content: South Korea's stock market has gone from the world's hottest to its coldest in just a few months. The Kospi, the world's best-performing major stock benchmark in the first half of 2026, has since fallen about 24%, making it the worst-performing major market in the second half. It's still more than 50% higher this year. The AI trade isn't losing its appeal. But investors are increasingly looking beyond South Korea's memory-chip giants to companies with broader exposure to the AI hardware boom. In July, analysts at GlobalData.TS Lombard pointed out that much of the earnings growth at Korean memory-chip makers came from higher memory-chip prices. By contrast, TSMC and Japanese chip-equipment makers relied more on advanced manufacturing and process expertise, giving them more durable growth prospects, they added. Taiwan's Taiex has climbed about 7% in the second half of the year, taking its year-to-date gains to about 70% as investors broaden their bets across the AI hardware supply chain. South Korea's rally was driven largely by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose soaring memory-chip profits made them among the biggest winners of the AI boom. Together, the companies account for more than half of the Kospi, leaving the market unusually dependent on a single segment of the semiconductor industry. Even blockbuster earnings are no longer enough to excite investors. Last Thursday, Samsung forecast a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, yet its shares have fallen for two straight trading sessions. The reversal followed months of extraordinary volatility. The Kospi plunged 22% in July, its worst month since the 2008 financial crisis, before rebounding 18% on the month's final trading day for its biggest one-day gain on record. The swings triggered multiple market-wide circuit breakers as leveraged bets on chip stocks amplified the moves. Young South Koreans flooded social media with memes and dark humor about their battered portfolios, while regulators tightened rules on leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds after concerns the products had fueled speculation. Turnover has dropped 70% from its late-May peak, while foreign investors have continued pulling money from Korean equities. The shift didn't happen overnight. Even before Korea's selloff, investors were debating whether the next phase of the AI boom would continue rewarding memory-chip makers or broaden to companies with exposure across the semiconductor supply chain. Taiwan appears to be benefiting from that shift. Its market offers exposure across AI infrastructure, from advanced chip manufacturing and packaging to servers and networking equipment. That includes TSMC as well as companies involved in advanced packaging, servers, networking equipment, and other AI infrastructure. The Taiex outperformed the Kospi by more than 23 percentage points in the third quarter, as Taiwan's benchmark gained nearly 4% while South Korea's plunged more than 19%. The quantum computing company is adding a zero-trust security business as it pitches protection against future quantum attacks. 	Niccolo de Masi, chairman and chief executive of IonQ. The Maryland-based quantum computing company announced the deal on Monday. IonQ wants its security arm to guard against attacks aided by AI and, one day, quantum machines. Founded in 2019, Elisity makes software that stops attackers and ransomware from moving through a company’s network. Hospitals and healthcare firms are among its main customers. IonQ says Elisity has more than 100 customers using its tools, including a growing number of Fortune 500 firms. It says sales and the customer base doubled in a year, and none of those customers left. Boss James Winebrenner will keep running the business. The deal should close by the end of the year, once regulators sign off. “We will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era,” IonQ chief executive Niccolo de Masi said. “Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets,” Winebrenner said. IonQ is the biggest listed firm that only does quantum. It is worth about $16bn. It bought chipmaker SkyWater for $1.8bn in January and UK startup Oxford Ionics for $1.1bn last year. Its security arm already sells tools built to resist quantum attacks. It has built quantum-safe national networks in Switzerland, Poland, Romania and Slovakia. Future quantum machines could crack the codes that protect data online today. Rivals are raising money on the stock market too. France’s Pasqal listed via a SPAC. IonQ is also among the firms in DARPA’s final test stage for useful quantum computers.                                        Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. Editor Editor  				Edited by Laura Michelle Davis  October 12, 2026, 3:23 pm ET Grand Theft Auto 6 is the most-anticipated game of 2026, and it’s already being blamed for gaming console shortages, especially the PlayStation 5 Pro. The high-end Sony console is currently out of stock on Sony.com and is selling on auction sites for $1,100 and over. Part of the reason for high console demand is that GTA 6 will be exclusive to PlayStation 5/Pro and Xbox Series X/S when it comes out on Nov. 19, and no other platforms have been announced yet. In September, Sony reportedly advised distributors that the PlayStation 5 Pro would be in short supply until 2027, citing “temporary market supply constraints and high demand.” The most severe bottleneck limiting PlayStation distribution is a global crisis in memory and storage components driven by the AI infrastructure squeeze, or RAMageddon.  More from CNET The PS 5 Pro promises better frame rates for a number of games as well as enhanced 4K processing, while the Rockstar Studios game is also designed to work on the “vanilla” PS5. Yet, GTA 6 isn’t the only recent high-profile PlayStation release: The PS5-exclusive Wolverine — by the makers of Spider-Man and Spider-Man 2 — has reportedly sold 2.16 million copies since September. The PlayStation 5 Pro debuted in November 2024 for $700, but its retail price has since increased to $900. Grand Theft Auto 6 is the long-awaited sequel to Grand Theft Auto 5, which first appeared in 2013. The crime-based game reportedly offers a playable area twice the size of the previous game’s. It’s available for preorder for $80. Representatives for Sony did not respond immediately to CNET’s request for more information.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Move aside priority boarding and extra legroom — airlines are investing in high-speed in-flight WiFi as a key amenity to attract customers. This year, Skytrax's World Airline Awards added a World's Best Onboard WiFi category "to reflect the importance to today's customer experience of fast and free onboard connectivity," Skytrax wrote in a press release. The ranking was determined by surveying passengers from over 100 nationalities between September 2025 and August 2026 in the world's largest airline passenger satisfaction survey. One WiFi provider popped up again and again in Skytrax's ranking of winning airlines: Starlink. Of the top 10 airlines recognized for having the best in-flight WiFi offerings, seven have partnerships with Elon Musk's high-speed internet company — an indication of how Starlink is cornering the market. Over 40 carriers worldwide have partnered with Starlink, which provides streaming-quality WiFi on flights via its network of over 11,000 satellites. Here are the top 10 airlines with the best onboard WiFi, ranked by passengers. Emirates was one of the first airlines to offer Starlink WiFi on its A380 aircraft, and plans to add Starlink to its fleet by mid-2027. EVA Air's onboard WiFi service is provided by Panasonic Avionics Corporation. As the first UK airline to partner with Starlink, Virgin Atlantic began offering flights equipped with streaming-quality WiFi in May. Singapore Airlines will begin rolling out Starlink WiFi on its Airbus A350 and Airbus A380 planes in 2027. Hawaiian Airlines became the first major US carrier to offer Starlink in February 2024 before merging with Alaska Airlines that September. Amazon Leo, which operates around 400 low-orbit satellites, will be available on JetBlue flights starting in 2027. Alaska Airlines announced its deal with Starlink in August 2025 after merging with Hawaiian Airlines, and is rolling out Starlink WiFi across its fleet. As of September, United offers Starlink on 560 aircraft, and plans to add it to its entire fleet. United has made efforts to lure Delta customers by touting its Starlink WiFi. Amazon Leo will be available on Delta Air Lines flights starting in 2028. Delta and Musk have been at odds over Delta's decision not to choose Starlink, with Musk criticizing the airline and its CEO, Ed Bastian, in posts on X. Bastian told CNBC on Friday that he pays little heed to the feud. "I'm a big fan of Starlink," Bastian said. "I'm a fan of what Elon does. I drive a Tesla. OK? So there's nothing. All this nonsense about being personal is not true at all." Qatar Airways won Skytrax's inaugural World's Best Onboard WiFi award. All of Qatar Airways' Boeing 777s and Airbus A350s feature Starlink. Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time? The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mindâ¦ it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations -  can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working? "I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation. The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators. Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years. The view that privatisation ultimately failed, leaving unreliable services and high fares, may be widespread. However, Prof Glaister argues that for a few years in the 1990s, the old privatised system actually worked well. Operating costs and subsidies were falling while the number of train services and passengers went up, he says. And in the current context, it's important to be clear about what nationalisation really means. The railways Labour inherited weren't, in truth, completely privatised, and nationalisation doesn't mean a return to British Rail. For example, the infrastructure manager Network Rail has been fully under public control for over two decades. A number of train companies including LNER and Northern had already been nationalised under the Conservatives. Scotrail, Transport for Wales and Caledonian Sleeper are controlled by devolved national governments. And even those operators still on contracts issued by the DfT at Westminster have been heavily controlled by the government for years. During Covid, private operators started being paid a fixed fee to run services, while the taxpayer took on the financial risk. The terms of the contracts meant train companies had to "ask government for permission to blow their nose", according to one senior industry executive, who asked not to be named so they could speak freely. Highly profitable rolling stock companies ("ROSCOS") still own the actual trains. Freight companies operate privately too, and there are a handful of fully commercial "open access operators" on the rails like Lumo, Hull Trains and Grand Central - although there are concerns within the industry that these could end up squeezed. So what is often referred to as the nationalisation of the railways, in fact amounts to gradually returning passenger train operators run by private companies to public hands as their contracts expire - and making this the default. This is not all that's happening, though. The government hopes that re-organising the railways under a new publicly run body, Great British Railways (GBR), will make a big difference. This will bring together the running of trains and tracks, ending the current fragmented system. A botched rail timetable introduction in 2018 was the spark for the then-Conservative government to eventually propose GBR as a new overarching body - although the Tories believe private competition should not be excluded from the system. Some trains are already covered in distinctive GBR branding, but the organisation still doesn't exist. A new law to create it is making its way through parliament. Unknowns remain, like exactly how GBR will interact with devolved governments, and who its senior leaders will be. GBR's livery has already been unveiled Transport expert and author Prof Jon Shaw, of the University of Plymouth, says the idea of a "single guiding mind" should create "a better planned railway that's more aligned to the customer". Prof Shaw thinks potential benefits include better long-term planning around rolling-stock and timetables, and the removal of "the compensation merry-go-round", where train companies and Network Rail argue about whose fault a delay was. Hynes says: "The way you get the railway to work is you get the infrastructure and the trains and the people working in harmony because it's a system. And we can do that in a publicly owned GBR railway in a way that we haven't been able to do for a generation." But Prof Shaw cautions of potential pitfalls. For example, "there remains very little money", and "a massive issue is whether or not the rail minister or DfT more generally - or the Treasury - will be able to butt out" and leave rail leaders to run the railway. Prof Glaister also fears politically sensitive aspects such as fares and levels of service could lead to politicians trying to run the railways themselves, because of the amount of public money involved. "Actually, governments are not very good at running railways," he says. "So you want management who are somewhat independent and able to run it." Lord Hendy insists that despite the Transport Secretary having ultimate sign-off on GBR's strategy, the body will be genuinely arms-length from government. "The point of this is to get a cadre of people who are committed to the outcomes that the secretary of state and I want for it, who can go off and run it on their own," he says, adding: "They'll have a lot more chance in the future than they've had in the last 20 years." The railways are currently subsidised to the tune of around Â£12bn a year - not including spending on major projects like HS2. The Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander says that she wants to see subsidy levels fall. Meanwhile, Network Rail has acknowledged a squeezed budget means difficult choices, and shoring up the network against the effects of more extreme weather requires investment. Prof Glaister says: "When the public is hoping for a better level of service, more reliability, fewer breakdowns and lower fares, what they're really asking for is more money to be put into the railway. "I don't think it's likely the government is going to be able to find more money, probably [it will have] less, actually. And so I think there's a real problem with ministers raising expectations from this policy." Commuters in Woking are hoping for improvements But Hynes doesn't see a contradiction between reducing taxpayer subsidy and making train services better. "My two north stars are performance up and subsidy down," he says. "If the service is better, we get more customers, we get more revenue." Lord Hendy and Hynes also push back on the idea that the answer to improving reliability might be running fewer trains. Hynes says: "In an industry with high fixed costs, the best way of getting the subsidy down is to go for growth." Questions also remain about how GBR will manage industrial relations. Terms and conditions currently vary across operators. What will cost-conscious ministers do if unions seek to standardise these at the most generous level across the network? While ministers argue they are getting on with improvements that people will notice, there's acknowledgement that the speed of improvement will vary between operators. Lord Hendy says some changes "ought to be dead boringâ¦ to make sure tomorrow is a little better than today if you can do it". But he says "more than 30 years worth of behaviors" will need altering to make the railway run solely in the interests of the customer. At Woking, is there optimism that things will improve in the long run? "I really hope so," says Leo, "it would be amazing - as it's not the best service now." The Lagos payments and lending app could list in November, with Standard Bank investing up to $200mn. Pay, a Nigerian payments and lending app, has filed to list on the New York Stock Exchange, Yinka Adegoke reported for Semafor. Earlier reports put its likely valuation at about $4bn. The company filed on 9 October, bne IntelliNews reported. It will trade under the ticker OPAY, and investors expect it to price in mid-November, Semafor said. OPay has not set a price range. OPay’s revenue rose 137% to $467mn in the first half of 2026, its filing shows. Net income more than quadrupled to $91mn. Lending is now its biggest source of income, ahead of payments. Nearly nine-tenths of revenue comes from Nigeria. OPay launched in 2018 and is controlled by Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui. It once chased super-app plans, with motorbike taxis and food delivery, before narrowing to financial services. It raised $570mn from investors led by SoftBank between 2018 and 2021. Standard Bank’s Africa arm has agreed to invest up to $200mn, capped at a 4.99% stake after the listing. Its Africa head, Lungisa Fuzile, is expected to join OPay’s board. OPay also plans a second listing in Lagos. Its filing warns that shares there may not be swappable for those traded in New York. It would be the first fintech with mostly Nigerian customers to list in the US. Earlier African listings in New York, such as Jumia, have had mixed results. Meta's autonomous agent app is losing downloads and daily-user growth, and a short seller is pressing the point; the insider selling, though scheduled months in advance, has run one way. The stock closed near $719, about 8% under Zuckerberg's sale price and far below the Street's highest target, $1,000 at Wells Fargo. Meta▲+3.16% — Meta, up 3.16 percent today launched Muse, its autonomous AI agent app, on September 8, built to carry out tasks rather than just answer questions 1. It drew five million downloads in 22 days↗, an opening only 23 apps have ever beaten, and topped the US free-app charts 23. By the estimate of Hunterbrook, a short-selling research firm, the run added about $200 billion of market value 3. Downloads have slowed since. They averaged about 165,000 a day in the seven days to October 7, down 8.1% from roughly 180,000 the week before 14. The October 6 reading, about 170,000, sat 21.1% below the September 24 peak of about 215,000 3. User growth cooled faster than downloads: net new daily users fell from about 198,000 a day in the week of September 15 to 87,000 the next week and 74,000 in the week to October 6, a 62.4% drop, while weekly reviews fell 11.6% to 4,716 13. Daily actives set a record, 2.73 million on October 6, but trailed Threads at the same age, and Threads had launched globally and lost users faster after its debut 3. Sensor Tower, a second tracker, counts lower levels: 1.8 million daily users on 6.6 million downloads 5. Muse's net new daily users fell 62% in three weeks Hunterbrook disclosed the Meta short on October 9↗ alongside the data, betting enthusiasm had run ahead of usage 4. Weeks earlier its investigative arm, then holding no Meta position, reported the agent could be prompted to compile lists of Facebook and Instagram accounts tied to undocumented immigrants, transgender teachers and women who ordered abortion pills 3. Useful agents need deep access to accounts and personal data, which is where the risk sits 1. Amazon▼−1.08% — Amazon, down 1.08 percent today said in September it had blocked Muse from shopping for customers, and TickerTrends, the app-data firm whose metrics underpin the short, tracks user reports of restrictions at Costco and Netflix▲+0.65% — Netflix, up 0.65 percent today as well 3. Zuckerberg has called Muse "the centerpiece of our vision for what we're building" 3. An agent shut out of Amazon has a narrower pitch than the one Meta advertised. Unusual Whales, an insider-trading tracker, counted 172 insider transactions at Meta over six months, none a purchase 6. Zuckerberg sold $21.4 million of stock on September 24 with shares near $778; Javier Olivan, Meta's chief operating officer, sold about $24 million; chief financial officer Susan Li also sold 6. EDGAR logs 40 of the filings, the insider trade disclosures↗, between June 17 and October 7 7. The filings cut both ways: the sales ran under Rule 10b5-1 plans set months in advance, some entries were tax withholding, and one filing states it "does not represent a sale" 6. A preset plan explains the selling; nothing in the filings explains why no insider has bought. The stock closed Friday near $719, about 8% under Zuckerberg's sale price 6. Wells Fargo raised its Meta target to $1,000 from $796↗ on October 6, tied for the highest on the Street, and 56 of 63 analysts rate the stock a buy or strong buy 8. Analyst Ken Gawrelski expects earnings per share to bottom in 2027, a spending cycle he compares to Reels in 2022 though "potentially much larger," with little Muse revenue before then 8. The June-quarter accounts↗ show the bill: total costs up 55% to $42.03 billion, operating margin down to 31% from 43%, free cash flow at $784 million after lease payments and $1.7 billion before them, as the chart shows 910. Downloads measure curiosity and daily actives measure habit 1. Both are slowing, and the habit measure, net daily additions, is slowing far faster; Q3 will show whether that is a launch lull or the product's shape 34. Range anxiety? That's so 2026. The auto industry is slowly flipping its calendars into the 2027 model year, and the transition is bringing a new crop of EVs with 400-plus miles of range. That was once a rare bragging point reserved for ultra-luxury sedans and gargantuan electric trucks. It's an important development, especially for the US market. While the rest of the world has started to embrace fully electric driving amid sky-high fuel costs, American drivers have lagged China and Europe in adopting EVs, held back by range anxiety, high vehicle prices, and limited public charging access. Automakers' response: Make EVs go farther in the US market. European manufacturers are leading that charge. BMW's next-generation EVs, called Neue Klasse, are the clearest example. The coming i3 sedan is expected to travel up to 468 miles on a charge, while BMW says its new iX4 SUV coupe can go as far as 428 miles. Those are preliminary estimates based on EPA testing procedures. Its iX3 crossover SUV, meanwhile, has an official EPA rating of up to 434 miles. Strikingly vibrant.                                       Introducing THE NEW BMW iX4.                                      #BMWiX4 #BMW #BMWNewEra #NeueKlasse #BMWGroup https://t.co/4kqvYE1E9s Fellow German luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz is also joining the race. The coming electric C-Class has a range of up to 474 miles, under Europe's more generous range testing system. Swedish automaker Volvo is also releasing the EX60 next year, including a trim with 400 miles of range. The cars are largely priced in the mid-$60,000 range. America has seen some 400-mile electric vehicles before, but so far, they've remained in a small corner of the consumer market. The Lucid Air, priced between $70,000 and $250,500, boasts a 400-plus-mile range for consumers willing to make mortgage-like payments on a vehicle. GM's electric trucks and Cadillac Escalade IQ can also clear 400 miles, but their longest-range versions rely on enormous 205-kilowatt-hour battery packs. The fresh EVs coming from luxury European carmakers feature smaller, more energy-dense battery cells that use their power more efficiently. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… New York’s Gaming Commission unanimously advanced proposals to restrict how licensed mobile sportsbooks use AI to personalize promotions and wagering advice, alongside new requirements to identify and contact patrons who may be at risk of problem gambling. The revised measures remain proposals, not rules in effect. The commission’s action puts both marketing systems and operator responses to risky betting behavior into the next stage of state review. The AI measure would restrict sportsbooks, their affiliates and vendors from using artificial intelligence, algorithmic profiling, machine learning, generative systems or other automated decision tools to analyze customer data and tailor promotions, bonuses, odds, betting limits, messages or product recommendations. It would also bar operators from suggesting particular wagers, types of bets or betting amounts. The proposal would prohibit promotions intended to increase customers’ spending, revenue or engagement. It would not apply to parimutuel horse racing; the commission’s account also describes a customer-consent exception, but does not specify its scope. A separate proposal would require licensees to identify customers who may be at risk of problem-gambling behavior and assign a person to engage them about those behaviors and related issues. New York has nine licensed mobile operators: Bally Bet, BetMGM, Caesars Sportsbook, DraftKings, Fanatics, FanDuel, Resorts World Bet, Rush Street Interactive and theScore Bet. The state taxes mobile sports-betting gross gaming revenue at 51%. Commission Chairman Brian O’Dwyer raised the risk that a customer restricted by one sportsbook could simply move to another licensed operator. He urged companies to work together and share data so that customers could not avoid intervention by switching platforms. “The industry is on notice by me and this Commission that they need to solve this problem,” O’Dwyer said. “It’s a problem that this Commission will require to be addressed and if the industry does not address it, then we will address it, and they may not like it or the solution we come up with.” The measures were included in Gov. Kathy Hochul’s 2026 State of the State program, announced in March, which addressed underage gambling, marketing to at-risk customers and gambling addiction. New York’s AI proposal draws on a similar New Jersey regulation, according to CDC Gaming, but does not amount to an outright ban on the technology. The New York action is part of a wider debate over how sportsbooks use customer data in marketing and how regulators should respond to gambling-related risks. ProPublica reported that the commission’s proposed rules would adopt specific thresholds for identifying at-risk bettors, followed by a required check-in; the details could change as the proposals proceed. Sports Betting Alliance President Joe Maloney said the group would continue working with regulators to ensure the proposals strengthen New York’s regulated market. He also described licensed operators as accountable to state regulators for consumer protection, responsibility and integrity. “Since 2022, New Yorkers aged 21 plus have been able to place legal wagers in a trusted, regulated market with licensed operators held to account by regulators that ensure commitments to consumer protection, responsibility, and integrity,” Maloney said in a statement. Maloney also said the legal framework had ended the illegal market’s monopoly and that regulated operators now generate more than $1 billion annually in tax revenue. Those figures are the alliance president’s characterization of the market, not a commission finding cited in the reporting. The revised AI rules will receive additional public comment before returning to the commission for discussion and a possible vote. Regulators have not set a date for a final vote, leaving room for further changes before any requirements take effect. Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details. Last Friday, Nikkei Asia reported that, according to “multiple people familiar with the matter,” Apple had told select suppliers to cut component production for the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” The report sent Apple shares down roughly 2.5% in early trading, although the stock has recovered much of that loss and closed at $340.97 today. That said, JP Morgan released a new investor note today (via AppleInsider), arguing that the reported cuts are consistent with Apple’s usual production patterns and don’t necessarily point to an unexpected drop in demand. The report also comments on Apple’s staggered iPhone launch schedule, with JP Morgan expecting the iPhone Duo to offset the sales shortfall caused by the absence of the regular iPhone 18, which is expected to hit shelves early next year. Interestingly, earlier today, a separate report from China’s Securities Times claimed that Apple had increased its iPhone Duo orders by 30%, potentially bringing its production for the remainder of 2026 close to 10 million units. Looking ahead to the December quarter, JP Morgan expects Apple to sell 8.5 million iPhone Duo units. JP Morgan also projects a roughly 2% decline in iPhone revenue year-over-year, but a 2% increase in Apple’s overall revenue. The firm also continues to flag supply constraints and broader economic pressures that could affect consumer demand. All in all, JP Morgan raised its AAPL price target from $340 to $360, while maintaining its Overweight rating on the stock. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. According to Counterpoint Research, Apple saw its share of global smartphone shipments cross 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite an industry-wide decline. Here are the details. In a report released today, Counterpoint Research says memory constraints and rising prices have pushed global smartphone shipments to their lowest third-quarter level in 14 years, with a 20% year-over-year decline. That helped it narrow the gap with Samsung, which remained in first place with a 23% share. The top five also included Xiaomi (10%), OPPO (9%), and vivo (8%), all of which saw their shipment shares decline compared to Q3 2025. Here’s Counterpoint Research on Apple’s performance for the period: Apple’s market share crossed 20% for the first time in any Q3, reaching 22%, despite a YoY decline in shipments. Iâm a DevOps architect, musician and all-round geek.  When Iâm not writing code or fiddling with computers for a living, I produce my own music and provide the low-end rumble for my band in West Sussex. A look at the tools, techniques and challenges of creating a retro-style 'crack intro'  Updated: October 12, 2026 Download Now View on pouet.net In the late 80s, I spent an embarrassing number of hours hunched over my ZX Spectrum, typing in Sinclair BASIC programs and rudimentary assembler routines copied from magazines, trying to re-create the Amiga crack intros Iâd seen round at a friendâs house. Obviously, they never came even slightly close - but now, many decades later, Iâve finally managed it! Iâm now the proud author of a hand-rolled retro demoscene intro that runs on a stock 128Kb Spectrum. It features all those late 80s tropes: A smooth scrolltext (with âleet custom fonts!), a three-channel AY soundtrack, bouncing VU meters and the essential parallax starfield. Itâs currently 10287 bytes of code, or 19552 bytes as a complete tape image - which, given Iâve been working on this since December 13th last year, means my average rate of code-production is a paltry ~ 455 bytes per week! This blog post is a technical overview of how I got there, some cool tricks I picked up, and everything I had to learn (and re-learn) about the Speccy and Z80 assembly along the way. It simultaneously rates as one of my favourite side-projects ever, and also the one that most often nearly triggered a foot put through my monitor in frustration. Iâll reflect on all that at the end, but for now if you just want to see the finished product, the download button is at the top of the article and the included .tap cassette tape image should load into any emulator. Thereâs also a YouTube capture, links to the production on pouet.net, and you can run it from within a web browser by visiting my TNFS site portal - check option 4 for recent uploads. But letâs skip back briefly to the late 80s. Coming from the world of an 8-bit, cassette tape loading computer, seeing an Amiga for the first time was like encountering something from outer space. Like everyone who saw one back in the day, I was blown away by the amazing graphics and sound on display, not to mention the library of ground-breaking games. But I found myself even more captivated by the mysterious (and totally badass) âintrosâ displayed at the beginning of pirated games. Created by the software piracy groups that had cracked the copy protection and distributed the floppy-disk based games, they were mini works of art in their own right - music, graphics and usually some cool-looking effect to show off the groupâs prowess. Thereâs a great collection of these intros (or âcracktrosâ) archived on YouTube. Watch a few of those videos and youâll quickly notice the âdesignâ tropes that almost every cracktro shares: a cool, edgy logo at the top of the screen (bonus points if itâs dripping blood or in any way âmetalâ), some boastful text displayed on top of an effect of some sort - usually a scrolling parallax starfield, or rotating 3d object - and a further scroll-text full of shout outs, greetings to fellow pseudonymous crackers and adverts for illegal BBS systems galore. Needless to say, to a kid in the 80s/early 90s this was possibly the coolest thing ever. I thought this one was the absolute bomb when I first saw it. Sine-scroller, pirate BBS adverts, cool logo with a sword - and of course, a starfield. Thereâs something for everyone here. The music from this is burned into my brain. I think pretty much everyone of my classmates knew this intro given the popularity of Lemmings in the early 90s. Skid Row as a group are still active to this day and this is probably the quintessential Amiga cracktro of the period. Endless Piracy. Edgy. Another cool logo, sine-wave scroller, starfield and boasting text. The classics never go out of style. Another great combination of all the essential ingredients. Cool logo, even cooler text font, scrolling starfield and a scroll-text running along the bottom. Vintage stuff. Logo. Text. Scroller. But no starfield - otherwise a solid effort from Anthrox here :) The demoscene grew out of these intros. The cracking eventually faded into the background, and coders, âgraphiciansâ and musicians all contributed to feature-length productions that showcased their abilities, competed with other groups and pushed the machine to its limits. In amazing feats of ingenuity and pure âcode as an art formâ, the scene lives on today, with groups producing breathtaking productions like this and this - bear in mind, both of those are running on a 7Mhz home computer equipped with a floppy disk, 1Mb of memory and a sound chip from 1985. But much as I admire the sheer skill and dedication that takes, itâs the early âsingle screenâ scrolly-text-and-starfield cracktros Iâve always found captivating. They took on a sort of mystical quality for me, hinting at a scene and a culture I could only ever experience from the outside - which is exactly why I spent all those hours in Sinclair BASIC, trying in vain to re-create them, and dreaming of the day Iâd eventually have an Amiga of my own. I eventually did trade up to a range of Amiga systems, joined a few âsceneâ groups myself and threw myself into a variety of activities until exams and the end of my teenage years beckoned. I dabbled with Z80 code back then, and at one point knew enough 68k assembly to bluff my way through - partly from the Amigaâs heyday, partly from a few âembedded systemsâ modules at University where I had to program a set of traffic lights or lift-controllers. Given thereâs not much call for that sort of thing at my $DAYJOB, though, it had all pretty much faded from my memory. I have kept working on a bunch of projects in my spare time, and one of my favourites is my TNFS site - sort of an old-school BBS system or interactive âwebsiteâ for the Spectrum, which grew out of a fun experiment to see how far I could push Sinclair BASIC. It relies on a modern network card fitted to the Spectrum, which is how I came to be chatting to âDesertkunâ, another TNFS-protocol enthusiast. Heâs now producing a great new WiFi network card for the Speccy, and was kind enough to send me a few of the prototypes to test out for him. I was massively inspired by his hardware and low-level coding chops, and during one of our video calls where weâd been comparing our development setups, he asked why I didnât write any Z80 assembly myself. A throw-away comment, but the challenge was set! Now, I couldnât face re-writing the whole site in asm, but I figured I could produce a self-contained intro to promote it in the style of the early âBBStrosâ, and finally be one of the cool kids with a scene production of my own :) I mean, how hard could it be ? (ooooh - foreshadowing!) My development environment through this was pretty straightforward, and is the same stack I use for developing my TNFS site. I just used a Makefile-driven build system which ran my code through the Pasmo assembler, my fork of zmakebas to build BASIC files, and the FUSE emulator for testing. For final testing on the real hardware, I uploaded my .tap files to my local TNFS server where I could run them on my +3. A few additional tools I have to call out because they ended up making a big difference - one is the amazing web-based âasm-editorâ I discovered while looking up Z80 instructions. Not only does this site have a great reference of all the Z80 instructions, but it also has an editor where you can run example code and see how the memory and/or various registers change state. Take for example, the djnz instruction - you can build it and step through the example loop construct one instruction at a time. Or try my example of an add instruction in the screenshot to see how the carry flag works when a bit gets shifted out of a register. Although it uses a slightly different syntax to Pasmo (so I couldnât drop my code directly in it), it massively helped when manually stepping through things. And lastly, probably the most significant debugging tools I used on this project - a notepad and pen, and my two dogs (say âHi!â to Biscuit & Pebbleâ¦) Iâll write some more about this in the wrap-up, but this really was a highly unusual project for me, coming from decades of much higher-level languages and constructs. Most of my z80 code I only ever really understood after drawing out the bytes and bitmasks, keeping a table of register flags and drawing chunks of screen memory out by hand. And I found my evening walks with the two dogs provided ideal rubber duck exercises, although Iâm not sure what they both made of my protracted mutterings about the hl register pair. Either way, debugging-by-dog is highly recommended! So, letâs get started. I followed a great âHello, world!â example from futurice.com to validate my build environment. Beyond that, the first thing I wanted to do was load in my logo and background image Iâd use as a âstageâ for the remainder of the planned intro. I wasnât really sure what I was going to do at this point, just that I wanted my logo at the top, and a scrolltext along the bottom row of the screen. As my TNFS site header already looked kinda demoscene-y, I made a quick edit putting in place two blue guide-bars inside which Iâd put further content. Memory map courtesy of breakintoprogram.co.uk A Spectrum SCREEN$ file (usually displayed as loading screens) is just a dump of screen memory, starting from byte 16384, and running for 6912 bytes. The weird layout of this is very relevant later, but in order to display it all you need to do is load your file into that memory location. After a few hourâs work of reviewing Speccy internals and following various guides, I had a very simple starting point for my demo that served as the basis for everything else that came after. Not much to look at now, but this simple starting point introduced me to important concepts like interfacing with the Spectrumâs hardware (ULA chip to start with, and AY sound chip later) via the out instruction, how to pull in binary files using Pasmoâs INCBIN directive, using the Z80âs block copy ldir instruction, the use of register pairs for 16-bit addressing, and simple branching to labels. The next step was to print something on the screen and explore some of the Speccyâs built-in ROM routines, which are somewhat analagous to syscalls on modern operating systems. There are plenty of disassemblies and guides to the Spectrum ROM available on the internet, one of the best commented and linked one is at https://skoolkid.github.io/rom/. Using this as a reference alongside the various âHello, world!â tutorials showed me how this sort of thing is built up: I ended up mostly not using the ROM routines in my code as they dragged in all sorts of things I didnât need, but it was massively useful to understand how they worked as they introduced me to yet more commonly-used constructs. For example, the PR_STRING routine defined here shows how you can build a loop over each character. If youâre just starting out, I highly recommend going over the 8 lines in that routine with a notepad and pen, working out the contents of the registers and following the loop constructs. I also made a version of it in asm-editor you can try. If you click that link, youâll see a version of the code loaded into the web editor. Click âBuildâ, and then step through the code using the âStepâ button - although no text will be actually displayed (I skipped over the call to the Spectrum ROM ârestartâ vector that does this), youâll see the various states of the registers and for example the BC register counting down as each byte of the string is processed. Problem is, the Speccyâs built-in font is not exactly dripping with demoscene credibility. I wanted to use some stylish fonts and this turned out to be super easy - a quick search turned up Jim Blimeyâs awesome font collection, which included a ready-to-use set of assembler files and some instructions which soon led me to these additions in my code: There we go! Now thatâs looking a little more elite. Sorry, I mean 31337. Strap in folks, weâre leaving lamer cityâ¦ So at this point, a month or so in to my dabblings and Iâd started to get a reasonable understanding of common idioms and was starting to feel like this was a project that might actually go somewhere. The problem started when I moved on to trying to implement actual demo effects: It became very apparent, very quickly, just how much I didnât know about how this all worked. Not to mention the fact that at this level, youâre really closely exposed to the physical hardware intricacies, including the design decisions and trade-offs that the hardware designers had to make when working with the extremely limited specs of the early 1980s. The first such problem - and the cause of probably 90% of my pain - is the Speccyâs extremely weird screen layout. Rather than standard bitmapped display you might expect on more modern hardware, it is instead split into 3 sections, each with a set of interleaved rows (so if you keep adding 1 to a screen address, eventually instead of reaching the next row, youâll instead end up 8 rows down, and so on until you hit the bottom of the section and then loop back to the row underneath where you started!) followed by a block of âattributeâ bytes which determine the colours of each 8x8 block. The attribute blocks are the reason why each 8x8 character cell can only have two colours (a PAPER and INK attribute) which led to the garish âcolour-clashâ of spectrum games and distinctive style where artists try to keep inside 8x8 blocks as much as possible. But it was the layout of the bitmap portion that is such a mind twister. You can see this illustrated whenever a game reads in a loading screen from tape. You can see each section built up with the interleaved rows one at a time, and then finally the colour and other attributes (like flashing ). Thereâs a lot of detail at the fantastic Break Into Program site. In the defense of the designers, they were working with extremely limited hardware and I donât think the Speccy was ever imagined as a games machine. When you start shuffling bytes around, you realise that this approach is really optimised for displaying text which is neatly arranged into 8x8 character boundaries. For example, using this âscrambledâ bit order, if you have a screen address in the hl register pair, you can quickly get to the next pixel line of a given address by simply incrementing the âhighâ byte. Thereâs a bunch of other âcheap movesâ you can make by simply shifting bits around: It was a reasonable choice for a machine that would probably spend a lot of itâs time displaying BASIC program listings - itâs only when you start trying to write demo or sprite routines that it starts to feel really weird. This also means youâll pretty quickly need a routine to convert X,Y addresses to the relevant memory addresses. Again, L Break Into Program has a useful routine and if you disassemble more or less any spectrum game or demo, youâll find a version of this procedure somewhere. And yes, this all became horribly relevant later onâ¦ Admittedly, not the most interesting demonstration - but this was the first time I had made something move on the Spectrumâs screen with assembly! I watched this with pride more times than I care to admit :) I had a snazzy logo and âHello Worldâ text, but that doesnât make for a very interesting intro! The first effect I wanted was the scrolltext - without that, itâs not really an intro. Now, the Amiga had all kinds of hardware sprites, blitter operations, custom chips but the Spectrum had none of that. I was going to have to work out how to do things the hard way - âbanging on the metalâ, literally by shifting bits around the screen memory by hand and having the CPU do all the work. This is where understanding the Speccyâs weird screen and character cell layout is so important. It turns out thereâs a neat trick as long as I stay inside one character row - thereâs a RL instruction, which takes a byte and ârotatesâ it left. It inserts whatever is in the carry flag into the rightmost bit, and whatever gets shifted out ends up in the carry bit again. That means if you string a bunch of them together, you can move a set of pixels across the screen - the moment they âfall offâ one character cell, they end up in the carry flag and then the next rl instruction inserts them at the beginning of the next character cell to the left. Repeat 32 times, and youâve just moved a pixel (or set of pixels) across a line of the screen: Hell yeah. Itâs almost a proper scrolltext now! Wrapping this in another loop that increments h each time (remember - that gets us moving down a scanline) gets us moving an entire character cell. Here you can see it moving an entire row of my âHello worldâ message. There was however a lot more work needed to make a proper scrolltext, with each letter appearing smoothly. I started off by just printing an entire character at a time on the right-hand edge of the screen - it worked, but was pretty ugly as you saw each new character appear at once in the right-hand side of the screen, scrolling 8 pixels over and then the next character flashed up. Instead, I wanted to make each character appear pixel by pixel and that required a bit more bit juggling. The routine I ended up with effectively streams each character in, line by line, pixel by pixel using the font data directly instead of calling the ROM print character routine. It does this by looking up the ASCII code for a character, and then fetching the corresponding font representation into a 8-byte buffer, one byte for each line of data. The font data starts with the space character (character code 32), so a lookup is simply font code base address + (ascii code - 32) * 8 to get to the bits for that letter. Arranged into an 8x8 grid, the bits for the letter H in the font data look like this. For each row of bits, I shift the line left using a neat trick. The byte is loaded into the a register, and then by adding itself to itself - add a,a we shift the value left (in binary, multiplying by 2 moves everything over one bit) so that the pixel I want to draw ends up dropping into the carry flag. This is an idiomatic way of doing it in Z80 code as itâs faster and smaller than the sla instruction. And every cycle quickly adds up when youâre re-drawing 256 bytes every frame! The character buffer then looks like this, with the top line shifted. Now, with the hl register pair pointing at the correct location on the screen, I can then use the rl trick discussed above. This shifts a scanline from the bottom character row of the screen left by one pixel and draws my pixel in the rightmost position by moving it in from the carry flag. Looping 32 times over this moves the entire row by 1 pixel with my new pixel inserted at the right. I then repeat this step again using inc h to move down one scan line until the entire character column has been drawn. At this point, the character buffer looks like this, and all 8 lines of the bottom screen row have all been shifted left by one bit by looping over all 32 character columns. The whole thing then repeats another 7 times until the entire character has been smoothly scrolled onto the screen. So just to re-state this because I think itâs worth the emphasis - just to scroll a message across the bottom of the screen, weâre having to loop over and re-draw 256 pixels every frame! It shows how much faster assembly is than the BASIC interpreter built into the spectrumâs ROM. I found it amazing to see my code finally working and imagining all the bits flying around and registers flapping away. It really makes me appreciate just how much effort went into creating the games I played back then. The original Amiga module I converted. A proper 1980s ear-worm! Of course, any good intro needs some music. On the Amiga, the standard was the âtrackerâ module format, which has a long and involved history of different forks, versions and tweaks. A song is built up from a series of patterns, each made up of rows of instructions. Each instruction usually includes note or pitch information, which sample to play and various parameters such as volume, effects - or in the case of some instructions, which position in the song to jump to. In many ways, itâs almost like a programming language for music. Using ProTracker as an example, a typical note cell is 4 bytes, shown on-screen as something like C-2 01 C20. That breaks down into three fields: the note and octave (C-2), the sample number (01), and the effect and its parameter (C20 - in this case, âset the volume to $20â, which is half of the maximum $40). A close-up of Protracker playing a tune. Note the VUmeters - another classic demo effect I would pinch later on! For an impressive demonstration of whatâs possible with a tracker and to see what the note data looks like on-screen, check out the work of h0ffman, and in particular his winning âProfessional Trackerâ entry from the Revision 2014 competition. Heâs an undisputed master of the science (or art!) of tracking, and his âSecrets of Protrackerâ talk gives a great overview of whatâs possible. The Amigaâs sound hardware far eclipsed anything else on the market at the time, and the ZX Spectrum is paltry by comparison. The original 48K models only offered a rudimentary âbeeperâ, but the later 128K models included a 3-channel AY-3-8912 sound chip. This was very popular in 8-bit micros of the time, and a more-or-less identical variant was also used in the Atari ST. While it only offers basic waveforms and sound processing, it does enable multi-channel âchip musicâ, and so it became the mainstay of the ZX Spectrum demoscene. It also spawned a variety of SoundTracker clones on the Spectrum itself, although most musicians these days prefer to work in modern tools like Vortex Tracker II, which runs natively under Windows. Pex looking back on his demos - this starts at the point where he features my letter and plays a bit of my cover version! For my intro, I wanted to port an Amiga module - and I had the perfect one in mind. One of my favourite Amiga music disks was âSounds Of Gnomeâ, released in 1989 by the Swedish duo âMahoney & Kaktusâ. Mahoney also wrote NoiseTracker, one of the first really widely used trackers on the Amiga, and the program that served as my teenage introduction to making computer music of my own. Back in 2018 I made a rock cover of one of the other tunes on that disk, and wrote to Mahoney (real name âPexâ) about it. He ended up showing my âmusic videoâ at a demo conference, which I am eternally grateful for! So it seemed only fitting that I mangle another song from that collection with a Spectrum conversionâ¦ Sorry, guys! I picked the track âMilkmanâ which was written by âGlue Masterâ, an associate of Mahoneyâs who had a few of his tracks featured on the compilation. Itâs an ideal track for converting: Itâs short (only 7 patterns in total), most of those patterns share the same chord sequence, and it looked fairly easy to squeeze the original 4 channels down into the Spectrumâs 3. Plus, itâs an incredibly catchy tune and I knew it well - Iâve been listening to it for 35+ years and often jam along to it on guitar or bass. The conversion started off pretty easily: all I really had to do was copy the patterns note-for-note from the Amiga mod, which I had open in OpenMPT as my Windows tracker. Below is a session with both trackers open on the same pattern - the original Amiga mod on the left, and my 3-channel Spectrum conversion on the right. Note the 11.7 in the 3rd channel of the Spectrum version. This is a âpitch slide downâ effect in Vortex Tracker syntax, which drops the pitch by about a quarter-tone. Itâs repeated on the next line, so the overall effect is a slide down from the A# that leads in to the next bass note. The original Amiga mod does the same thing using its own syntax - those are the 202s you can see on the same notes, at the bottom of the 4th track. Using just a single âbeepâ sound for everything was enough to check everything was working, and after a few weeks of hacking on it and re-arranging things in the evenings, I had a basic version which sounded surprisingly good for a first draft: I have to give a special mention to this forum post which was a massive help getting me started. Itâs probably the best introduction to Vortex Tracker Iâve found - many, many thanks to the original author for taking the time to write it all up! The real challenge was making it sound as close to the original as possible. That meant building up a library of better-sounding samples for the different parts, and making extensive use of Vortex Trackerâs âornamentsâ. Vortex Tracker comes with a great selection of sounds, and fortunately Iâm also a weirdo who likes to listen to chiptunes in the background while I work! So whenever I found something particularly enticing, I filed it away for later pilfering inspiration. A Vortex Tracker sample isnât really a âsampleâ in the Amiga sense of a recorded sound - itâs a definition of how a note sounds, one line per frame. Each line can mix in a tone or the white noise generator (useful for snare effects and suchlike), along with various other parameters. Ornaments, on the other hand, give you extra control over what pitch a note plays - and this enables really useful tricks like âarpeggio chordsâ. For example, an ornament of 0,4 makes the channel switch rapidly (25 times a second) between the note being played and the one 4 semitones above it. It happens so quickly that it sounds much like two notes played at the same time, which means you can build up full-sounding triad chords using only two channels. Take the opening chord in my fully converted version, Cm: It plays C in the first channel and the minor 3rd (D#) in the second, then I apply an ornament to the second channel to bring it up 4 semitones to the 5th (G). That gives all three notes of the chord, while keeping the 3rd channel free for other parts. As well as making much more efficient use of the limited 3 channels, this also gives Spectrum music that characteristic âwarblingâ sound, which I find really appealing in a retro kind of way! Between tricks like this and samples that mix tones with white noise (to make a combined âbass-snareâ sound, for example), I managed to condense the full track down to 3 channels. Many months later, I have to say Iâm really pleased with the final result. The original site that was home to Vortex Tracker, documentation and other resources appears to be offline at the moment. I managed to grab a copy of everything I needed from archive.org - youâll want the PTxTools.7z file for the playback routines discussed here. The playback was simple in theory: As this overview notes, you basically just pull in the player routine, include your module file and call the playback routine once per frame in your main loop. The catch is, none of the source code versions supplied in the archive worked with my Pasmo assembler. Fortunately, there is a pre-compiled binary object shipped alongside the source (VTII10bG in the PTxTools/PT3Play directory). This just has to be loaded in at address $C000 - this cannot be changed, as it has lots of absolute addresses baked in. My code to handle module playback now looks something like this, with the binary module loaded in place: Well, that didnât work as hoped. TNFStro - tortoise edition. This brings me to the main event. No self-respecting cracktro is complete without a starfield! My first, naive approach to the classic starfield effect was to scatter random stars across the screen, then move down each scan-line applying the same rl trick Iâd used for the scroll-text. I figured I could get parallax by shifting each row a different amount: One pixel for the first row, two for the second, three for the third, then back to one again, all the way down the screen to give the impression of several âfieldsâ of stars moving at different speeds. It turned out there were two major problems with that approach. Firstly, shifting an entire row smeared whatever else was on it along with the stars - which Iâd expected, and had filed away as a problem for future me. The bigger issue was speed: by the time Iâd finished the first three rows Iâd already performed hundreds of shift operations, and it was nowhere near fast enough to fit inside a single frame. Everything crawled across the screen, and the music playback slowed down so much that you could actually hear the arpeggio ornaments warbling away as separate notes. Clearly I was going to have to keep track of the individual stars instead. I found this routine, which was more-or-less what I had in mind and started me off with the idea of a structure to hold the state of each star. It also uses a screen address lookup much like the one from âBreak Into Programâ. Dammit. Back with another funeral dirge rendition :( That got things moving, but the co-ordinate lookup and tracking proved expensive to do (it has to run for every star, every frame as well as keep track of the old position for erasing) and Iâd been ignoring the bigger question how to display stuff on top of the starfield. My original idea was simply to draw the stars and then paint text over them each frame, which blew the frame budget just as comprehensively as my first attempt. If I wanted something more interesting than an empty starfield, Iâd have to keep track of which cells were occupied by text and avoid drawing stars in them in the first place, rather than over-painting them every time. After lots of scribbling in my notepad and visualising rows of bits, I eventually solved both challenges by âcheatingâ fairly liberally. So now, I donât generate a random starfield at all. Instead, I built a table of pre-calculated Y and X position pairs: This saves faffing about with an RNG, and once I have a layout that looks good I know itâll always look good. I can also âfudgeâ things and ensure no two stars share the same y co-ordinate which sidesteps a whole class of problems like stars sharing a scanline, and having to deal with them overtaking each other. The ârandomâ layout is generated by a simple Ruby script: When the routine initialises, I convert those co-ordinate pairs into a table that tracks the state of each star. So rather than storing a position and translating it to a screen address every frame, each of my star records now looks like this (offsets from the base address): The key thing is that there are no X/Y co-ordinates at all. For each star I store the screen byte it sits in and the bit mask within that byte, so itâs already in the form the screen writes need. That means no address conversion per frame, just simple bit shifting and rotation. Moving a star is then dead simple. I rotate its mask left with rlca, and when the bit rotates out of bit 7, it lands back in bit 0 with the carry flag set. Thatâs the signal I need to move the star one character cell to the left, which is one of the âcheap movesâ from earlier. Because Iâm tracking which cell each star is in, the collision check comes almost for free. Thatâs what the second pointer is for: STOCC (Star Occupancy) moves in step with STSCR through a table holding one byte per character cell. The âtypewriterâ routine sets a byte to 1 for every cell containing a text character or the cursor, so checking whether a star is hidden behind text is a single or instruction. If the cell is occupied, I skip drawing the star but carry on rotating and stepping it along until it reaches a cell where it can be displayed: Parallax is still handled by moving each star a different number of pixels per frame, but the cost is a lot lower this time as Iâm only touching the cells the stars actually occupy, rather than every byte of every row. Thatâs looking more like it! The typewriter routine is a simple copy of the font data from memory, and is very cheap as we can use the âcheap movesâ to quickly fetch the 8x8 block. I also skip drawing any space character so it leaves the âoccupancy cellâ unmarked. This means the stars keep drifting through the gaps in the text - you can see here the odd star passing in between the words. I switched to ALL CAPS writing for the final version which helps the effect even more as the font is quite blocky, so you donât really notice stars skipping the spaces inside a glyph at all. A few odds and ends that didnât warrant a section of their ownâ¦ Some sort of graphic display bouncing along with the audio playback was another common early demo trope. I did originally consider a real-time graphic equaliser, but that would have been far too complex, probably in terms of spare cycles per frame, and definitely in terms of my limited mental capacity at this point! So I settled for a simple set of bouncing meter bars instead. Itâs worth a mention mostly because it gives me an excuse to link to the awesome chibiakumas website! I just love the late 90s web design on display - one can argue that readability and accessibility take a hit, but itâs just so much fun to encounter a site that still looks like this. Itâs a clear labour of love and thereâs a wealth of content there as well, if your eyeballs are up to it. Their guide on Making Sound with the AY-3-8910 was what showed me how to get the data I needed to draw the meter bars. The examples write a register number to $FFFD to select a register, and I realised that once a register is selected, I could use the in instruction to read its value back out instead of writing a new one. As the page says, R8, R9 and R10 hold the channel amplitudes, so they feed nicely into the height parameter for drawing a bar. Getting the amplitude for channel A is then as simple as: This is a simple effect that makes the header logo a little more interesting. Iâm not sure where I originally got the idea - Iâve definitely seen something like it on a few late 80s/early 90s demos, though. All I wanted was to pick random star dots in the logo background and animate them. Hereâs the header image loaded in ZXPaintbrush with the character cell grid showing. By happy chance, there are four stars which each sit neatly inside a single character cell with enough surrounding space, so they can be used to give an animated âtwinkleâ effect by drawing a cross out from the centre point and back in again. These dots map to the following co-ordinates, which target the top scanline of each fully-grown star (two pixels up from the centre): The âtwinkleâ routine itself is simple enough: it adds a pixel on either axis to grow the star, waits a few frames, then shrinks it back down again. The interesting bit was how I made the twinkle order pseudo-random. Remember that my starfield was entirely pre-calculated from a data table generated by a Ruby script, which meant Iâd never actually needed a random number generator in assembly. From Jonathan Cauldwellâs âHow To Write Spectrum Gamesâ e-book, I found another great âhackâ which simply walks through the start of the Spectrumâs ROM, picking out random-looking bytes as it goes. As he says, he uses it in most of his games, and it does the job in a really simple way - as long as you stay below the block of structured, repeating data that sits 8Kb into the ROM. About halfway through writing the intro, I hit a fairly predictable problem: I had run out of memory. In an attempt to keep everything self-contained in one block of code, I was pulling all of the assets (the screen background, the player binary, the music file etc.) into the program itself, and then using the ldir block copy instruction to move each one into its correct location. Since that meant effectively storing every block twice, and the player routine had a hard-coded start address of $C000, I quickly ran out of room and my code started crashing into the playback routine. The simplest option was to split things out into separate code blocks, load each one directly to the address it needed to live at, and wrap the lot in a multi-stage BASIC tape loader: This loads the main program, then the player routine directly into $C000, and finally the background screen straight into screen memory. It does mean the background starts appearing before the demo has fully loaded, but as I imagine most people will be seeing this running in an emulator or on my TNFS site, it doesnât really matter. Plus, at this point I was in danger of disappearing down yet more rabbit holes (I still really want to work out how to do multi-colour border effects!) and Iâd never have got this thing released. This whole project is a really weird one to look back at. On the one hand, Iâve fulfilled a childhood ambition and have something Iâm very proud of. Itâs also pretty unusual these days to end up with a binary where you can say pretty much what every single byte is doing and the story of how it got there. But on the other hand - I now have an answer for why I donât code in assembly: Itâs because I value (whatâs left) of my sanity! The thing is, in order to write code like this you have to start thinking like the machine itself. You have to visualise the registers and the status flags flapping away, graphics as lines of bits slotted into strange orders, loops and conditionals as binary logic and so on. Getting this close to the hardware definitely brought about a greater sense of attachment to the hardware of my childhood, and itâs easy to see why assembly coders and sceners get so passionate about it. That said, Iâm in no hurry to start re-writing my body of work in assembly! The projects I really enjoy are those that give me an excuse to learn something for the sheer hell of it, and to slow down a little from the ever-increasing velocity and demands of the modern work world. Going back to Z80 code is probably about the furthest I could have taken this, short of going into hardware hacking. I found it at times an intriguing puzzle, often a frustrating exercise that nearly had me throwing in the towel at several stages. This project has certainly taken the longest to go from the âideaâ stage of any given feature to any kind of meaningful output. True, I didnât spend every day of the last year working on it - my actual coding time was probably only a few hours over a couple of evenings a week. But Iâve certainly been thinking about it and pondering it most days (as my dogs will attest). The biggest breakthroughs and âaha!â moments usually didnât come from behind the keyboard; they came from scribbles in my notebook and thinking about processor states while doing something unrelated. It has however given me massive appreciation and respect for the coders who pull this stuff off and make it look easy. And that goes double for those kids and bedroom coding superstars who managed all of this back in the 80s, and had to work it all out by experiment themselves. I only managed to get this far because of numerous books, online tutorials, GitHub repositories with sample code, YouTube videosâ¦ I canât imagine how much longer this would have all taken me if the only resources I had were my Spectrum, a cassette tape recorder and a notepad. So, as I draw a line under this project - for now! - I raise a glass, and in the words of h0ffman: âShout out to the hackers, graphicians and protrackers.â   Categories:   spectrum   The opinions and views expressed on this website are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of my employer, past or present.
