Markets     Hot Stocks     Fear & Greed Index                  Latest Market News                  Hot Stocks                  Four years ago, with inflation at multi-decade highs, then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a blunt message to Americans: Getting inflation under control would come at a cost.                   The Fed needed to act “forcefully,” Powell told attendees at a key central banker conference that August. Doing so, he cautioned, would bring “some pain” for consumers.                   Now, with the Fed back to raising interest rates for the first time in three years, a familiar warning about the economic fallout is resurfacing.                   Inflation across the country is being driven primarily by fuel prices, which have skyrocketed since the war with Iran broke out in February. The Fed has little control over oil production, but by raising interest rates, it is seeking to prevent higher energy costs from spilling over into other parts of the economy and fueling broader inflation.                   While this type of supply-driven inflation may be easier to bring under control than the post-pandemic demand-driven inflation, “it won’t be painless either,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said last month.                   For central bankers, the challenge is balancing two competing priorities: keeping inflation in check and preserving a healthy labor market. When price increases become too rapid, the Fed typically raises interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses. That, in turn, can curb spending and cool demand, easing pressure on prices.                   But that slowdown can come at a cost to workers, often leading to weaker hiring, fewer job openings, and, in some cases, job losses, as businesses struggle with higher borrowing costs.                   “Inflation is the disease. And now the Fed comes with a cure: higher interest rates,” Beth Ann Bovino, chief economist at US Bank, said. “I don’t know which is more painful because they both hurt.”                   Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity, making it a key driver of growth. If Americans pull back — either because prices are eating up more of their budgets or because higher borrowing costs force them to set aside more money for expenses such as a home purchase — the economy could slow. In a worst-case scenario, that pullback could help tip the economy into a recession, Bovino told CNN.                   For now, though, economic pain isn’t being felt equally. Americans with substantial investments in the stock market, which is hovering near record highs, may be doing just fine. Those who rely more heavily on their paychecks to cover everyday expenses have less of a cushion against rising prices.                   “Those are the people being hurt,” she said.                   With the risks of higher interest rates in mind, a growing chorus of Fed officials have recently been advocating for a more patient approach as they tackle the issue of inflation. Rather than trying to get a head start at fighting the potential for more or broader-based inflation, several central bankers have said they’d like more time to observe how economic conditions evolve to get a better idea of how many more rate hikes, if any, are needed.                   “There is no need for urgency,” New York Fed President John Williams said last month.                   Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson echoed that sentiment. “Any future adjustments in policy should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks,” he said earlier this month.                   But waiting to act carries risks of its own. With the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge more than a percentage point above its 2% annual target, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that delaying action could make the fight against inflation even more painful.                   “The longer inflation stays above our objective, the harder it will be for us to bring it back down, and the more pain that individuals and businesses are going to be experiencing,” Hammack said in an August CNBC interview.                   For the Fed, the challenge is figuring out how much pain the economy can withstand — and which risk is worse: acting too soon or waiting too long. Either way, consumers are likely to pay the price.                   The September Consumer Price Index report due Wednesday may give officials some valuable clues. So why did the Big Five publishers just kill the mass market paperback? The cheap mass-market paperback gave us a truly popular yet sophisticated literary culture. Its decline has at least as much to do with corporate consolidation as shifting consumer preferences. (Evening Standard / Hulton Archive / Getty Images) Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20. It seems every week a new piece about the decline and fall of the American reading habit goes viral. The idea that we’re entering a literary apocalypse that threatens to destabilize our democracy is perhaps overstated, but nobody is denying the book-reading trend is grim. In the most recent international assessment of adult skills, conducted in 2023, 28 percent of American adults scored at or below the lowest level of literacy — up from 19 percent just six years earlier. By one widely cited estimate, more than half of American adults read below a sixth-grade level. It’s interesting to note that these hand-wringing, sky-is-falling pieces unfailingly focus on external issues. Few of us doubt what we feel in our bones to be true — that long-form reading is being harmed by disruptive technologies and other beyond-our-control societal issues (political dysfunction and a decrepit educational system) that apply to the demand side of the equation. But what about the supply side? Could it be that corporatized publishing — with all of its consolidations and centralization — may have enshittified the product to the point where it has abetted the decline in consumer demand? Consider the death of the mass-market paperback last year. When the Big Five publishing houses (Penguin Random House, Macmillan, HarperCollins, Hachette, and Simon & Schuster) took the most affordable book format in America — known for its modest price and compact size — off of life support in 2025, it had long ago failed to live up to the “mass” part of its name. At that point, the books under that banner were recognizable but lacking the vitality and freshness that had first driven them to national attention in the twentieth century. Until the 1940s, book retail was dominated by hardcovers — books held between cloth- or paper-covered boards, the pages secured by sewn spines. Penguin in the UK and Pocket Books here in the United States were the first to make successful use of an alternative book format that rivaled — and, for many decades, far outsold — the hardback. This cheaper-to-manufacture book had a soft cover and relied upon a glued (versus stitched) binding. The resulting tome was easier to carry and much easier to afford. The new format was as much commercial opportunism as it was any attempt to democratize reading or to improve the citizenry’s understanding of the world. If you make a dime on each purchase of one hundred thousand paperbacks, that’s more than making a buck each on 2,500 hardcovers, which was the average unit sale back then. Better yet, these books were sold all over middle America — in drugstores, grocery stores, and gas stations — not just in the little metropolitan oases. In the post–Great Depression years, American bookstores were hardly ubiquitous. Large metro areas with a sufficient intelligentsia density might have a few, but in the 1930s there were only about five hundred dedicated bookshops across all of America. At the same time, basic literacy was nearly universal — by the 1930 census, some 96 percent of Americans over the age of ten could read and write — but the average American only knew books through schools (which used to buy a lot more books than they do now), libraries (which used to contain a lot more books than they do now), and catalogs (which used to sell a lot more books than they do now). Unless you lived in an affluent area with a bookstore or were near a department store or gift shop — which also sometimes had small book sections — you simply did not encounter them as a working adult. But when these cheap little books dubbed “mass-market paperbacks” began showing up, they were a hit. America’s Pocket Books launched in 1939 and sold 8.5 million copies within two years. Which is even more remarkable considering they were not yet being sold “north of Boston, west of Chicago, or south of Washington [DC].” The books were averaging close to one hundred thousand units each, with a population a little over a third the size of today’s United States. When the industry discontinued the format in 2024, the highest-selling new mass-market title — a Danielle Steel book — sold 53,000 units. It’s no wonder the executives decided to scuttle the whole thing and to blame the customer for it. One of the bigger recent pieces on the supposed new trend in anti-literacy was an Atlantic piece called “The End of Reading Is Here,” and it was typical in its emphasis on the failures of the society that is degenerating outside the walls of the Big Five. The piece gives us the history of publishing from Mesopotamia to Ptolemy to Johannes Gutenberg and emphasizes the importance that our nation’s founders and civil war heroes placed on long-form print. Marshall McLuhan, Neil Postman, Walter J. Ong, and Alexander Luria are name-checked. The tech-happy media and educational industries are decried, and the system that allows kids to spend 4.5 hours a day on social media is called out, but nowhere in the massive piece is any shade thrown at the book publishing industry with whom The Atlantic, for 169 years, has been cozy, and to which the article’s Yale-educated writer likely — as with most staff writers — means to sell manuscripts over the course of a career. There is plenty of good reason for gloom. We are told that 80 percent of elementary school teachers report that their students have, by kindergarten, received school-issued personal video devices. But the Atlantic piece contains no implication that one possible reason books and long-form reading are falling away, a theoretically contributory factor to the mass market’s extinction and the plummeting demand for books, involves the supply-side of the equation. Any thought that what the publishing industry is printing, or how it has been pricing it, or where it has been placing it, just might have harmed our nation’s reading habit is never mentioned. The writer has good company in blaming the people on the outside. None of the publishing executives and pundits that attended the mass-market paperback’s funeral ceremonies last year did any self-implication either. “We follow the consumer,” said Dennis Abboud, CEO of ReaderLink, America’s largest book distributor, upon announcing the death of the mass-market paperback. “It seems the consumer has spoken,” said Steve Zacharius, CEO of one of the biggest publishers in the format. “As a format, I would say it’s pretty much over,” said Ivan Held of Penguin Random House. All this shrugging and hand-washing for the book format that, as one regretful publisher eloquently put it, saved (or at least forestalled the decline of) America. “I believe that mass-market paperbacks democratized America,” said Esther Margolis of Newmarket Press. “For basically the equivalent of a dollar or two, you know, you could be educated. You could pick them up at the school book fair. You could pick them up at a local gas station . . . You didn’t have to be an elitist.” But could the mega-consolidated Big Five American publishing industry bear any blame for this state of affairs? Consumer scientists have long understood that that popular habits are not just among the hardest things to break but are also very difficult to make. Many companies try to integrate their products into preexisting habits, but it’s rare that a company touches off an entirely new one, much less one at the scale of the mass-market paperback. Those 8.5 million paperbacks sold by Pocket Books from 1939 to 1941 were arguably proof of a bigger, more instantaneous habit birth than that of even the iPhone, which sold a comparable amount of their own product but to a population that had grown three times larger. But America’s decades-long mass-market paperback binge (which in 1979 topped out at 387 million annual units sold) suggests that we, as a people, are capable of — and perhaps even prone to — falling into a book-reading habit. So was there anything publishers could have done to prevent the death of the mass-market paperback and the decline of our national reading habit? In 1939, television didn’t exist, movies lasted only a couple hours — versus the days you can occupy through a single book — and even there you were stuck with whatever was playing at the non-multiplex cinema. You also had at best a dozen radio stations to choose from versus the cheap time-killing options we have on this side of the digital revolution. The new landscape obviously comprises external demand-affecting features that exist beyond the reach of even the most powerful book industry executive. And judging whether books are more or less attractive seems like a hard one to quantify. Proving that publishers have gotten better or worse at designing attractive book jackets, executing motivating marketing campaigns, and delivering compelling manuscripts would doubtless be largely subjective. But one aspect of appeal for which it is much easier to hold the publishers’ feet to the fire is range. There is a bigger story to be told here, but let’s take a snapshot and consider the first ten mass-market paperbacks that Pocket Books published: Emily Brontë, Bambi, Dorothy Parker, Agatha Christie, Shakespeare, a Victorian bildungsroman and a Pulitzer Prize–winning novel by Thornton Wilder. That’s quite a broad spectrum! Now let’s hold this mini-catalog up against the mass-market bestsellers list from the very month in 2025 that Dennis Abboud, CEO of ReaderLink — a former managing partner at a private equity firm — announced that the mass-market paperback was to be put out to pasture: Comparing the first ten paperbacks ever published — which sold millions of copies in a very different world — to the last ten is not entirely unfair. Those were the industry’s ten priority titles of 1939; the latter ones are the ten priority titles of the industry eighty-six years later. In other words, decisions — curations, really — made by the companies. The former are effectively the ten books a person of 1939 was most likely to have encountered while shopping, and the latter are the ten books a person is most likely to have encountered while doing the same in February 2025. In 1939, we have adventure books, plays, poems, a story about a deer, a murder mystery, a prize-winning literary novel, and a movie tie-in — all by a set of authors ranging in age, if they were living at time of publication, from thirty-eight to sixty-nine. In 2025, we have only contemporary commercial fiction options, half of which are series titles (one of which had a whopping thirty-five prior installments) and by eight brand-name authors, average age seventy-four, plus two whose franchise author is a man who would have been eighty-six at the time of publication, at least had he not died in 2004. There’s nothing wrong with pursuing safe bets: all these old brand authors and their long-established readerships are obviously dependable, at least from a quarterly earnings standpoint, versus Pocket Books’ unscientific, consumer-data-lacking, instinct-driven — albeit extremely successful — strategy from 1939. But given that variety is an important part of attracting consumers, is it possible our twenty-first century publishers have diminished the wider appeal of their product — for readers and potential readers outside the dependable boomer commercial-fiction core — even just a little bit? As to affordability, ¢25 (the price of each of Pocket Books’ titles) went a lot further in 1939 than it does now but was still a consumer-friendly price point. It was just slightly higher than what our great-great-grandparents would have paid for a gallon of gas and slightly lower than what they’d have paid for a dozen eggs. In 2024, the format’s last year of full national distribution, a new mass-market paperback would set you back three times as much as a dozen eggs or a gallon of gas. One might suspect that materials, distribution, or other book-specific costs had risen over the intervening decades. But how then to explain that the mass-market paperback’s older sibling — the hidebound hardcover — hasn’t seen an inflation nearly so dramatic? Today’s hardback novel has a cover price between $28 and $32. That’s 40 percent cheaper than it would have been back in the 1940s, and this is before a typical national retailer discount of more than 20 percent (and often up to 50 percent) for best-selling titles. In 1939, you could buy ten mass-market paperbacks for the cost of a single new hardback. In 2024, you could barely buy two. Which means that under the leadership of the Big Five and their equally hegemonic national retail partners, the flagship product favored by elite-facing bookstores in wealthy enclaves got cheaper, and the format with the proven mass potential got many times more expensive. Finally, let’s consider availability. Even before the mass-market paperback was discontinued, books were being carried in fewer and fewer places. Supermarkets, drugstores, truck stops, newsstands, and department stores,had all gotten out of the business. And the bookselling stalwarts of recent decades have been faltering too. In 2024, Costco, which used to sell millions of units a year, stopped carrying books in most of its stores. The big national book retailer Borders, with an assist from private equity, went out of business in 2011. Barnes & Noble has been roughly holding steady, but it has just around six hundred outlets in at best 19 percent of our nation’s counties. The trends the publishers and the media cite to justify this availability crisis are real. But were they unavoidable? And are they excusable? And are they perhaps also driven by problems the two other As — appeal and affordability — over which the industry has even more direct control? Could and should the US publishing industry in fact be visibly exploring solutions or putting up a public fight to maintain a more significant non-digital distribution of its titles? Could and should the industry notice that the mass-market paperback is still for sale in Canada — where, in that same 2023 assessment, just 18 percent of adults scored at or below the lowest literacy level, compared with 28 percent here — and at a price less than half of what it rose to in the United States? It’s difficult to see how the corporatized, highly centralized industry is walking away blameless from killing off one of its former darlings — the affordable paperback. Clearly it’s easier to focus on fewer higher-income readers than on a multitude of Americans whose lives you have no social connection to. Clearly decisions were made — ones that no doubt have had a major effect on American reading habits. And clearly the highly intertwined media establishment is not going to second-guess them. But maybe you should. Ned Rust is a researcher at the Center for Working-Class Politics. {{ message }} Thanks for signing up! → Already on our list? Get our print magazine for just $20 a year. Tech > Mobile > Phones Higher phone prices are seriously squeezing consumers' wallets, says Counterpoint Research. October 12, 2026, 5:35 pm ET If you’re holding on to your phone despite a wave of new, high-powered options, you’re not alone. Hitting the lowest mark since 2012, smartphone shipments worldwide continued a months-long skid, slumping 20% in the third quarter of 2026 due to the RAMageddon memory shortage, according to a new analysis by Counterpoint Research. Counterpoint said that the cost of DRAM and NAND — the two main memory chips used in smartphones, computers and data centers — continues to rise, forcing manufacturers to raise phone prices, which are up 20% overall this year. Memory costs more because there’s less of it to go around, thanks to the massive AI infrastructure buildup and its voracious appetite for chips. It was the second consecutive quarter to take “the full brunt of the memory crisis,” Shilpi Jain, a senior analyst at Counterpoint, said in a statement Monday. More from CNET Research firm Gartner has estimated that companies will spend $1.4 trillion on AI infrastructure this year and $2.6 trillion overall. More than 70% of global memory chip production will go toward AI investment, TrendForce said. Global fears about rising inflation for most products and services are also likely suppressing phone sales. Some manufacturers fared all right during the third quarter, according to Counterpoint. Samsung’s market share was 23%, up from 19% in 2025, thanks in part to “robust initial demand” for the Galaxy Fold 8. Apple’s third-quarter market share was 22%, the first time the company has surpassed 20% in that three-month period. But both companies saw a year-over-year decline in shipments. Things aren’t looking rosy for customers’ wallets, either. Earlier this month, Samsung hiked prices by $100 for its Galaxy S26 phones, and Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched last month with prices set $100 above the previous generation. The third quarter saw a number of notable smartphone introductions, including Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, the Google Pixel 11 and, in the period’s waning days, the iPhone 18 Pro line and Apple’s first foldable, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin on Friday. Shoppers will be cautious about buying the latest and greatest in smartphones because of higher prices, says TMT analyst Paolo Pescatore. “New design features, including foldables, may generate excitement and appeal, but their steep price premiums remain hard to justify when most people want a device that delivers robust, reliable connectivity,” Pescatore told CNET via email. “For many, the question is straightforward: why replace a perfectly functioning smartphone that continues to meet their everyday needs?” Counterpoint Research found in a recent survey that half of respondents — spanning the US, UK, India, China and Germany — would wait until holiday sales to buy a new phone. That number rises to 56% among Gen Z consumers. Counterpoint’s Jain said consumers are increasingly shopping for “refurbished devices and prioritizing higher-value devices.” With sales down, phonemakers might resort to different strategies for customers, including refurbished handsets, repairs and trade-in schemes, Pescatore said. Cellphone carriers like T-Mobile, Verizon Wireless and AT&T could also use financing plans and bundled services as enticements. As AI investment continues to devour memory supply, phone prices won’t be falling anytime soon. And with companies focusing more on premium devices, there could be fewer budget alternatives available for customers, Counterpoint Research said.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Forward-deployed engineers are all the rage in AI, and Anthropic is going to other companies to train up top talent. The AI company announced a $100 million investment into an FDE training initiative earlier this month. It's a quasi-fellowship that engineers from other firms have already begun applying for. They'll attend four-day on-site intensives and then complete 12-week "residencies" working with Anthropic's Claude tools at their own companies. The company says it hopes to train 10,000 people through the program by the end of 2027. As Anthropic approaches its gigantic initial public offering, it's using the new training model to get more of the corporate world used to AI — and ramp up Claude spending. Job postings for FDEs have boomed over the last couple of years, as more companies buy software from AI firms and need help deploying it. Two Anthropic executives leading the push told Business Insider that their customers see AI's advances, notice competitors grabbing market share, and feel pressure to change their own work. "Everybody understands the model capability is expanding extremely fast," said Shambhavi Shambhavi, Anthropic's head of go-to-market strategy and operations for partnerships. "So, what can be done with the technology is greatly appreciated by the customers." Enter the FDE — which Anthropic calls "Frontier Deployed Engineers," rather than the standard "forward-deployed engineer" title that Palantir helped popularize. Both roles essentially mean someone with deep technical expertise in AI and the mandate to create new modes of work at a company. Shambhavi and Steve Corfield, Anthropic's head of global business development and partnerships, broke down the FDE role as they see it and how Anthropic hopes to set a "gold standard" with its new skills push. Shambhavi said that the best FDEs have four main attributes. They are familiar with agentic AI systems. They're good problem-solvers. They're excellent communicators. And they're experienced, skilled engineers. Corfield tacked on a point he thinks helps Anthropic thrive: "You've got to be super, super curious. If you walk around this organization, everybody talks about curiosity." Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. She said that as companies try to overhaul entire workflows and approach agentic AI holistically, someone who can navigate the interpersonal dynamics goes a long way. "Our own Frontier Deployed Engineers work with these kinds of problems day in and day out," Shambhavi said. "And so we kind of applied the mindset of, we need to take this skill and bring it to our customers and partners and to the top engineers in those organizations, so that they can derive the benefits from Claude." Engineers who can expand their teams' use of AI have become a hot commodity in Silicon Valley. Salesforce, a major Anthropic partner, announced a plan in May to recruit 1,000 early-career workers into "AI builder" roles. Anthropic's program, in Corfield's view, goes a step above other industry attempts to recruit and train FDEs. Combined with other company initiatives to teach people AI, he hopes Anthropic will set "the gold standard for AI skilling." The first cohorts have begun in New York and San Francisco, including engineers from Accenture, Bain, Novo Nordisk, and other organizations. Companies nominate engineers for the training, and Anthropic interviews candidates. If they're accepted, they work for the four-day residency on a "simulated environment," an agentic system that they have to learn how to build and deploy. Then they take a practical test, before returning to their companies while staying in touch with Anthropic mentors for 12 more weeks. Anthropic is still building its assessments throughout the program. Shambhavi said they'll focus on "what does a great FDE look like" — articulation, problem solving, coding skills. Corfield said corporate customers wanted a program like this to help them figure out how to deploy Claude more effectively, and the holdup isn't motivation. "This is a skills gap problem, and that creates a market problem," he said.  "What we're trying to do is fill that gap," he added. Have a tip? The white-collar sector is doing more with less. While the number of total jobs has slid in industries like finance, tech, and professional services, output has been on a tear. Gad Levanon, the chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, examined how employment in white-collar-heavy sectors compares with real gross domestic product. He wrote in a Substack article that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional and business services is collectively down roughly 2% since the end of 2022, while real output for these sectors has soared by 16%. The ongoing slow decline in employment for this group goes against historical patterns and highlights how workers and job seekers are facing a largely frozen, low-hire, low-fire job market. "A growing share of the work businesses used to get done by consultants, contractors, call centers and their own back-office staff is now delivered by software, cloud and IT firms, which produce far more per worker and add almost no staff," Levanon told Business Insider. "That is why the sector's output keeps rising while its hiring has stopped." The divergence also risks breaking the traditional link between economic growth and rising fortunes for everyday Americans. "Even a strong, continual growth in GDP may not translate into jobs for people, may not translate into a higher quality of life for people as well," said Cory Stahle, an economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. People looking in these kinds of sectors may be having a challenging time. "It's important to remember for these job seekers that a career is not necessarily built over the course of two or three years," Stahle said. "It's usually built over the course of two or three decades. So what the pattern is now could easily shift a couple of years from now. So it's important to be reactive but not overreact to what we're seeing in the data, either." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? Have you had to make a career pivot? Levanon said on Substack that there's demand in these white-collar fields, but firms can meet it with fewer workers. Part of that could be due to employers shifting their priorities toward leveraging AI. Levanon said "the back-office and junior tasks" that AI performs best at are concentrated in the white-collar sectors he looked at.  Dante DeAntonio, senior director at Moody's Analytics, previously told Business Insider that the lack of hiring in white-collar fields is largely due to uncertainty around economic policy and AI. Other job market experts have noted that in Big Tech, employers pulled back after the pandemic-era hiring surge. The job market's woes can be especially difficult for people who lack years of experience. "Firms, I think, are certainly diving in with both feet, trying to find ways to gain efficiency from AI," DeAntonio said. "And certainly the first domino to fall is likely to be a pullback in hiring amongst younger workers, new college grads, positions where firms think they might be able to get some uptick from AI, and some sort of replacement value from AI." Whether companies are actually more productive because they're incorporating AI tools remains a question. Eric Kutcher, a senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, recently said that there are individual productivity increases, rather than institutional-level gains. "You have people that are getting more productive as individuals, but they're just changing some of the work that they're doing," he said. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed general labor productivity has increased, but not at a wildly accelerated clip. "We have seen that things have slowed down in the last few years, but output per worker and productivity was climbing even before we saw ChatGPT and AI starting to come onto the scene," Stahle said. "To me, that says that AI is part of the story here, but not the complete story. This is part of a longer-term trend." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? Jaclyn Diaz        Loading...  For hours, bullets tore through the home, hitting neighboring houses and cars. Inside, a man wanted by police for allegedly killing his ex-girlfriend was holed up with his new girlfriend. As the SWAT team prepared to enter, Kevin Fennessy with the Ocean County Sheriff's Office tried something new first. He sent in a tiny assistant: a small drone equipped with a camera. From a safe position outside, Fennessy slowly piloted the device through a blasted-in window, while he and other officers watched on a monitor. The video, viewed by NPR, showed hallway walls and furniture riddled with bullet holes. As it entered a back bedroom where the couple had holed up, footage showed the man's body on the floor. He had killed himself. With the drone still hovering above the macabre scene, police deployed two flash bangs into the room. The woman rushed out and surrendered. The incident, which happened about three years ago, sticks in Fennessy's mind when he considers the value of his department's drone program, which he heads. "No one's hurt. Everyone's safe," Fennessy says. "Forty-one times they shot out the house at us. But at the end of the day, we were able to clear the house."                  Chief Warrant Officer Kevin Fennessy lifts an Ocean County Sheriff's Office DJI Matrice 300 RTK drone out of the custom-built bed of a department SUV at Robert J. Miller Airpark on Sept. 4.                                                           Albert Yee for NPR                                       hide caption  New Jersey's Ocean County Sheriff's Office is one of an estimated 6,000 law enforcement agencies across the country that now have drones, used for search and rescue, fire and traffic crash investigations, and tactical response, according to the Law Enforcement Drone Association. It's an organization that advises, trains and certifies police across the country on their drone programs. Ocean County's entire fleet is from DJI, a Chinese manufacturer of drones. LEDA estimates that about 80% to 90% of law enforcement agencies flying drones use DJI devices. China controls a vast majority of the global drone market, and it's the dominant source for the minerals and raw materials needed to build them, researchers say. The Trump administration wants that to end. It's made several moves to bolster U.S. drone makers, including by banning many new foreign-made drones from entering the American market. Most recently, his administration announced tariffs of 15% to 100% on some foreign-made drones, making it much more expensive for agencies to buy these devices. Critics of these moves say the American drone industry is not yet able to keep up with demand, nor can it match the high-quality and low-cost drones made in China. Law enforcement agencies that rely on these drones are getting caught up in the fight as the federal government pushes back on the dominance of Chinese technology. "We're seeing lives being saved with the use of this technology," says Jon Beal, head of LEDA. He says the organization supports efforts to boost the American drone industry, but that reducing access to Chinese drones is not a good solution. "What that's going to do is cancel out perfectly viable drone programs that are doing great work out there," he says. "We don't want to cut off our nose to spite our face." Agencies pay for drone programs in various ways, including with grants and fundraising. The Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses profits from asset forfeiture and through their municipal operating budget to cover their fleet of 25 drones. "We have to be cost-effective. And to do that, get the best product that's available to us," Ocean County Sheriff Michael Mastronardy says.  Loading...                   A Seabob rescue vehicle inside the garage of the Seaside Heights Volunteer Fire Department Ocean Rescue office in Seaside Heights, N.J. This vehicle propels rescue swimmers during water rescues. The department is looking into aerial drones equipped with flotation devices and unmanned water drones like the ones the Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses to aid in water rescue.                                                           Albert Yee for NPR                                       hide caption  For them, that meant turning to DJI drones. In the parking lot of the Ocean County Sheriff's Office in early August, Fennessy breaks down the costs of the equipment one of his deputies carries in his vehicle. A DJI Matrice 300 RTK: $13,699 A set of two batteries: $1,400 A camera with infrared thermal imaging: $11,499 A (very fancy) remote controller: $1,600 A RESTUBE Automatic, a flotation device that can be dropped into water for rescues by the drone: $130.99 A payload release system: $1,099 That comes to a total of $29,427.99 Fennessy acknowledges this is a huge investment, but says the devices are well-used and well worth it — especially in the summertime, when Ocean County's population nearly doubles. Major events constantly pose a policing challenge for the department, and they've found that drones have helped keep an eye on big crowds. In July, the department used a drone to drop flotation devices to two swimmers in distress, and rescuers were able to bring them to shore. Fennessy has become passionate about drones professionally and as a hobbyist. He's done a lot of research, including into the American drone market. "All their stuff is good," he says. "I've flown almost all of them. And I like them. I do. They make good products, but probably about three times the cost" of the DJI tools. Beal, who says his organization is "agnostic" when it comes to what drones departments use, says he thinks Chinese-made drones are "light years ahead of what our American drones are able to do." For instance, Beal says DJI offers a drone with an impressive, high-resolution thermal camera that costs less than $10,000 right now. He says American-made drones have worse flight-time capabilities, thermal imaging and zoom. And still they usually cost between $20,000 and $50,000, depending on the type and the model. NPR compared the cost of two drones with similar features. The DJI Matrice 400 drone retails for about $10,500. The American-made Inspired Flight IF800 TOMCAT is going for $21,000. Ocean County is closely monitoring recent actions by the Trump administration that could limit options for updating its fleet in the future. Agencies in other states like Florida, Texas, Mississippi and Tennessee have had to terminate their drone programs or plans for one after state lawmakers passed bans on agencies using foreign drones. Beal says some were left scrambling to find ways to pay for more expensive American alternatives when tight department budgets couldn't cover the additional costs. And there are more federal actions in the works. The Federal Communications Commission is considering a new rule that would reclassify drones that use tech like thermal imaging as "military grade" — effectively banning many Chinese-made drones that have this integrated technology. Ocean County and other law enforcement use thermal imaging to assist in finding lost people or pets.                  An aerial view of an Ocean County Sheriff's Office DJI Matrice 300 RTK drone with a thermal-capable camera payload at the Ocean County Fairgrounds with the New Jersey Pinelands stretching into the distance. A propeller plane can be seen below and right of the drone.                                                           Albert Yee for NPR                                       hide caption  The FCC already bans the sale of some new models of foreign-made drones without the agency's approval. Federal agencies and contractors cannot use certain foreign-made drones. The FCC said in response to NPR's questions, "Thanks to President Trump's leadership, America's drone industry is booming with new investment, manufacturing, and jobs. At the FCC, we're doing our part — working hand-in-glove across government and the private sector to make sure that U.S. drone and counter-drone supply chains are safe, secure, and reliable for all." The administration says that Chinese-made drones, and DJI drones specifically, pose a threat to national security — with, for instance, their potential for major attacks during large public gatherings, like the recent World Cup games, among other concerns. DJI has pushed back against claims that its tech is shared with the Chinese government or that it accesses cameras and other footage collected by users, even hiring a U.S.-based cybersecurity firm to test the company's products for vulnerabilities. Adam Welsh, head of global policy at DJI said in a statement published in May, "These findings confirm what DJI has consistently maintained: our products are secure, our data practices are transparent" and the concerns that led to the company being banned "are not supported by technical evidence." There's also the allegation that DJI uses forced labor from Uyghurs, a primarily Muslim ethnic group facing human rights abuses under the Chinese government, to build its products. In 2024, the Customs and Border Protection blocked certain DJI drone imports under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. DJI has strongly denied these allegations, too. Fennessy says he understands these concerns. "But to be honest, right now," he says, "I want something that's capable to go out there and do the job. And I have it." Beal says he's seen no hard evidence that China is using these drones or its technology to spy on communities that are using them. He says he can understand the argument to bring more of the drone supply chain stateside. But that's a problem too, right now. "We don't have a lot of the minerals. We can't produce the battery now. Even the American companies are using Chinese batteries," he says. "We're kind of limited to the resources that we have in-country or in an allied country, and sometimes that's just not there." The National Sheriffs' Association, which represents more than 3,000 sheriffs, has called for the FCC to reconsider the proposed reclassification of certain drones as military grade. In a recent letter, the association wrote that it "recommends that the FCC confirm the adequacy of the domestic market for [Unmanned Aircraft Systems] and [Unmanned Aircraft Systems]-critical components for sheriffs and their colleagues in public safety to acquire drones to fulfill their various mission types, including drones that meet the definition of military grade." In addition to thermal imaging, that classification includes capabilities such as the ability to spray aerosols and lidar, or laser-based sensors. The NSA recommends that otherwise the FCC add an exemption for state, local, tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to continue to purchase and operate this equipment until the domestic market is built up.                  An Ocean County Sheriff's Office drone lifts off at the Ocean County Fairgrounds on Sept. 4 as Chief Warrant Officer Kevin Fennessy (left) and Officer Adam Wright (at right, with the controller) stand near a department SUV.                                           Albert Yee for NPR                                       hide caption  Keith Miao, the CEO and founder of Birdstop, a Detroit-based manufacturer of autonomous drone technology, says China "hands down" dominated what he calls "the first era" of drone technology. He says American manufacturers have the potential to "define the next era of enterprise and government use of drone technology." To Miao, the federal government's latest moves are an acknowledgment that this is a critical technology that, if not manufactured at home, could be a serious problem down the road. "I think this is going to give American manufacturers an opportunity to rethink … and build out drone manufacturing," Miao says. "We are going all in on manufacturing drones in America and building up the supply chains to do that long term. And so we obviously believe it can be done." There are several federal and state grants that law enforcement can use to buy American-made drones. But they are competitive. Fennessy hopes more federal funding comes through, especially if the government eventually wants them to park their DJI drones for good. "If the federal government wants to say, hey, listen, you can't fly your DJI drone anymore, well, that's cool. Um, how am I going to afford to buy the drones that you want me to fly? The taxpayers of Ocean County are going to absorb that," he says. "The funding's got to be there." NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. It's been a quarter century since Honda had a new Prelude arriving at dealerships. The coupe — which was popular in the 1990s with enthusiasts who liked to tinker with tuner cars — was discontinued in 2001. So, I wouldn't blame you if you don't recognize the nameplate. I also wouldn't blame you if you do remember it and find Honda's new approach to the beloved car a little surprising. Unlike the Prelude of yesteryear, the new one is certainly not cheap. My Boost Blue tester has a sticker price of $43,650, including destination. Optional summer tires pushed the suggested price to $44,850. On paper, this car makes almost no sense. Who exactly is the buyer? Prelude purists may bristle at the hybrid powertrain and price. Young shoppers looking for an affordable coupe have cheaper options. Drivers chasing outright performance can get substantially more power elsewhere. After 400 miles, I started to think the Prelude makes more sense for Honda than it does for any one obvious customer. Honda calls the new version a sporty grand tourer. It's aiming for a niche part of the US market: It's comfortable and efficient enough for long drives, while maintaining a visual appeal that's very different from the vehicular blobs filling today's grocery store parking lot. I say it nails the aesthetics. My Boost Blue tester was almost aggressively photogenic, with bulging wheel arches and a sloping roofline that gave it a poor man's Porsche vibe. As I drove slowly past a construction site in Brooklyn, a worker asked me to lower my window. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    "Sweet car!" he said. As I drove away, I heard him yell to a coworker: "Damn, that's a Honda?" Underneath its curvy coupe body sits Honda's deeply engineered two-motor hybrid system, good for 200 horsepower and an EPA-estimated 44 mpg combined. It also borrows suspension, steering, and Brembo brake hardware from the Civic Type R and luxury interior elements from its high-end luxury brand, Acura. It's not particularly fast. That trade-off became obvious pretty quickly. The Prelude's getup is plenty for merging onto the highway, and it actually felt sprightlier once moving at speed. But its immediate shove is nowhere near what I've felt in similarly priced performance cars — or some EVs, like the Tesla Model 3. What it lacks in outright speed, though, it makes up for elsewhere. The car stays impressively flat through bends, the steering feels direct, and the Brembos are grabby enough to remind you that Honda raided the fun-loving Type R's parts bin. Good news, too, for drivers mourning the death of manuals: Honda's new S+ Shift system does a surprisingly convincing impersonation of a traditional transmission. There aren't actually eight gears, but steering-wheel-mounted paddle shifters, simulated rev-matched downshifts, and surprisingly natural engine sounds add some fun driving nostalgia theater. More useful was the fuel economy. I averaged 43.5 mpg on my mostly highway drive, almost exactly matching Honda's 44-mpg combined estimate. Its backseat, however, is nearly useless. The second row is difficult to get into because of the sloping roofline, has virtually no headroom, and will only fit riders with calves as thick as a sheet of paper. Is this car a fit for most American buyers? Not really. It's effectively an expensive two-seater with a Honda badge and a luxury interior. On paper, it doesn't really stack up against its competition: the Ford Mustang is more powerful, the Mazda MX-5 Miata is sportier, and the Toyota GR-86 is nearly $10,000 cheaper. That's a particularly small cubbyhole of a market for the Prelude. Honda may not need the Prelude to become a volume seller. Dealers I've spoken with said supply is limited, and one told me there's already a waitlist to get one onto the lot. Another dealer said the Prelude could draw curious shoppers into the showroom — even if many ultimately leave in something like the ever-popular CR-V. So maybe there's a better question surrounding this car: Is the Honda Prelude attention-grabbing? The construction worker clearly thought so. No comments right now, check back later. Cathy Valentine lost her job as a transformation lead in 2023. After three years struggling to find a comparable full-time job, the 61-year-old is now a prep cook at a cafe. She said she earns about an eighth of her previous salary. "It just feels like I tried to do everything right and I still am stuck," said Valentine, who lives in Florida. Some older workers who lose their jobs can afford to retire, while others find a comparable role fairly quickly. But those who don't risk getting stuck in a job search that drags on for months or even years — and is getting longer. On some metrics, older Americans are doing just fine in the job market. As of September, older workers had lower unemployment rates than younger workers, and when they were jobless, the median length of that unemployment was shorter. But those figures obscure a worse trend for older job seekers. While half of 55 to 64-year-olds were jobless for a relatively low three months, the group's average unemployment duration was more than eight months in September. That means some older workers have been unemployed for so long that they're pulling the average way up.  The gap between the average and median has widened in recent months, suggesting the longest job searches may be growing even longer. In September, about 173,000 unemployed Americans ages 55 to 64 had been out of work for at least six months, and some are facing far longer stretches of unemployment. A Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis found that only 57% of workers ages 55 to 64 who lost their long-held jobs any time between 2023 and 2025 had found new jobs as of January 2026. By contrast, 73% of workers ages 25 to 54 who lost long-held jobs in that period had found new work. Some older workers may have taken their job loss as a sign they should retire. But for others, it marked the beginning of an uphill battle to find another job. The construction workers building Meta's largest-ever data center are arriving in a tiny Louisiana town with more than specialized skills and manpower. They've also got cash to spend. It's a fact that local entrepreneurs are leveraging to build new businesses. "It's been a good opportunity for everybody," David Rodgers, the cofounder of Ice Queen, a local business, told Business Insider. "I tell people, you can't stop it unless you have $50 billion. You might as well get on board and go with the flow." Meta said the data center, dubbed Hyperion, will span nearly 10 million square feet in rural Holly Ridge and will support more than 7,500 jobs at peak construction. That's a workforce larger than the population of Aspen, Colorado. While the influx of workers is straining the local housing market and disrupting aspects of daily life, their presence has also boosted the region's economy. Holly Ridge is a very small sliver of the nearly 19,600 residents in Richland Parish, where agriculture has been the main industry for decades. Before Meta arrived, the smattering of towns, villages, and unincorporated areas that make up Richland Parish hadn't seen significant economic growth in years. Tim Allen, a Richland Parish restaurant owner, lived through that stagnation in the nearby town of Rayville. "Rayville has been a small community my whole life, and it's been in decline over the last several years. We have a lot of people whose children are moving out, and they usually don't come back," Allen said. "Growing up, downtown Rayville had multiple businesses, hardware stores, and clothing stores. One by one, they shut down until only a couple of stores were left." Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. When Meta announced its project in 2024, Allen and his family were among those who saw an opportunity to turn things around. "Since Meta's announcement, we've seen old businesses revitalize and new ones open, including ours," Allen said. Holy Tacos opened in April 2025. TJ and Kaycie Weed, also based in Rayville, said the new demographic created by Meta's project has boosted their sales. They first opened their café, HeBrews Coffee & Eats, near the end of 2021. "When we first started, we thought 30 tickets was a good day," TJ said. "Now, we're hitting 30 tickets before the first hour and a half through the drive-thru alone. We're probably hitting 130 tickets now." The café in Rayville is a brick-and-mortar, but the couple has two franchise locations, including a food truck that opened in 2025 directly across the street from the construction site in Holly Ridge. They said the Holly Ridge location opened specifically because of Meta. "Holly Ridge does most of the catering. If it's any of the businesses under the umbrella of Meta, I send it to Holly Ridge," TJ said. The wave of construction workers inspired Rodgers and his former business partner, Linda Edwards, to cofound Ice Queen in 2025. The business sells $3 bags of ice to subcontractors and companies working on the Meta project. The parish has weathered several heat waves this summer, making ice a necessity for outdoor trade workers. Since July, residents have seen temperatures reach 100 degrees Fahrenheit more than two dozen times. The pair keeps the ice bags in a large tractor-trailer parked near the construction site and has a separate ice truck available to make deliveries. Ice was only the beginning, though, and soon Ice Queen transformed into a one-stop shop of sorts for the work crews. Coffee machines. Cups. Sugar packets. Fridges. Microwaves. Straws. You name it, Ice Queen tries to supply it. Robert Cleveland, president and CEO of the local economic development authority, Grow NELA, said the economic growth happening in Richland Parish is undeniable. Data collected by Grow NELA shows that Richland Parish's annual sales tax revenue jumped from $21 million in 2024 to $39 million in 2025. At the end of 2026, Grow NELA expects the parish will see $92 million in annual sales tax revenue. Richland Parish has gained more annual sales tax revenue in 2025 alone than in the last 20 years combined, Grow NELA says. "We have a number of small businesses that have propped up and have grown significantly because of the project," Cleveland said. Part of the business growth in Richland Parish is supplying construction workers with what they need while they are away from home: lodging, food, and basic necessities. Angel and Bryan Crawford, for example, chose to address the housing market gap with their rental company, Parish Line Properties. The couple owns a mobile home park called Antley Pines that opened in 2025. "We added two homes last December, four this May, and our last four in July. All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. A fully-furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom mobile home that's eight miles from the construction site costs an average of $3,000. The couple previously worked in the nursing field, but decided to dive into real estate and property management after becoming empty nesters. "In 2024, we started buying older houses that had been on the market for a long time or needed a lot of work. We had a vision to create a mobile home park and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center," Angel said. The company now owns 18 rental properties, 14 of which the owners have set aside as workforce housing. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," she said. Those long days can be taxing, making places like HeBrews Coffee & Eats popular with workers. Shelbie Stephenson, owner of the Holly Ridge location, said they deliver 450 lunch plates to the Meta work site twice a month. Stephenson said they also do breakfast and coffee catering several times a month. "We have done 900 burritos and 2,500 cups of coffee during safety week," she said. Stephenson said the crews tend to order breakfast burritos, muffins, and scones in the morning. For lunch, they typically purchase pulled pork nachos, steak bites with peppers over rice, chicken bits over rice, or a sandwich. Holy Tacos also fulfills lunch catering orders for workers on Meta's project, in addition to serving at its brick-and-mortar location. "We've been out to the man camps, which are the temporary housing for construction workers, took our mobile setup, and cooked for them," Allen said. He said the crews will order from catering from Holy Tacos between one and four times a month. "Catering costs anywhere from $4,000 to $7,000, depending on the size," Allen said. "We have a good local following, but when you add the catering, probably 40% of our monthly business is directly related to Meta." Staying hydrated is also a must in northeast Louisiana, where a series of heatwaves blanketed the region this summer. "Pallets of water are where we make most of our money because it's a safety issue out here. The heat and all that," Rodgers, the owner of Ice Queen, said. "I buy truckloads of water and deliver probably 30 to 40 pallets of water a week to these guys." Ice Queen sells a pallet of water for about $600. Liquid I.V., an electrolyte drink that helps with hydration, costs just over a $1 per pouch and is another notable product. "The Liquid I.V.'s were one of the most important products because the guys would get so dehydrated," Edwards, a real estate agent with John Rea Realty, said. "They had never, ever encountered the humidity and the heat. It probably got up to 110 degrees out there." In June, a study commissioned by Grow NELA said that consumer spending and capital investments made during the data center's construction period will generate $162.9 million in sales tax revenues at the local and state levels. While Meta has temporarily transformed Richland Parish into a modern-day boomtown, most of the construction workers will eventually move on to other jobs, taking their spending with them. It's a reality that business owners in Richland Parish know is on the horizon. Allen said Holy Tacos would likely continue catering for other businesses in the area and selling out of their restaurant. TJ and Kaycie said HeBrews Coffee & Eats will lean on the clientele it built before Meta arrived. The Crawfords said they are considering either selling the properties or continuing to rent them after construction ends. Ice Queen has diversified and plans to rely on other large-scale clients in the area. Louisiana Economic Development said Meta is expected to work on the Richland Parish site through 2030. What happens after that is anyone's guess. For now, though, there's money to be made. No comments right now, check back later. Comments are unavailable right now. Jump to

Home > Law and Politics >                          The Entertainment Software Association has asked the U.S. Government to label the Denuvo cracker ‘voices38’ as a notorious piracy market. The game industry group argues that the cracker is an essential source in the game piracy ecosystem, feeding repackers and torrent sites. A notorious market flag is no guarantee of success, however, as FitGirl's previous listings show.          Every year, the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) asks rightsholders to nominate the foreign piracy sites and services they see as the biggest threats. The resulting list of ‘notorious markets‘ traditionally features torrent sites, cyberlockers and streaming portals. In recent years, hosting companies and other intermediaries were added as well. Last week, the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which represents many of the major video game companies, submitted its latest recommendations. These include the usual suspects, but also a target that doesn’t have a website of its own. ESA’s submission lists ‘voices38’ as one of its new threats. The game industry group describes the anonymous cracker as a persistent operation that specializes in beating Denuvo Anti-Tamper, the popular technical protection measure that’s used by at least nine of its members. Voices38 According to ESA, Reddit’s r/CrackWatch index attributes roughly two dozen cracked or bypassed games to ‘voices38’. The gaming group stresses that the cracker plays a key role in the piracy ecosystem as its releases are picked up by repackers, torrent sites, cyberlockers and piracy forums. “Each crack therefore unlocks an entire downstream market for an unauthorized copy of that title. For a title that no other actor has made usable, but for Voices38’s crack there would be no functioning pirated copy for those markets to offer,” the submission notes. “Treating only those downstream services as markets would overlook the upstream operation that determines whether protected games can be offered by them at all.” The fact that the cracker has no public identity or “traditional homepage” shouldn’t stand in the way of a Notorious Markets listing either, ESA notes. In fact, it argues that a listing could help rightsholders crack down on the cracking operation. “Designation would focus attention on identifying the operator, preserving evidence, disrupting distribution accounts and donation channels, and coordinating action across the forums, repositories, hosting services, peer-to-peer infrastructure, and other intermediaries used to seed each release,” ESA writes. ESA’s recommendation     Ideally, ESA would like to identify the person or people behind the popular cracker handle and it’s not alone in this. Identifying the operator is also what Denuvo is trying to do through a U.S. federal court.  Last month, Denuvo sued ‘voices38’ at a California federal court and it recently asked for permission to subpoena Discord, Valve and Reddit. ESA’s submission doesn’t mention this lawsuit. So far, this hasn’t stopped the cracks from coming out. After a few quiet weeks, ‘voices38’ released cracks for Atomfall and The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales last week, as well as a crackfix for Dead Space Remake. Atomfall-voices38     These releases swiftly spread over torrent sites and cyberlockers. Popular repacker FitGirl has already picked them up too, which brings us to ESA’s next target. After already being included in USTR’s 2024 and 2025 notorious markets lists, FitGirl gets a recommendation from ESA for the next installment.  FitGirl’s site is currently blocked in Germany, Italy, Spain and elsewhere, but ESA notes that these measures didn’t change much. The repack site received 41.77 million visits in August and continues to offer games published by ESA members. “FitGirl’s scale and persistence demonstrate that prior blocking and designation have not induced meaningful remediation by its operator. ESA’s takedown notices to the site are ignored, with zero links removed between August 2025 and August 2026,” ESA writes. The game companies also put a billion-dollar price tag on the losses, which they report down to the last cent. “Between March and August 2026 alone, ESA detected 15,484,145 users in peer-to-peer swarms for games repacked by FitGirl, with an estimated lost value of $1,083,735,308.55,” the submission notes. A footnote explains that this figure is based on a retail price of $69.99 for every user ESA spotted in a swarm. Hypothetical Losses     Other targets are not very responsive either. DODI-Repacks removed 22% of the reported links and RuTracker, the Russian torrent site, complied with just 3% of ESA’s notices over the past year. While these sites are not responding, ESA highlights that tracking their finances, including crypto transactions that go to KYC-vetted platforms such as Binance, could help to identify these targets.  This year, the USTR’s review has a special focus on high-quality counterfeit goods, known as superfakes. ESA uses this opportunity to highlight handheld consoles that come preloaded with pirated games, which it sees as the video game equivalent of superfakes. The group nominates Anbernic.com, the official store for a widely sold line of handheld emulation devices. ESA says these are routinely offered or shipped with memory cards that hold hundreds or thousands of unauthorized games, and notes that they are sold through Amazon and eBay as well. The submission further lists G2A, FunPay and Eldorado.gg, where game accounts and in-game items are traded, as well as cheat sellers including Cronus Zen. ESA argues that cheats belong on a piracy list because they circumvent the technological protection measures of games. It’s now up to the USTR to decide which of these recommendations make the final list. The previous edition was published in March, so we might have to wait a while before the final Notorious Markets list arrives. — A copy of ESA’s submission for the 2026 Notorious Markets review is available here (pdf). Asian makers of AI hardware gain most, Kristalina Georgieva said, while warning AI will reshape 40% of jobs. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at Wall Street Journal House during Climate Week NYC, September 2025. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday that spending on AI infrastructure is helping the world economy grow by about 3% each year, even though energy prices are high. She made these comments in Bangkok at the start of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, according to Reuters. According to Georgieva, Asian economies that produce AI hardware, like Thailand, benefit the most. She estimated that advanced Asian economies could see growth increase by 0.5 to 1 percentage point, while emerging Asian economies might gain 0.2 to 0.8 points. The scale of that trade is large. In a speech in Singapore last week, Georgieva said AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than a tenth of global trade in goods. Apart from the US, China, and India, most leading countries in this trade are Asian suppliers of chips, chip-making equipment, and robots. This demand is rising as major tech companies plan to spend between $660 billion and $690 billion on AI this year. In its July outlook, the IMF said that AI demand is boosting tech-exporting countries, while conflicts are affecting energy importers. The IMF also predicted 3% growth for 2026. Georgieva also cautioned about the impact of AI on jobs. She described AI as a “slow-moving tsunami” that will transform jobs, education, and how governments collect taxes. According to the Fund, AI will eventually affect about four out of ten jobs worldwide, improving some and making others worse or unnecessary. Georgieva said, as reported by CNBC, that richer countries are most exposed, with about 60% of jobs affected, compared to 23% in the poorest countries. Young people entering the job market face the first hit, Georgieva said, because the routine roles they usually start in are disappearing. Singapore’s President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking on the same panel, said, “The first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand.” Tharman also warned that if governments do not act, AI could increase the gap in growth and jobs between wealthy and developing countries. Ajay Banga, the head of the World Bank, said the bank is supporting small AI tools that do not rely on large language models. These tools are designed to help farmers, health systems, and teachers in emerging markets. The IMF has also pointed out risks from the AI boom. In June, Georgieva warned that Mythos-class AI models could be used to attack the financial system. The Fund will release its updated growth forecasts on Tuesday.                                        Alina Maria Stan builds connections that people actually feel. It’s one of the great mysteries of computing, how somehow in the Year Of OLlama 2026, tape remains the god of cheap storage. A while back [Ben Pettis] recounted his experience setting up an LTO-5 tape drive in his homelab, an experience which only becomes more relevant as hard drive prices stay high. LTO-5 is already well out of date in the professional world, after all– a new server install would be debating the merits of LTO-9 versus LTO-10, but for the homelab it’s a matter of what’s affordable on the used market with decently-sized cartridges. If you can live with 1.5 TB of uncompressed data on a roughly palm-sized Linear Tape, Open cartridge then LTO-5 could be good enough. Yes, the tapes are advertized as 3TB, but that’s assuming a 2:1 compression ratio on the data, which you’re not likely to get on the photos and video that make up much of a data horder’s storage. That’s one thing [Ben] was quick to clear up for us. He also detailed his adventures with the cheaper-to-buy fiber channel model of drive. Tape drives usually come with an SAS or fiber channel interface– fiber channel being, you guessed it, an optical solution unlike the SCSI-like SAS connection you may be familiar with for block storage devices. With a PCIe adapter it’s not hard to set up, provided you get the cables the right way around! That’s another detail we’re glad [Ben] shared so we can find it again if we have the same problem: with no switch in the circuit, you need a crossover cable to bring TX to RX. Which is obvious in retrospect, but obscure to those of us just learning about the standard. The advantage, as [Ben] makes clear and everyone has always known is simply price. As of this writing, diskprices.com has 16$/TB as the lowest cost, while [Ben] was able to pick up lightly-used tapes on eBay for only 2$/TB. If you have a lot of data, those savings amortize the drive costs relatively quickly, since a used drive like [Ben]’s can be had for a few hundred bucks. Is it the ultimate solution for our data storage woes? That depends on your needs, but perhaps not considering we get as many tips on storing data on reel-to-reel as we do on LTO. Disney's new tech chief said in a memo to employees that he "won't pretend it will be easy" to win in the changing media environment. Karandeep Anand, the Mouse House's first-ever companywide CTO, was hired by CEO Josh D'Amaro to lead Disney's tech transformation. He started in early October. Under D'Amaro, Disney is investing in tech to better compete with Netflix and YouTube in streaming. Anand previously ran Character.AI, an AI startup that Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter to last fall. (Disney told Character.AI not to make chatbots from its copyrighted characters without permission, and the startup complied.) Anand told staffers on Friday afternoon that the media business is "at an inflection point," adding that he's confident Disney has a strong hand thanks to its deep, iconic content library and a passionate fan base. "With our rich IP and global fan community, I strongly believe we are uniquely positioned to win," Anand said in his memo, which was obtained by Business Insider. The new tech chief said that winning in this highly competitive media landscape "will take focus, speed, and the willingness to say no to good ideas so we can say yes to great ones." Anand also said he's "admired Disney for as long as I can remember" and said he had constructive conversations in his first full week inside the Mouse House. "What stands out most is the talent and care this team puts into its work, the craft Disney has perfected, and the strong foundation you've built," Anand said. Disney has leaned into tech this year by embracing AI and further unifying Disney+ and Hulu — the first step in building a streaming super app that includes games and merchandise. Beijing will also cut tariffs on some EU goods and ease rare earth licensing. EU leaders must still approve the curb on hybrid car exports, which Šefčovič called only a first step. China has agreed to moderate its exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars to the EU, which EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said could cut them by more than half. He announced it on Friday in press remarks in Beijing, after the second round of EU-China trade and investment consultations. “It is unsustainable and it demands a credible path to rebalancing,” Šefčovič said of the EU’s trade deficit with China. He called the results three “shared understandings”. China will also cut its tariffs on some EU goods, including car parts, olive oil and footwear. Those exports are worth almost €4bn, and the cuts would save at least €225m in duties. China will further ease export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, Šefčovič said. The Commission has not published a written agreement. Its statement gives no volumes, timeframe or mechanism for the cut in car exports. Šefčovič also spoke to reporters in Beijing, the Associated Press reported. “By this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union,” Šefčovič said. AP described the cut as covering electric and plug-in hybrid imports. The Commission’s statement names only hybrids and plug-in hybrids. The consultations began at a meeting with China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, in Brussels on 29 June. In Beijing, Šefčovič also met Vice Premier He Lifeng. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will assess the results and discuss next steps with EU leaders at the upcoming European Council. The final decision lies with the leaders, Šefčovič said, and he called the results “only a first step”. Where talks cannot deliver, the EU will use its tools to force a rebalancing, he said. Officials will meet again by January, and a third round of consultations is planned for March. Šefčovič has pushed for a new tool to cut Europe’s dependence on Chinese supply chains. In September he said he would ask CEOs how much decoupling they can afford. Wang expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures, China’s Commerce Ministry said. He said China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them, AP reported. China has also pushed the EU to stop blocking its imports of advanced chipmaking machines, AP reported. The EU imposed those limits on national security grounds at Washington’s request. Sigrid de Vries, head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, said the deal appears to avert further instability. “It can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way,” de Vries said. China’s trade surplus with the EU reached €360bn last year, according to AP. In Europe, hybrids are outselling every other powertrain. By Liz Shackleton  pmc-media-editor-2024  	Five independent producer organizations from Korea, Indonesia, Philippines, Hong Kong and Taiwan launched a coalition, the Asian Producers Alliance (APA), at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).  	The five bodies include the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK), Indonesian Film Producers Association (APROFI), Philippine Independent Producers Group (PIPG), Hong Kong Movie Production Executives Association (HKMPEA) and the Taiwan Producers Association (TPA).  	In the initial stages, the alliance aims to support regional and international co-production and protect creators’ intellectual property, while evolving into a consensus body with a formal decision-making structure. For years, we have faced the same changes alone – in our own markets, in our own languages. Today we choose to face them together. We will advance co-production across Asia, so that our stories can be made together and travel further.”     			Watch on Deadline		       	The alliance was launched at the close of a seminar entitled ‘Empowering Asian Cinema: Solidarity and Creative Alliance’, hosted by PGK at the ACFM Producers Hub.  	Moderated by Han Jin, Director of PGK’s International Committee, the panel brought together producers Yulia Evina Bhara (Indonesia’s KawanKawan Media), Rhee Handae (CEO of Korea’s Sidus) and Shin Yamaguchi (Japan’s Knockonwood) to discuss the state of their industries and the possibilities of co-production in an environment reshaped by streaming platforms and short-form content.  	APA’s inaugural team includes PGK President Lee Dong-ha and APROFI Chairman Edwin Nazir as Co-Representatives, with Han Jin and Yulia Evina Bhara as Co-Sectretary Generals. The Representatives and Secretary Generals willserve one-year terms and are elected each year at the General Assembly held during ACFM.  	           	PGK President Lee Dong-ha said: “Asian producers have faced the same challenges separately, market by market. Starting today, we face them together. APA is not a declaration – it is a practice of solidarity that begins now.”  	APROFI Chairman Edwin Nazir said: “APA gives Asian producers a foundation to connect and collaborate. Stronger together, we reach further.”  	PIPG Founder Member Bianca Balbuena said: “In a time where divisiveness has dominance, the creation of APA signals a safe space for producers in Asia where we cultivate harmony and collaboration in the film industry, and where collective resources, expertise and vision are shared in solidarity.”  	HKMPEA Chairman Johnny Wang said: “In the past, we as producers were accustomed to following the paths paved by our predecessors. Now, with the birth of the APA, we are embarking on an entirely new and unprecedented journey. We believe that in today’s globalized context, international co-productions will bring powerful synergies to every APA member.”  	TPA Chairperson Yating Chang said: “It is truly our honor to participate in APA. We are really looking forward to connecting with other producers’ associations around Asia.”  	APA will hold regular online meetings every quarter, with a General Assembly convening each year during ACFM in Busan. The alliance is welcoming other producers bodies across the region to join and stress that membership is not limited to one organization per territory.
