I considered pulling out the soldering iron to implement a fix that would speed up the Flash memory storage, but I feared that I might accidentally ruin the board. I expected that PINE64 would issue an new version of the PinePhone that would fix the problems, but instead PINE64 dismissed the screen flicker as a problem and hasn’t changed the eMMC’s voltage from 3.3 to 1.8 volts, which would have increased its sequential read speed from 55 to 125 MB/s. I was also annoyed that PINE64 provided no way to communicate with its hardware developers, so I wasn’t able to get errors fixed that I found in the PinePhone schematics. Unlike the Pinephone which I rarely used, I kept using the Librem 5, because its better CPU and memory performance made its interface much more responsive than the PinePhone. Nonetheless, the Librem 5’s screen and aluminum frame got hot, since Purism used thermal paste to join the i.MX 8M Quad to the LCD’s backplate to dissipate the processor’s heat through the screen and aluminum frame. I often felt like I was walking around with a heater in my pocket. The battery drained fast, so I was constantly having to charge the Librem 5. Eventually the Purism developers got the Librem 5’s camera to work, and I tried out each new version of the Millipixels app. It was fun playing with the camera and I learned a lot about how cameras work trying to adjust the settings to get a good photo. However, the Librem 5 took a long time to process each photo in software after taking a picture, since its i.MX 8M Quad processor lacked an image signal processor and hardware encoder in the VPU. It also took me way too long fiddling with the Millipixels’ settings for me to rely on the camera. Whenever I wanted to make sure that I would get a decent photo, I pulled out my Xiaomi Redmi Note 7 running LineageOS to take the photo. Eventually it was possible to shoot video on the Librem 5 at a low resolution and frame rate, but it took so long to process the video and the quality was so limited, that I never bothered using it. In the end, the PinePhone sat most of the time in a drawer in my desk, and the Librem 5 sat charging on my desk. They were good entertainment for the geek in me, but I didn’t use either of them as my primary phone. Many of the early adopters appear to have had similar experiences with their Linux phones. It was hard to justify buying another Linux phone, when there was already one sitting unused in the drawer. Many people were unwilling to take a chance on another Linux phone after witnessing how the community developers abandoned PINE64 in 2022, and software development stalled for the PinePhone Pro and how Purism refused to refund cancelled orders for the Librem 5. When FuriLabs announced its upcoming FLX1 in June 2024, it solved many of the problems with the Librem 5 and PinePhone. It contained a 6nm MediaTek Dimensity 900, which was powerful enough shoot video and run 3D games with Vulkan. It offers three hardware privacy switches and multi-booting to run multiple operating systems on the phone. The phone’s software was developed by Bardia Moshiri, who is the lead developer of Droidian, which runs Phosh in a Debian-based distro on top of Halium with an Android kernel. It was based on well-supported projects and software which had already been developed, so its costs would be low, but it had an experienced developer to provide software support. In other words, it would avoid the high costs that troubled the Librem 5 and the lack of software support that bedeviled the PinePhone Pro. People report that the FLX1 and its following FLX1s and FLX1s+ variants work well, but the Linux phone is not well-known and appears to have gotten a limited number of orders. The company’s forum has been frozen and there has been limited activity on the Droidian forum, indicating that the phone has gained little traction in the Linux community. Revision 1.1 of the Divine D. circuit board arrived on Aug 10, 2026. In January 2025, Liberux, a startup based in Madrid, Spain, announced its upcoming NEXX Linux phone based on the RK3588S with specs to make nerds salivate: 4×2.4GHz Cortex-A76, 4x Cortex-A55, Mali-G610 MP4 GPU, 32GB LPDDR4X RAM, 256GB eMMC, 5G modem and 3 hardware kill switches. In June 2025, Liberux started the crowdfunding for the phone, and a couple days later announced a modular and open architecture that would allow the RAM board with an FPC connector to be upgraded up to 32GB, the eMMC board with a standard socket to be upgraded up to 512GB, and the cellular modem with a custom adapter board to be replaced/upgraded. The price varied between €790 and €1310, depending on the selected configuration. In addition, the NEXX would have two USB-C 3.1 ports to facilitate the phone being used a convergent desktop PC and an AW8737SCSR amplifier and a 3.5mm audio jack for better analog audio. The NEXX was a revolutionary design, promising to be the first phone in history with two USB ports and the first one with the RAM and eMMC on separate boards, so it could be upgraded and connected like a normal PC. Liberux was attempting to offer the first truly convergent smartphone that had the right software and hardware to replace a desktop PC, yet it hardly generated any headlines in the tech press. It only got 120 pre-orders in a month, which generated a tenth of the $1.7 million in crowdfunding that it needed. When its crowdfunding campaign failed, Liberux reported that it was negotiating with investors for raise the funds to build a prototype. However, its last post on the company’s Mastadon account was in November 2025 about “moving forward with new self-funding.” After 11 months of silence, it is looking increasingly doubtful that the NEXX will ever come to market. There is more hope for the Dawndrums Divine D. phone, which is being produced by a startup in Tunisia. The startup has continued to make slow progress according to its Mastodon posts. They are now on the second revision of their main board and have produced a breakout board for debugging it. They are developing their own distro known as DawnOS, which is based on Mobian and planning to support both the Phosh and Plasma Mobile interfaces. They are asking for donations, but appear to be largely self funded at this point. Like the NEXX, the Divine D. also promises to be an outstanding convergent phone, supporting up to 32GB RAM and offering a separate HDMI port for video out. It also offers a LoRa (long-range radio) chip, and a pogo pin interface to add accessories to the phone. While the failed crowdfunding of the Liberux NEXX and the limited sales of the FuriLabs FLX1 would suggest that there isn’t much hope for Linux phones, it is important to keep in mind that these phones were poorly advertised and produced by unknown startups that had no prior track record, so people were reluctant to order them. Bitter experience with the Librem 5 refunds, the failures of the PinePhone Pro, and all the cancelled Linux mobile devices over the years, such as the Ubuntu Edge in 2013, the Firefox OS phones in 2015, the Jolla Tablet in 2015 and the Necunos NC_1 in 2019, has taught Linux enthusiasts to be cautious about crowdfunding mobile devices. However, there are reasons to believe that there is quite a bit of pent-up demand for mobile Linux, and it only requires the right kind of promotion and a company with a credible track record to unlock it. Ironically, the company demonstrating that people still want to use Linux phones is tiny Jolla, which has somehow managed to survive over the years. The Finnish engineers who used to work on Nokia’s MeeGo founded their own company named Jolla Oy in 2011 to keep developing that code as Sailfish OS. They took the FOSS parts of MeeGo and added their proprietary Silica interface based on Qt QML, which imitates the Swipe UI that Nokia had developed for MeeGo on the N900/N9. They also licensed the proprietary Alien Dalvik from Myriad Group to run Android apps inside Linux, and now markets it as AppSupport, which has been updated to run more recent versions of AOSP in an LXC container. Jolla deserves credit for developing libhybris and helping to maintain much of the code developed by Nokia, including the oFono telephony library and the Maliit virtual keyboard. Remarkably, the small Finnish company managed to survive nearly going bankrupt in late 2015, when it cancelled its crowdfunded Jolla Tablet, and was only able to return half of the money to the customers who pre-ordered the tablet. After killing off the original company in 2024, because it was majority owned by Russian investors, who were politically toxic due to the war in Ukraine, Jolla reemerged under a new company named JollaBoys that bought the old company’s assets from Jolla Oy. The new Jolla company has returned to the business of selling hardware. Jolla announced its Jolla C2 Community Phone in May 2024, and started delivering them four months later, which helped reestablish the credibility of the company. When Jolla started taking preorders for its new Jolla Phone on December 5, 2025, it sold out its crowdfunding goal of 2000 phones within the first 48 hours and 5000 phones within the first week. People were pre-ordering the Jolla Phone without having seen any reviews of the phone and not even knowing what processor it would contain. The phone, which initially cost $499 and now costs was €679, was marketed as containing 12GB RAM, 256GB storage, a user-replaceable battery and a physical privacy switch. Jolla’s advertising for the phone clearly struck a chord with European consumers, which proclaimed it to be a “Do It Together (DIT) Linux phone, shaped by the people who use it.” The Finnish company emphasized the independence of the phone from the rest of the mobile phone industry, stating on the order page: “The Jolla Phone is not based on Big Tech technology. It is governed by European privacy thinking and a community-led model.” Jolla has sold 15,000 units of its phone as of August 2026 just by taking pre-orders for production batches from its web site, and it probably could have sold far more units if it had paid for advertising, expanded beyond the European market, and kept the phone in stock, so customers didn’t have to wait months for the next production batch. Clearly, there is an untapped market of people who are dissatisfied with the reigning Android/iOS duopoly. Today the use of Linux is growing on the desktop. Many people are installing Linux on their PCs, because they have become disgusted by how Microsoft has turned Windows into an advertising platform for surveillance capitalism and a vehicle for AI slop. Rather than buying new PCs, a growing number of people have decided to install Linux, because support for Windows 10 has ended and they can’t upgrade their old PCs to Windows 11 due to Microsoft’s arbitrary TPM restrictions. Likewise, many people are equally disenchanted with Android and iOS on their phones. More people have grown distrustful of the surveillance capitalism which undergirds the Android market and the restrictions and rising prices of Apple’s “walled garden” on the iPhone, yet the options to escape the smartphone duopoly keep shrinking. In the past, people who wanted to gain some control over their digital lives could unlock the bootloader on their phone and install an AOSP derivative such as LineageOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS or GrapheneOS, however the mobile phone industry is increasingly shutting off this escape valve. Every year there are fewer Android phone models on the market which allow the bootloader to be unlocked. The rise of Chinese brands, which now control roughly 60% of the global smartphone market, has driven many of the traditional phones brands out of the market which did allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Many of the phone brands that were mod-friendly, such as LG, BQ, LeEco, WileyFox, Essential and Razer, are now gone from the market, and other mod-friendly brands like Sony and HTC now have so few sales that they are no longer relevant in the global smartphone market. Huawei stopped allowing its bootloaders to be unlocked in 2018. In the last couple years, Samsung, ASUS and Realme all followed Huawei’s bad example and no longer allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Xiaomi, which rose to fame as a mod-friendly brand, has recently implemented so many restrictions to obtain its unlock codes, that it is unlikely that modders will bother porting custom ROMs to future Xiaomi models. As noted in my article on LineageOS statistics, the brands which have good policies for bootloader unlocking has shrunk from 42.5% to about 7% of the global smartphone market over the last couple years. The brands which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked (without major restrictions like Xiaomi) only sold about 87 million phones in 2025, including Lenovo/Motorola (60M), Google (12M), OnePlus (11.6M), Nothing (2M), GigaSet (>1M), Sony (400k), Fairphone (145k), SHIFT (10k), Teracube, Volla and Brax. Together those brands only represent 7% of the 1245.5 million total smartphones sold in 2025. However, that is an overestimate, since most phone models never get good custom ROMs made for them. A good portion of Motorola and Google phones are sold through carriers, and many carriers like Verizon don’t allow their phones to ever be unlocked, even if they are no longer under contract. MediaTek Dimensity and UNISOC Tiger processors have gained market share in recent years, and those chipmakers don’t publish the source code for their kernels like Qualcomm does for its Snapdragon processors. A few brands that use MediaTek SoC’s, such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Volla, Gigaset, TeraCube and Brax, do publish their kernel code, but that code for many other MediaTek phones will never get published, nor will custom ROMs be made for them. UNISOC processors are basically black boxes for the modding community. The bootloaders of all phones with Apple A-series, Huawei Kirin and recent Samsung Exynos processors are locked, so the modding community is restricted to just Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and some MediaTek Dimensity processors. Motorola and Xiaomi have switched most of their budget model lines from Snapdragon to MediaTek Dimensity processors, so they are harder to mod. Aside from the Motorola Moto G05, which was released in Jan 2025 and replaced 8 months later by the G06, there has not been a single budget phone released by a major phone maker in 2025 or 2026 that has gained official support by LineageOS. Gaining official LineageOS support is important, because many of the other custom ROMs are based on LineageOS and only port to its officially supported models. Just looking at phone models with official LineageOS support which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked, only about 20 million or 2% of smarphones sold each year are good for installing custom ROMs. The situation is about to get much worse. Sadly, Oppo just announced that it will pull its OnePlus brand from the North American and European markets. OnePlus phones will still be sold in India and China (where the bootloader can be unlocked if the user presents an official Chinese ID card), but OnePlus is essentially gone for the modding community. Nothing, which was a rising star in the modding world, has been losing sales. The London-based company denies rumors that it will pull out of a third of the countries where it currently sells phones, but confirms that it plans to cut 100 jobs, which comprise 12% of its workforce. At any rate, none of the phones which Nothing has released in the last two years have gained official LineageOS support.Samsung has been making it more and more difficult to mod its phones over the last decade, so the Korean company’s decision to lock the bootloader for all its phones getting its ONE UI 8 interface wasn’t a surprise, but Xiaomi’s decision to start restricting its bootloader unlock codes was a major blow for the modding community. The only major global brand left for modding is Motorola, but there are only unofficial ports available for recent Motorola models, meaning that some things don’t work correctly or security patches aren’t being provided. Motorola promises to launch phones with GrapheneOS in 2027, but they will be flagship models which probably cost over $1000 and be limited to a few select countries. Aside from the Motorola Moto G15 (released in December 2024), people are unlikely to find a new phone where they can install an official LineageOS port for sale in Africa, most of Latin America (except Mexico) and most of Asia (except India, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia). The only option to run a custom ROM in most of the world is to buy a used Motorola or Xiaomi phone from a couple years ago, such as the Moto G (2024), Moto G32, Moto G34, Moto G84, POCO F5, POCO F5 Pro, POCO F6 Pro or Redmi Note 13 Pro. There are more recent phones like the Moto Edge 70, which have unofficial LineageOS ports, but it is a gamble if they will ever be officially supported by LineageOS. As Google has pushed phone makers to support their phones for longer, many companies have decided to collect more personal data from their users for better targeted advertising and for training artificial intelligences. The smartphone industry is moving away from a business model based on planned obsolescence toward one based on surveillance capitalism, and the phone makers don’t want their users to opt out of the system, so they have removed the option to unlock the bootloader and made it harder to gain root access. That way they can recoup the cost of providing more years of support for their phones by monetizing their users’ data. In addition, Google has made it harder to maintain custom ROMs, because it has moved more and more functionality from AOSP into its proprietary libraries and services (starting with Android 4.1 in 2012), and largely abandoned the development of many of the free/open source apps in AOSP in favor of its proprietary apps. Starting with AOSP 16 in 2025, Google stopped including the device trees and driver binaries for Pixel devices in AOSP, so ROM developers no longer had target devices, where they could easily test out and adapt the latest versions of AOSP on running hardware. Now custom ROM developers have to do painful trial and error to make the device trees for Pixel phones just like all the other phone brands. Google also squashed the kernel’s commit history, which makes it very difficult for ROMs like GrapheneOS to create their own custom kernels, because they can’t easily take new features, bug fixes and security patches from Google’s kernels. Given how the smartphone industry is locking down their hardware and pushing business models that are inimical to users’ privacy, there is increased opportunity for Linux phones to be marketed to people who want to escape the Android/iOS duopoly and surveillance capitalism. In the past, it was much harder to bring a Linux phone to market, but now there are three viable types of Linux phones that can be brought to market, and all of them have better prospects than in the past. The first type is the pure Linux phone which runs a Linux kernel, like the Librem 5, Liberty, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. These phones previously didn’t have the processing power to offer the functionality that people expect in a smartphone. They often lacked components such image signal processors, audio digital signal processors, hardware video encoders, Vulkan graphics, neural processors and encryption engines, or they lacked the FOSS drivers to support those components. The RK3588S and the upcoming RK3668, however, will give pure Linux phones the processing power to be viable alternatives to Android and iOS phones for the first time. The pure Linux phone is the riskiest type because it requires the most investment in engineering the hardware. Companies can’t just modify a reference phone design from Qualcomm or MediaTek or call up a phone ODM and ask them to modify one of their existing designs. They have to work with a design house or ODM that has some experience with radio frequencies to custom design a phone with 2 to 3 times more components than a standard smartphone. This means many iterations of the circuit board to get it right, and some kernel work to use all those different chips. It will take a long time to get to market, which can lead to customer complaints and reputational loss if using crowdfunding to finance the dev work. The benefit of the pure Linux approach is that it allows for true hardware kill switches that cut the current to separate components, rather than the use of pins on an integrated mobile SoC or software to turn off the WiFi/Bluetooth, cellular modem and GPS/GNSS. The second benefit is the ability to select components that have free/open source drivers, which allows for greater software freedom and more transparency to address security and privacy concerns. The use of proprietary blobs in the drivers often prevents the kernel from being upgraded because the blobs are often only compatible with a specific kernel version number, which allows the chipmakers to dictate the lifespan of devices. Another benefit of not using a reference design from an SoC maker or an ODM is the phone maker has full control over the design and can publish the schematics and board views for the circuit boards, so the hardware is as free as the software. In the past, Qualcomm didn’t produce powerful Internet of Things processors with Linux support, but now it is possible to build a good Linux phone based on an Internet of Things processor, like the QCM6490 or QCM8850 with an integrated cellular modem. These Dragonwing processors are not as up-to-date as the latest Snapdragon processors, but most of them receive 10 years or 15 years of software support, and many of them will eventually get partial support in mainline Linux, so they can live on with community support after they are no longer supported by Qualcomm. The third kind of Linux phone is built on an integrated mobile SoC, which runs a standard Linux stack on top of an Android kernel using libhybris to translate glib calls to Android’s Bionic. This used to not be a good option because Android SoC’s were not supported long enough for the long development cycles and lower annual sales of Linux phones, but now it is possible for the high-end processors that are getting 8 years of software support from Qualcomm and MediaTek. This approach is the most economical way to bring a Linux phone to market, since many phone ODMs already have reference models available and are willing to work with phone sellers to tweak those models to their specifications. It is not impossible to work with an ODM to add privacy switches to a design, as FuriLabs demonstrated with its FLX1, but it takes longer to get a custom design to market, so it is important to select an SoC that gets 7 or 8 years of software support, so the phone will enjoy a reasonable lifespan. It is no longer necessary for Linux phone companies to expend huge amounts of capital in developing mobile Linux, because there are now three good mobile interfaces—Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri—which offer a reasonably complete complement of applications, so hardware companies don’t need to risk bankruptcy developing the software like before. Because Phosh and now Plasma Mobile are based on a well-supported desktop stack and convergent applications, they will require much less work to maintain and it is easier and less costly to keep providing software updates for the phone. Companies offering Linux phones will still need to hire developers to work on things like power management and camera support, but they don’t have to bet the farm like Purism did with the Librem 5 or provide no software support as PINE64 did with the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. This reduction in software development costs, however, probably won’t result in more economical Linux phones. The shorter software support for the QMC4490 and the mid-range and low range Snapdragon and Dimensity processors rules out the making of an economical Linux phone. It is possible to make an upper mid-range Linux phone based on a Snapdragon 7 or Dimensity 8000 series processor, but it won’t support video out via DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, so it can’t be used as a convergent PC, which is a major selling point for Linux phones. Given that the QMC6490 does support DisplayPort Alt Mode, it is probably the best option for making an upper mid-range phone. Companies like Jolla, FuriLabs, Volla and Brax may choose to continue making mid-range Linux phones, but they will likely suffer from the same problem as the FLX1 and C2, where the Android kernel is unsupported and no longer getting security updates, so it is better to move up to a more expensive SoC that gets 8 years of support. Ideally, these companies will stop using MediaTek processors, and select Snapdragon processors that get partially supported in mainline Linux, so people can run a distro like Nura on them after they are no longer supported. Now that the available SoC’s and software are no longer holding back the making of compelling Linux phones, the real barrier to creating a viable Linux phone market are the companies to make and sell those phones. There aren’t many companies with the experience and passion to make Linux phones, which historically have lost money. PINE64 recently announced that it is pausing production of most of its devices due to the high prices of RAM and eMMC. Essentially PINE64 is admitting that it can’t raise the price of many of its products, because they don’t have the needed software support, so many people won’t pay elevated prices for them. It appears unlikely at this point that PINE64 will change its business model to pay for software developers to work on the kernels for its hardware, nor is it repairing its relationship with the distributions and volunteer developers who have abandoned the company, so it is unlikely to ever produce the rumored PinePhone 2 using the RK3566. In theory another community-based Linux hardware company could arise, that charges a bit more so it has the necessary funds to pay developers to work on the kernel support for the hardware, but it appears highly unlikely that another community-based hardware company like PINE64 will appear. In contrast, Purism is clearly planning to produce a second version of its phone. In its July 2026 newsletter, Purism stated that it “is in the early stages of planning the Librem 5 v2 and Liberty 5 v2.” It is preparing a “crowdfunding campaign in the coming months” to “gauge customer interest and traction, which will help fund the production of our second version.” The problem is that Purism’s public reputation has been stained by its refusal to refund the Librem 5 backers who cancelled their orders. Refunding the 600 customers who are still waiting for their Librem 5 refunds would do a lot to restore the company’s public reputation, and it would cost the company less than $400k. Without taking that step, it seems unlikely that Purism will be able to crowdfund the “over $2 million” that it projects will be needed to produce its next Linux phone. Maybe Purism can charge a lesser amount (such as $99) to pre-order the phone, and then use those numbers to raise capital privately to develop the phone. At any rate, the time and cost of producing the Librem 5 v2 will be much less than the first version of the phone, because Phosh and its applications have already been developed and the mainline Linux driver support for the RK3588S is already in a good state due to the last four years of work by Collabora. Hopefully, Purism will either provide funding or developers to help Collabora get the ISP and hardware video encoding working. The challenge for Purism is that it also needs to finance the development of its next generation of Librem 14 notebook, Librem 11 tablet and Librem Mini. The Librem 11 and Mini are rebadged ODM designs, so they don’t require as much work, but the Librem 14 is a custom design, which requires quite a bit more work and financing to create. In addition, Purism reported in its July newsletter that it has been pre-approved to get over $50 million in funding from the CHIPS Act to develop a Librem Core-V processor based on the RISC-V architecture, which will be a huge undertaking for the tiny company which doesn’t have any prior experience in chip design. Presumably, Purism will have to raise some matching funds to get the government funding for its chip project. In other words, many projects will be competing for Purism’s attention in the future, and the Librem 5 v2 could be neglected and postponed in favor of other products. Presumably Dawndrums will launch a crowdfunding campaign once it has a working prototype of its RK3588S-based phone to show to the public, but the company based in Tunis has been very tight lipped about its future plans to bring the phone to market. There has been no news from FuriLabs about a new phone model to follow the FLX1s+. The implementation of Ubuntu Touch on the BraX3 phone has been stalled for months, and it appears that Brax Technologies is depending on the UBports community to finish the porting work. Volla Phone continues to offer Ubuntu Touch as an alternative operating system on its phones, but the German company’s primary focus is on developing its own Volla OS, which is an AOSP derivative oriented toward privacy. Jolla is making the right moves to create a viable Linux phone market. The Finnish company says that it plans to move to mass production of its Jolla Phone, so the phone will be in stock, and to offer the phone to the North American market. However, many in the Linux community will be reluctant to embrace Jolla’s phones, because of the proprietary software in its Silica interface and its AppSupport (aka AlienDalvik) to run Android apps. People who believe in free and open source software won’t want to buy a phone from a company that has been violating the GPL 2.0 license by not published the kernel code for its Jolla C2 and Jolla Phone. In addition, these phones use UNISOC and MediaTek processors that don’t have any mainline Linux support, and they will probably have short lifespans, since their kernel are unlikely to ever be upgraded. A critical factor in the success of Linux phones is publicizing the phones to attract the niche customers who care about Linux, software freedom, privacy or security. Liberux appears to have failed because it did such a poor job of publicizing its future NEXX phone and didn’t attract enough crowdfunding. FuriLabs similarly has done a very poor job of publicizing its phone, so that most Linux enthusiasts have never heard of the phone. Likewise, Dawndrums has done a very poor job of publicizing it development work on a future RK3588S phone. In contrast, Jolla has very effectively used social media to market its Jolla Phone to European customers. There are several dozen companies that sell Linux PCs, which could potentially expand into the Linux phone market. Most of those companies, however, don’t have experience in the design of custom hardware. Most of them use standard notebook designs from one of the ODM’s that make specialty notebooks such as Clevo or Tongfang. Most of these companies also don’t have much experience doing kernel work, so they are probably better off just using a standard Android design provided by a phone ODM and installing Linux on top of Halium, so they can use a well-tested Android kernel and drivers. There are also a number of companies that make Linux single board computers (SBC’s), who could potentially jump into the Linux phone market. They have more experience in working with Chinese and Taiwanese companies to design and produce custom hardware. They are better equipped to undertake the engineering challenges of entering the Linux phone market, but most of them do a poor job of engaging the community. Many companies which sell Linux SBC’s don’t have public forums for their customers and do a poor job of using social media and online advertising to promote their products. Public opinion surveys show that people are increasingly aware that they are losing their privacy online. Ipsos polls found that 79% of global respondants and 84% of American respondants express worry about their online privacy. A Malwarebytes survey found that 89% of consumers are concerned regarding corporate and AI data misuse. 62% of Americans in a YouGov poll report worrying about how much personal data third parties have about them online. If Linux phones can be created that provide the same functionality and ease of use as Android or iOS phones, they could tap into that huge potential market of consumers who wish to preserve their privacy online. In order to appeal to mainstream users, Linux phones will need to support the usage of Android apps through Waydroid or a similar solution. In the same way that Murena and iodé sell AOSP phones which block third party trackers, Linux phones need to incorporate similar software. The conditions may be ripe for Linux phones, but it is unclear whether the companies selling Linux phones will take advantage of those conditions to create a viable alternative to the current Android/iOS duopoly. For the sake of software freedom, online privacy and the greater longevity of mobile devices, a concerted push is needed to promote mobile Linux. Whether it's eating gelato under the Mediterranean sun or exploring a medieval city, North Americans can't get enough of summer trips to Europe. Business Insider analyzed data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, to create four charts that show how Eurosummer is on the rise — and which destinations are the trendiest. We looked at the number of seats on flights from North America to Europe. Unlike just measuring the number of flights, this also accounts for the airplanes' capacity. Airlines scheduled 69% more seats in July 2026 than in July 2010. Meanwhile, the number of flights went up 59%, from roughly 15,700 to 24,900. As the data is based on flight schedules rather than border crossings, it does not necessarily reflect tourists' final destinations. Even so, passenger demand still informs where airlines send their fleets and launch new routes. Cirium's data also show that airlines are adding more seats in summer than in winter. In 2026, there were 77% more seats from North America to Europe in July than in January. In 2010, there was a 50% gap between those months. However, there is also some country-level data showing that the summer travel season is getting longer, as more people choose to fly later in the year. Spanish government statistics show that 57% more Americans arrived in the country in October 2025 than in October 2019. Overall arrivals during the summer months of 2019 and 2025 increased by a quarter. The UK has long been the most popular transatlantic market — its 15 million annual seats are nearly double those of France and Germany — due to strong business links and airline partnerships that make it a useful hub connecting to destinations elsewhere in Europe. To find where more North Americans are flocking, we focused on changes in flight capacity between the years ending in July 2023 and July 2026. This also helps minimize the fluctuation in recovery times from the pandemic. That expansion has not been spread evenly across Europe. Only four countries saw fewer seats across the period. There are no longer any flights to Ukraine due to the war. Norway and Sweden both saw their seats drop by more than half, and Belgium dipped by 3%. Three countries saw over 1 million seats added in that time. Unsurprisingly, they are already Europe's most popular for tourists: Italy, Spain, and France. However, percentage growth shows that the fastest-growing markets are not all traditional hot spots. We excluded destinations with fewer than 10,000 scheduled seats in the year ending July 2023, so that small base numbers wouldn't skew the results relative to busier destinations. It is clear that tourists are besotted with Italy. Airlines added more seats there than to any other European country, and it ranked fourth for proportional increase — up 52%. Czechia and Croatia stand out as the only two countries where airlines are sending at least double the capacity they had in the year ending July 2023. Over the past year, airlines have relaunched routes to Prague, known for its striking medieval Gothic architecture. Croatia also offers a dose of historic attractions plus a host of beaches on the Adriatic Sea. While the UK as a whole saw only a 4% increase in the number of seats, capacity on flights to Scotland increased by 70%. As well as the Highlands' mountainous vistas, Edinburgh attracts visitors from across the world for its performing-arts festival in August. Ireland also continues to rise in popularity. Dublin and Shannon are the only European airports where you can cross the American border before taking off for the US. Denmark is propping up travel to Scandinavia, thanks to fashionable Copenhagen and new flights to Billund, home of Lego. The picture gets more specific when you zoom into the airport level. We excluded airports that weren't served pre-pandemic or had fewer than 10,000 seats in the year ending July 2023. Flights to Naples, Italy, now have room for more than five times as many passengers as in the year ending July 2023. In the past few years, United Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and Air Canada have all launched new routes to the home of pizza and the gateway to the picturesque Amalfi Coast. Dubrovnik, a coastal Croatian city known for its medieval walls, found fame in the 2010s as a filming location for "Game of Thrones," but it has continued to soar in popularity. While flights to France as a whole saw only a 16% increase in capacity, three French airports made the top 10. Portugal is also proving popular, with two cities on the list. Last summer, United launched flights from Newark to Faro, the capital of Portugal's seaside Algarve region. In last week's Xbox Town Hall with the team, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma warned that the division will "not survive" if it relies entirely on existing game franchises. Xbox has been "restructuring" over the past summer, which has seen thousands of job losses via cuts and divestitures, and has left Xbox fans wondering what the aftermath will ultimately look like. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has made no secret of her intent for content moving forward: Microsoft will double down on its biggest and most visible Xbox franchises, including the likes of Fallout, Call of Duty, Candy Crush, World of Warcraft, among others. Some of Xbox's more eclectic studios, such as Ninja Theory, Double Fine, and Compulsion have either been spun off as separate, or outright shut down. These studios were all working on new franchises generally speaking, and while they didn't become financial success stories, the creativity was often award-winning. Sharma's comments about Xbox's biggest franchises have left many wondering if there'd still be space for creativity and newness at Xbox, and it seems the answer is "yes," complete with a warning on over-relying on existing franchises.      "On content, I think this is probably the thing that you are all seeing the most about as we're making a lot of changes," Sharma said at the Xbox Town Hall this past week, in wholly unauthorized transcripts shared to Windows Central via multiple trusted sources. Sharma reiterated the plan to focus on the biggest Xbox franchises, but also noted that relying on past victories won't help Xbox win the future. "We're backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences."  Sharma remarked upon opportunities to grow King and the casual gaming segment in general, where titles like Monopoly Go and Block Blast have eaten into Candy Crush's casual gaming market share in recent years. Asha Sharma also talked about simplifying their studios, reiterating decisions to move some IP, like Halo and Sea of Thieves under Activision, hinting that more "simplification" could be on the way ... what that "simplification" might look like remains to be seen.      Xbox has been aggressively exploring ways to drive down costs in general this year. The opportunity within Xbox's ecosystem has diminished as hardware stock levels collapse, owing to the RAMpocalypse. Xbox's disastrous multi-platform strategy of yesteryear saw the platform lose relevancy while boosting competitors, leading to declines for major third-party games like FIFA, Fortnite, and NBA 2K titles on Xbox Series X|S as well. Moving back to exclusive games has given Xbox a boost, with users returning to the platform for titles like Gears of War: E-Day and Forza Horizon 6, but growing Xbox again will probably take a multi-year, multi-game, multi-franchise effort, coupled with some sort of miracle on the hardware side. Xbox Series X|S and console hardware in general has moved wholly to being a luxury purchase, putting pressure on Xbox's chances. In an interview with Windows Central at the start of the year, Chief Content Officer Matt Booty remarked that "everything big once started as something small," in reference to investing in new IP, which has always resonated with me. Indeed, Microsoft has partnered up with Hideo Kojima of Metal Gear fame for PHYSINT, complete with movie and TV rights in development with Xbox's new XP entertainment licensing division. It'll be interesting to see if Sharma's Xbox does more in this space ... even if Xbox has made stark, quite devastating cuts within its existing teams. AI is muddying the water and blowing up component costs. There are more games than ever, and for many, less free time and money than ever. Micro-spend in service games continue eating up all the spend and users, and finding new cohorts seems more difficult than ever ... On my 36th birthday, I crossed the border from Uganda into Rwanda, commemorating my 100th country visited as a solo traveler. It was a gift — literally — to have this happen on my birthday, but also a huge feat for me. I took my first solo trip when I was a 25-year-old bartender in New York City. Since then, I've been all over — from popular tourist destinations to off-the-beaten-path destinations like rural Madagascar and tiny islands like Jeju and Nevis — documenting my ventures on my blog, No Man Nomad, along the way. After being privileged enough to see so many corners of the world, I can say with confidence that destinations are simply better suited for new solo travelers. If I had to start this wild, wacky journey all over again, here are five destinations I'd consider for a first-time solo trip. My first international trip was to Thailand, and though I've made my fair share of travel mistakes, this was, undoubtedly, the right choice. In my opinion, Thailand is one of the best solo-travel destinations. Ten years after my initial visit — where I visited my first Southeast Asian night market, met people in hostels who accompanied me to pubs and drag shows, and ate a crab curry that still lives in my head rent-free — I went back to Thailand, and can confirm that it's still true. What makes Thailand stand out is that there's really something for everyone. Bangkok has some of the world's best street food, but you'll also have no problem finding Michelin-starred meals. Backpacker culture is abundant, with plenty of hostels to choose from, but five-star hotels are easy to find, too. If islands are more your speed, try Koh Samui or Koh Phi Phi, which offer serene landscapes with world-class diving along white sandy coasts. If your goal is to truly get away from it all, might I suggest a New Zealand road trip? As a New Yorker who seldom finds herself behind a wheel, my time driving through New Zealand was as much of a reward as it was a challenge. By the end of my week cruising through the South Island, I — a city girl through and through — felt a deep appreciation for van life. New Zealand is exceptionally beautiful and peaceful. Hiking spots like Roys Peak offer views that beat out even the prettiest of postcards. Lakes like Pukaki are so blue you'd think they have a filter on them. Also, despite being alone and sleeping in a van each night, I never felt bothered or unsafe. There's a reason everyone who has been to New Zealand swears it's the prettiest place on the planet — after over 100 countries, I still believe that to be true. One of the biggest myths about travel is that you have to wait for a romantic partner to visit honeymoon destinations. Let me debunk that for you and encourage you to visit Italy, party of one. I highly recommend romanticizing your life on a gondola ride in Venice, where, yes, people will likely stare at you for being alone, but this won't stop you from having a great time. (Take it from someone who's done this twice.) If you're hungry to meet people, a food tour through Rome's Trastevere neighborhood is a delicious way to meet others, and a winery tour in the Tuscan countryside is just as fun. I've been to Italy more than anywhere else in the world, and it's a destination I continue to return to as a solo traveler. Just because I've been solo traveling for a decade doesn't mean there's not plenty left for me to explore, as proven by my recent trip to Uzbekistan. Before I started traveling, I probably couldn't have pointed to Uzbekistan on a map, but now, I'd recommend it to any and all solo travelers. One of the biggest pros was that, while traveling alone, I rarely felt like I was on my own. From walking tours to dining at local restaurants, I connected with other women traveling solo. The country as a whole, but specifically Samarkand, felt calm and peaceful — and also rich in culture and Silk Road history. I had a great time in Tashkent visiting historic landmarks like Chorsu Bazaar and Hotel Uzbekistan, and found it easy to get around on public transit. One of the most nuanced questions I'm asked about solo travel is, "Is that safe?" Safety is subjective, so what's a safe experience for me might be entirely different for someone else. That being said, a lot of stats indicate that Iceland is widely considered a safe place to travel. It was even ranked the most peaceful country in the 2026 Global Peace Index, based on criteria like ongoing conflicts, societal safety and security, and militarization. While there, I took a day trip out of Reykjavik to see the "Golden Circle," and almost everyone else on my tour was a solo female traveler. In Reykjavik, I noticed a plethora of queer spaces, including the National Museum of Iceland, home to "A Rainbow Thread," a guide to the country's queer history. It doesn't hurt that Iceland is a geographically stunning destination. Here, you can see geysers, active volcanoes, waterfalls, and — depending on when you visit — the northern lights. The only con about a solo trip to Iceland is that, as safe as it is, I found it equally expensive, with even shared hostel dorms generally starting around $50 a night. Every small business starts with a dream.   Whether it’s expanding into a new market, hiring a first employee or turning a side hustle into a lasting business, growth is what motivates entrepreneurs to take risks and build something of their own. But dreams only grow when the day-to-day works, when customers trust the business, operations run smoothly and unexpected setbacks don’t derail progress.   That’s why cybersecurity is no longer just an IT issue. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), cybersecurity is now fundamental to building trust, serving customers and growing with confidence.  As SMEs become more digital, they gain new opportunities to scale, streamline operations and serve customers more effectively. But digital transformation can be a double-edged sword: As impactful as it is, it also invites new forms of risk. Increasingly, understanding cyber risk is becoming just as important as understanding cash flow, customer acquisition or inventory management.  The most successful businesses won’t simply be the ones that respond effectively when an attack occurs. They’ll be the ones that build resilience into the way they operate from the beginning.  Small businesses today rely on digital tools at nearly every stage of their operations. They use cloud-based software to manage workflows, digital channels to acquire customers, online payment systems to facilitate transactions and connected platforms to collaborate with suppliers and partners.  This shift has created tremendous opportunities. Business owners can reach new customers, automate routine tasks and make more informed decisions than ever before.  But increased connectivity also means increased exposure.  For many entrepreneurs, a cyber incident can have consequences that extend far beyond the initial attack. A breach can disrupt operations, prevent a business from accepting payments, compromise customer information, delay order fulfillment or interrupt payroll. Trust that may have taken years to build can be damaged in a matter of hours.  The impact can be especially severe for smaller organizations that often lack dedicated security teams or specialized expertise.  Mastercard’s Global SME Cybersecurity Landscape research found that 46% of SMEs say their current business has experienced a cyberattack. Even more concerning, nearly one in five business owners whose companies experienced an attack reported subsequently filing for bankruptcy (18%) or closing their business (17%).  These statistics underscore an important reality: Cybersecurity is no longer solely about protecting systems. It is about protecting a business’s ability to operate, grow and earn customer trust.  One of the clearest findings from Mastercard’s Dreamonomics research, based on a survey of more than 6,600 SMEs across 18 markets, is that entrepreneurs are redefining what growth means. Increasingly, business owners are prioritizing stability, predictability and long-term sustainability alongside expansion. The most successful businesses are pursuing what could be described as controlled momentum: growth that is resilient and built to last.   In that environment, cybersecurity is becoming less about defense alone and more about enabling confidence.  That same research found that 71% of small businesses prioritize protection from cyber threats, yet only 37% currently use cybersecurity tools.   That gap is revealing.  Business owners recognize cybersecurity as important, but many still struggle to find solutions that are accessible, practical and relevant to the realities of running a small business.  The signal is clear: Entrepreneurs increasingly want smarter, simpler ways to understand and manage cyber risk without becoming cybersecurity experts themselves.  In many ways, cybersecurity is following the same trajectory as other business functions. Owners don’t necessarily want more technology to manage. They want solutions that reduce complexity and help them make better decisions with confidence.  Historically, many businesses have approached cybersecurity only after something goes wrong.  An attack occurs. A breach is discovered. Systems go down. Then the work of recovery begins. But recovery is often more expensive, disruptive and time-consuming than prevention.  As cyber threats become more sophisticated, the conversation is increasingly shifting from “How do we recover?” to “How do we identify risks before they become problems?”  This is a fundamentally different mindset.  Instead of treating cybersecurity as a response plan, businesses are beginning to view it as an ongoing capability that supports operational resilience and long-term growth.  The goal is not to eliminate every risk. No business can do that. The goal is to understand where vulnerabilities exist, prioritize the issues that matter most and take practical steps to address them before they become costly disruptions.  One of the biggest opportunities facing the industry today is making cybersecurity easier for small businesses to understand and act upon.  Many entrepreneurs don’t have the resources to employ dedicated cybersecurity teams. They need guidance that is practical, actionable and integrated into tools they already use every day.  This is where a growing number of financial institutions and technology providers are beginning to play a larger role. Rather than treating cybersecurity as a standalone service, providers are increasingly embedding protection directly into the products and experiences business owners already rely on.  That’s exactly why Mastercard integrated MyCyberRisk — a proactive risk assessment tool that enables businesses to pinpoint, prioritize and act on cybersecurity threats — into The Mastercard Collection for Business. Designed around the evolving needs of modern entrepreneurs, The Mastercard Collection for Business brings together growth resources, premium experiences and cybersecurity support in a single, connected offering.   It was designed to reflect a simple reality: Business owners shouldn’t have to choose between pursuing growth and protecting what they’ve built. When security is accessible and integrated into the tools they already use, entrepreneurs can address risks earlier and move forward with greater confidence.  Every small business starts with a dream. But dreams need more than ambition to succeed.  They need resilience. They need trust. They need the confidence that comes from knowing the business can withstand unexpected challenges and continue moving forward.   Cybersecurity has become an essential part of that foundation.  For SMEs, the most important first steps often include understanding where the business is exposed, prioritizing vulnerabilities that could create the greatest operational impact and building protection into existing workflows wherever possible.  When business owners understand where they are vulnerable and have access to tools that help them proactively address risk, security becomes more than protection. It becomes an enabler of innovation. It helps organizations adopt new technologies with greater confidence, serve customers more effectively and scale without introducing unnecessary risk.  Small businesses shouldn’t need cybersecurity teams to understand where they are vulnerable. The next step for the industry is to make cyber protection simpler, more accessible and more deeply integrated into the services entrepreneurs already use to run their businesses.  Because ultimately, the businesses best positioned for what’s next won’t simply be the ones that respond to cyber threats. They’ll be the ones that build trust, resilience and security into the way they grow, protecting what they’ve built while creating the confidence to pursue what comes next.  Every small business starts with a dream.   Whether it’s expanding into a new market, hiring a first employee or turning a side hustle into a lasting business, growth is what motivates entrepreneurs to take risks and build something of their own. But dreams only grow when the day-to-day works, when customers trust the business, operations run smoothly and unexpected setbacks don’t derail progress.   That’s why cybersecurity is no longer just an IT issue. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), cybersecurity is now fundamental to building trust, serving customers and growing with confidence.   We'll be in your inbox every morning Monday-Saturday with all the day’s top business news, inspiring stories, best advice and exclusive reporting from Entrepreneur.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition? Alexandra Rutkay, a makeup artist  on film and television sets, has a parent-friendly side hustle.  Copied to clipboard This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Alexandra Rutkay, 43, a New York City-based makeup artist who works on film and television sets. Currently, she is Mariska Hargitay’s personal makeup artist for Law & Order: SVU. Rutkay also runs a side hustle out of her apartment: citymouse, which sells a minimalist crossbody diaper bag for parents. Her side hustle, launched in 2022, hit seven figures within a couple of years — and even surpassed $50,000 in three days over one weekend. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.  When did you start your side hustle, and where did you find the inspiration for it?I launched citymouse at the end of 2022 out of our New York City apartment, and 2023 was our first real year. The night I realized the brand needed to exist was when my husband, son and I were heading to dinner post-pandemic. I reached for a cute small bag and realized I couldn’t fit my son’s sippy cup, diapers, baby wipes and a few of my things inside. I couldn’t find a diaper bag geared toward those in-between years where you don’t need everything but still need some things. Especially a transitional bag that a woman would want to grab or wear even if they didn’t have kids. The baby gear industry offers what I call “single-serve items” because so many of them never get touched again after a few months. I really wanted to change that. What were some of the first steps you took to get your side hustle off the ground? How much money did it take to launch?I invested about $8,500 from my own savings to start the side hustle. I began with a rough sketch of a crossbody-style bag that could hold a drink inside and keep everything organized. Then I sent it to a supplier I found on Alibaba, got a sample made and once that arrived, jumped right on Tiktok (which I had been avoiding until that moment), and it changed everything. Women were very interested, and I launched on preorder, which helped to fund some of the initial run. We are still fully bootstrapped.  Are there any free or paid resources that have been especially helpful for you in starting and running this business?Social media was a must, not an option. I also hired a publicist who worked with my budget right off the bat to help build credibility. I utilize the app Intro, which is an incredible resource — essentially paying for advice and mentorship of established entrepreneurs. Through that, I found out about Newbook, which I’ve used over and over again for models who I can hire within my budget as well. If you could go back in your business journey and change one process or approach, what would it be, and how do you wish you’d done it differently?I’d have set up systems for inventory and order fulfillment before we went viral, not during. When orders spiked, we were scrambling and packing out of our living room and counting stock by hand. We’ve sold out more times than I can count, and every time we do, we have to go back onto preorder, which kills the momentum.  When it comes to this specific business, what is something you’ve found particularly challenging and/or surprising that people who get into this type of work should be prepared for, but likely aren’t?How fast you get copied. We kicked off the small diaper bag trend in 2022, and now Target has essentially duped us, as well as random Amazon dropshippers. Both large and small brands saw the trend we started and made their own knockoffs. If your product works, assume someone will copy it within a year. Your brand and your relationship with customers are what they can’t copy, so invest and focus there early. Can you recall a specific instance when something went very wrong — how did you fix it?The first version of our bag isn’t what we sell today. We printed a rubber logo onto the regenerated nylon, and it was a disaster from the start: The logos kept peeling off. Luckily, that didn’t affect how the bag worked, but it taught me that a design choice can look great and still not hold up to everyday use. Sometimes you have to make concessions. Now we stitch the logo onto our Classic bags, and honestly, it looks just as cool. How long did it take you to see consistent monthly revenue? How much did the side hustle earn?Sales became consistent month to month in 2024. Our first full year, 2023, brought in about $135,000. Then TikTok shop took off in spring 2024, and we had our best three months ever — even a weekend where we sold $50,000 in 3 days. Across our website, TikTok Shop and wholesale, we hit seven figures in revenue within the first 18 to 24 months. What does growth and revenue look like now?Tiktok virality isn’t a business model you can bank on, so while the spikes are great, we’ve reached more normal baseline growth. We’ve surpassed $1.7 million in total sales and have over 20,000 customers. My husband left his career to run operations for the business full time, and this year, we launched on both Nordstrom.com and Maisonette.com. We just placed our biggest holiday order yet and are expanding the line with new bag styles. What do you enjoy most about running this business?It’s honestly an incredible creative outlet for me, but connecting with other moms has to be the best part. Hearing how it’s given them more confidence and made them feel good in a delicate postpartum period where nothing feels like you. Running into women on the streets of New York City wearing it is the biggest trip ever. I also love that it’s a business I built with and around my family, and even my 6-year-old is very invested in the brand and products. What is your best piece of specific, actionable business advice?It’s not a sexy answer, but if I’m being real, it gets old scrolling on social, and every other video is a kid in private equity quitting their cushy job to start a brand. I built mine while working more than 50 hours a week from set. It wasn’t “sexy” or easy, but it let me take risks and try things while still paying my bills. Keep your day job, and don’t take investors until you truly need them. My rule is simple: Don’t scale before you can afford to, and if something isn’t necessary, don’t buy it. It might be slower, but we’ve never answered to anyone, and every decision is still mine. Bootstrapping isn’t the fallback plan. It’s a power move. With the state of the job market these days, many realize it's close to impossible to find a job with their current qualifications. Think about it: how is it that every junior role out there demands 5 years of experience? How are people expected to find jobs when the demands keep getting harder and harder to reach? It has become standard practice to lie or polish your resume to fit whatever impossible qualifications hiring managers demand. However, if you decide to try it yourself, know that it isn't without risks. First, some lies are easy to verify, especially when it comes to past experience or education. There are enough workplaces out there that are willing to do the background check in order to ensure they aren't being lied to, and if someone gets caught in this lie, well, the conversation that follows is not something I would ever want to be a part of. Second, even if you aren't caught, when you choose to lie on your resume and then get a job because of that lie, you will then need to keep lying for your entire employment. If the lie is about a couple of months you added to your previous job, there's nothing to really worry about, but anything more than that will feel like a huge burden to carry. At the end of the day, is it really worth it? Lastly, the job candidate in the story below proves that not getting a job can be a better outcome than getting one and then having to admit you lied in the hiring process. Coming clean is never easy, and in this case, it could seriously damage the candidate's career.  Woman with a resume in hand sitting on a chair. Model portrayal. A job interview. Stock photo unrelated. The only thing I usually polish in my resume is the little gaps I might have during job search periods. Hiring managers hate to see those, even if there is a reasonable explanation, so I simply extended my time at one company to make it seem like the move to the next job was seamless. It's a little white lie that is almost impossible to catch.  I wouldn't dare to lie about a whole job or higher education, because those are so easy to verify. Not only that, but if I get accepted to a job after lying about something so big in my past, I would never feel at ease there. It doesn't seem worth it, and this story proves my case. Getting caught in a lie is never fun. Losing a job offer after getting caught in a lie on your resume is so much worse…  Here's to hoping this new hire will manage to hold on to the job, and that they are not completely blacklisted from the company. Did this story convince you to update your resume and delete everything that isn't the complete truth, or do you still think there are some white lies you can get away with during a hiring process? I am definitely taking this case as a lesson to be as honest as I can the next time I look for a job. Want More? Follow Us and Add Us as a Preferred Source on Google.

At 5 a.m. in Northern Virginia, chefs are already preparing chicken and chile roja enchiladas, fried shrimp tacos, and big batches of rice and beans to feed thousands of data center construction workers. By late morning, a crew brings the food from the off-site kitchen to a break tent where workers can pick up lunch without leaving the worksite. They don't pay: The Big Tech companies spending billions on AI infrastructure foot the bill. On an average day, National Jobsite Catering serves about 1,500 meals at each of its dozen data center construction sites across Northern Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Nevada, and Georgia, founder Scott Kaplan tells me. The busiest sites serve twice as many. After one to three years, the crews wrap up and move on. Kaplan, whose business used to consist of a fleet of food trucks catering one-off events along the East Coast, designed a venture that can follow them. If you build it, they will cook. National Jobsite Catering is part of the economic ecosystem being generated by America's data center boom. The tech giants leading the AI buildout are expected to spend more than $5 trillion on technology and data centers through 2030, with more than 1,500 data centers already in the works in the US. The room where a worker sleeps, the gym he hits before his shift, his parking spot, his lunch — these are all provided by a growing network of businesses. Local firms in the suburban and rural areas where the bulk of data centers are being built can get a windfall from a single project, but a more lasting proposition is the opportunity to serve site-to-site as construction crews move around. Whether that translates into lasting benefits for host towns is at the heart of growing pushback against the wave of data centers popping up across the country. Kaplan recognized the new opportunity a few years ago when a hyperscaler hired him to bring trucks to a site outside Philadelphia to feed 2,500 workers. "Literally the town that it was in had one restaurant — and it was in a strip club," he says. To avoid a lunch-hour bottleneck, Kaplan proposed preparing meals in a temporary kitchen and bringing them to the site. After replicating this model for other projects, his company now has 20 full-time employees and partners with established local vendors, helping them add equipment and plan production. He estimates a project can employ about 15 local people in kitchen, delivery, and distribution roles. "They know what they're doing," Kaplan says of the local partners. "But they've never cooked for 1,000 to 3,000 people." Since pivoting to data centers exclusively four years ago, revenue has gone up 10X, Kaplan says. Before thousands of construction workers can arrive on-site, they need somewhere to leave their cars — a logistical challenge that's creating a new market. WhereiPark began as a marketplace for city parking spots, but its fastest-growing business now comes from leasing lots near data center construction sites. General contractors have asked WhereiPark to find as many as 2,000 spaces for a project. A church lot used mainly on Sundays might work, as might a struggling shopping center or a nearby fairground or casino. In more remote locations, a contractor may need to grade and stripe land. Local landowners, meanwhile, earn temporary income from unused space without selling the farm. "If there's nowhere for the construction workers to park, the thing doesn't get built," says Joshua Eisen, WhereiPark's chief revenue officer. A team in Toronto does much of the search via property data, calls, and emails; a partner or the general contractor then inspects a prospective lot locally. The company also partners with shuttle operators to ferry workers between the lots and construction sites. For a builder juggling several projects, that means one contact and billing relationship instead of a new search and lease negotiation in every town. A completed facility the size of a Walmart might have just 50 spaces, so most lots return to their previous use. WhereiPark can repeat the search around another project without owning land. With global AI investment expected to exceed a trillion dollars in 2026 alone, companies of all sizes are getting in on the gold rush. Food services and facilities management giant Aramark launched a new division called Nexus earlier this year, which offers hotel-like amenities, fitness centers, and recreation to help attract skilled workers. The company noted that Nexus contracts carry higher-than-average profit margins. Executives projected that three initial data center sites could each generate Aramark about $150 million in annualized revenue once fully running. The data center housing business has a precedent in the oil patch, where companies have long followed temporary crews from project to project. Target Hospitality, a $1.8 billion company that has housed oilfield workers and operated two Texas detention centers for ICE, is building and operating accommodations for data center construction crews, including a $550 million deal for a 4,000-bed facility in North Texas. The company advertises furnished bedrooms equipped with small fridges and microwaves, as well as communal dining, gyms, and WiFi. Its modular assets can be redeployed elsewhere. In August, the company said it has secured contracts representing more than 9,000 beds and $1.4 billion since January. Facing growing opposition, hyperscalers have pitched the AI buildout as an engine of economic development, promising spillover benefits for local areas. Microsoft's "community-first" promise cited its experience in Washington state to estimate that for every direct construction job created, another is generated in sectors including security, maintenance, retail, and food service. While spillovers certainly occur, the exact level varies project to project. To capitalize on that before-and-after job creation, Salute sells data center clients security, safety oversight, and technical support during construction and facility management after it opens. The company, which has worked exclusively with data centers since its founding in 2013, brings in experienced staff to get sites running while recruiting and training locally. It tends to employ veterans and oil and gas workers accustomed to remote job sites, and hopes those who relocate will put down roots. While engineers move to the next project, guards, cleaners, and some technical workers can remain. After all, for a security guard, the job doesn't change much. "It's still the same perimeter. It still has the same fence line," CEO Erich Sanchack says. For local businesses, the work can be unpredictable. In Louisiana, a couple spent more than $40,000 on a food truck to serve workers building Meta's Hyperion data center, Fortune reported. Orders fell from more than 100 a day to fewer than 40 after a contractor brought in an out-of-state caterer. Business later picked up again after a local journalist covered their plight, and Meta gave them a catering job. Now they're serving about 80 orders a day, owner Katie Stewart told me. They went through a boom, a bust, and a recovery before construction was even over. Mark Muro, a senior fellow at Brookings Metro who has studied data centers' local economic impact, found that the drop in activity after construction can be steep — jobs can climb into the thousands during construction and fall to the low hundreds once the facilities open. But for small towns and rural areas, even those remaining jobs "should be acknowledged as a contribution," he says. "It is genuine economic activity." How long that activity lasts depends in part on the deal a town strikes with data center builders. Negotiations can include how much work goes to locals, tax revenue collected, and whether the developer helps meet demands on housing, roads, and other public services. Due in part to blowback against data centers, towns have more leverage than they realize, Muro says. They should ask for the infrastructure, training, or jobs they need, he adds, "If they need a $400,000 fire truck or whatever, ask for it."
