Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year. In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines. Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed. With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.  On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year. Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold. The cattle market tanked immediately. "So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry." "It just felt like a betrayal," she said. Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain. That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.  Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race. Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months. The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.  And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive. Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle. "All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas. Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing. Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own. The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry. But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning. "Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head. Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day. "It really makes a guy think," he said. A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left. But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market. "People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said. Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall. "The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit." Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago. But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said. He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House. Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.  But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate. That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago. Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper. He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.  That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry. "Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News. An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy". Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical". But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt. "We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it." But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction". Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things". But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed. "Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste." Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions. "I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said. Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture." Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said. Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later. But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter. "It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in. He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers. "I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'" Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state. "They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore." All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.  On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction. Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - do not pause for politics. Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude. "People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it." Who said all privacy protections had to be digital nowadays? In my line of work, traveling can be common, and working from a coffee shop, train, or hotel lounge is something I do on the regular. So when I came across this nifty privacy app that knows to blur your screen the second you look away, I was enthralled.  The app is called ShyGlass, and it comes from developer Max Rovensky, who posted a 10-second demo on X last month that has since racked up over 230,000 views. The way it works is pretty simple. While wearing a pair of AirPods, if you turn your head to a certain degree, your MacBook screen blurs. When you turn your head back, the screen unblurs itself. Behind the scenes, it’s using the motion sensors Apple uses for dynamic head tracking in Spatial Audio, the feature that keeps your music anchored when you look around. ShyGlass uses the same motion data but to detect presence. A user calibrates a center position from the menu bar, and anytime head positioning drifts past a set angle (15° by default, adjustable from 2° to 30°), a blur fades in over the display until it’s fully covered. Now this is Security Bite after all, so I have a couple of thoughts on the permission the app needs: Screen Recording. ShyGlass does need to pull a snapshot of a user’s display to apply the blur effect, which kind of sounds a little ironic for a privacy tool. According to the developer, the snapshot stays in memory and is never saved or uploaded, and capture stops the moment the blur does. I have no reason to doubt that. But it’s worth bring up the trade here. Screen Recording is one of the most powerful permissions on the Mac. An app with it can see everything you see, all the time, and macOS has no way of enforcing that it only looks when it says it does. So you’re basically taking the developer at his word. Still, I find its functionality useful more often than not. Like turning to chat with the person next to you on a flight, or digging through your bag in a public space. Any time your head leaves the screen, there’s a window where someone else’s eyes can land on whatever you’re working on. I hope to see Apple implement a macOS feature like this one day. But if you want to check out ShyGlass, the developer has it priced at $4. It’s available on macOS 14 or later and requires AirPods 3 or later, any AirPods Pro, or AirPods Max. As 2026 draws to a close, travelers are beginning to map out where they want to go next year. To help jump-start those plans, Lonely Planet in September released its annual "Best in Travel" guide for 2027, highlighting 25 destinations chosen by its global network of writers and contributors. The guide's destination picks span Argentina's mountains, Canada's red-rock beaches, a Caribbean island, and California's ancient redwood forests, among other places. Here are the 25 best travel destinations featured in Lonely Planet's annual list. The Tweed region is in far northeastern New South Wales, between the Gold Coast and Byron Bay. Visitors can enjoy activities such as hiking and biking. Veneto, the northeastern Italian region, is far more than just Venice. It stretches from the Prosecco Hill vineyards to the Dolomites and Lake Garda, offering visitors a bit of everything: historic cities, mountains, lakeside towns, and a top-class food and wine scene. New Mexico offers a range of activities and sights: desert landscapes, mountain towns, ancient sites, and a mix of Native American, Hispanic, and Anglo cultures. Prince Edward Island is Canada’s smallest province. However, it packs in red sandstone cliffs, fishing villages, and a food scene centered on the sea. Fans of "Anne of Green Gables" can also visit the places that inspired author Lucy Maud Montgomery’s novel. Bariloche is a great destination to explore Patagonia’s lakes and mountains. Located within Nahuel Huapi National Park, the city is known for its alpine scenery, outdoor activities, and chocolate shops, giving Bariloche a distinctly European feel. Skanör-Falsterbo is on the Falsterbo Peninsula in southwestern Skåne, dotted with beaches, cottages and beach huts. The two towns have medieval roots and were once important centers for the herring trade, when merchants traveled from across northern Europe to take part in the annual Scania Market. Known as the "Emerald Isle of the Caribbean" for its Irish heritage and lush, mountainous landscape, Montserrat offers black-sand beaches, hiking trails, and a quieter alternative to neighboring islands. The 1995 Soufrière Hills eruption and later ones buried much of the former capital, Plymouth. Visitors can tour the remains of Plymouth and learn about the volcano at the Montserrat Volcano Observatory. Granada, the former capital of Nicaragua, is filled with bright buildings, horse-drawn carriages, and churches, with the yellow Granada Cathedral serving as one of its best-known landmarks and a backdrop to the city. Dunedin and the nearby Waitaki District on New Zealand's South Island offer historic architecture, dramatic coastline, and outdoor escapes. Together, Tsavo East and Tsavo West form Kenya's largest protected area. Travelers can spot elephant herds, zebras, giraffes, and African wild dogs roaming across the two parks. Located in northwestern Spain with easy access to the Camino de Santiago, a trail that stretches across several European countries, León provides visitors with several museums to peruse, including the Castile and León Museum of Contemporary Art. History buffs can also visit the ancient Roman mining site of Las Médulas, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Panama's Bocas del Toro is a series of islands along the Caribbean coast, making for a lively, beach-filled destination for those seeking sunshine and a relaxing vacation. Pack goggles and a snorkel: the water is crystal clear, and a coral reef lies below. Maryland is a historic US state known for Harriet Tubman's Underground Railroad and several other sites on the Network to Freedom. The state also offers a plentiful seafood cuisine, as the Chesapeake blue crab is a highly prized local delicacy. Oman, a country bordering the United Arab Emirates, has a rocky mountain range backdrop and a subtle skyline in Muscat, the country's capital, that pays tribute to Omani and Islamic heritage. Visitors can see canyons and dunes and visit traditional markets and castles across the country. Québec, Canada, looks like it could be another European destination. French is Québec's official language, and most residents speak it. Quebec City, the capital of the province, is lined with cobblestone streets and historic fortress walls. Chengdu, the capital of China's Sichuan province, is the birthplace of the fiery Sichuan cuisine and the home of giant pandas. Okinawa, located in Japan's southernmost prefecture, is a chain of tropical islands with a culture quite different from that of Japan's mainland. The average annual temperature is about 73 degrees, and it is one of the world's few "Blue Zones," a region associated with health and longevity. Da Nang, located in central Vietnam, is a coastal city and one of Vietnam's largest by population.  Visitors can walk across Dragon Bridge, a dragon-shaped steel bridge over the Han River, or visit Golden Bridge in nearby Bà Nà Hills, which appears to be held up by giant hands. A small island in the Maldives, Fulidhoo, can be walked end to end in 30 minutes. Still, Lonely Planet recommends that travelers visit the island as both a getaway and a dive into the local culture. Dessau, now part of the German city of Dessau-Roßlau, became home to the Bauhaus school in 1925.  Visitors can view two UNESCO sites: the Bauhaus structures and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, an 18th-century landscape park system. The city is located about an hour and a half away from Berlin. Morocco's Rabat is a coastal city home to a UNESCO World Heritage site and known for its blend of traditional culture and modernity.  Since it has a Mediterranean climate, the city is easy to visit year-round, and visitors can take in its architecture and tour its numerous historical sites, such as Chellah, which holds remnants of the Roman and Merinid empires. Northern California's coastal redwoods are home to some of the world's tallest trees and offer plenty of outdoor activities, including fishing, kayaking, biking, rafting, backpacking, birding, and more. New Caledonia is a French special collectivity in the South Pacific, with a cultural mix shaped by Indigenous Kanak, French, Asian, and Pacific Islander communities. Crystal-clear waters and coral reefs surround the archipelago, along with turtles, rays, and dolphins, making it a great destination for those seeking a relaxing beach vacation. Gujarat, located on the western coast of India, is home to wild lions and salt flats, as well as elaborately carved mosques and shrines. The state has an archaeological history dating back more than 3,500 years — making it a fantastic place for history lovers. Šibenik is in Croatia's Dalmatia region, on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea. Visitors can take day trips to nearby Krka National Park or boat trips to the Kornati Islands. Desktop speakers usually have a pretty straightforward job and an equally straightforward appearance. That makes sense when all you want is music, but it doesn’t leave much room for personality. Divoom’s Astrotoo takes a different approach, putting a display and oversized physical controls into a speaker that looks like a tiny computer terminal. It definitely gives your desk something playful and personal, and your friends something to be jealous of. The rounded housing and recessed side panels give Astrotoo the appearance of equipment from an imagined future, albeit one with chunky buttons. White, pink, and green finishes offer different levels of restraint. At roughly 4.2 by 4.3 inches across its base, it won’t need the space of a computer, although its upright screen certainly makes it harder to overlook than a conventional speaker. Designer: Divoom         Of course, those buttons aren’t simply there to complete the retro disguise. Three raised mechanical keys, a joystick, and an orange Back button handle music and display functions. You can reach over to control playback without opening another app, though customizing the display still involves your phone. It’s a familiar division of labor, with physical controls for everyday actions and software for the changes. Despite the pixel art theme, Astrotoo doesn’t limit you to blocky characters and low-resolution graphics. Its 3.95-inch IPS display has a 480×480 pixel resolution, accommodating photographs and detailed clock faces as well. That means you can keep a family photo beside your monitor without making room for another frame. Music visualizations are also available, if you’d rather have your speaker put on a show.         The Divoom app lets you change visual content and clock faces, giving the device something to do when the music stops. Weather and stock information bring a more practical side to that small screen. That said, another dashboard isn’t necessarily what a busy desk needs. A favorite picture might be a better companion than financial numbers quietly competing for your attention all afternoon. Divoom positions the 20W speaker for listening nearby, so the desktop proportions aren’t entirely about appearance. Playing music while answering emails or listening to a podcast during a break fits that purpose. Of course, the power rating doesn’t tell us how balanced the sound will be. The styling is easier to judge than the audio, which needs listening rather than a specification sheet.    Bluetooth 6.0 handles wireless audio, while microSD playback lets you bring a collection of stored music along without keeping a phone connected. Wi-Fi supports the connected display features. There’s also a battery, with Divoom claiming up to six hours of operation. That’s enough to move it between rooms for a while, but don’t expect it to stay unplugged through an entire workday. The $199.99 US price makes this a considered desk accessory rather than a casual decoration. Divoom lists approximately 3.5 hours for USB-C charging, so it probably makes sense to leave a cable nearby. You can dress the screen as a futuristic control panel, but there’s nothing futuristic about discovering that your tiny computer needs plugging in before the afternoon playlist. If you own an Nvidia RTX graphics card, you probably use it mostly to play video games. However, GPUs can do more than just render the latest games. Nvidia graphics cards (and, by extension, AMD GPUs) are essential for generating images, and not just the AI kind. These GPUs can even make old pictures and videos look the way you remember them using the same technology they use to improve old video games. Nvidia RTX Video Super Resolution (VSR) is an upscaling technology that combines the power of an RTX's Tensor Cores (the hardware components that enable computer graphics rendering) and AI to improve video quality. Unlike most Nvidia technology, which focuses on video game graphics, Super Resolution applies to any video that passes through the GPU. Whether you're watching a live Twitch stream or a home movie you converted from physical format to digital, VSR upscales it all. Enabling Nvidia RTX VSR is easy. All you need to do is follow these simple steps: Open the Nvidia Control Panel. Select "Adjust video image settings" under "Video." Click the " Super Resolution " box under "RTX Video Enhancement." Use the dropdown menu under "Quality" to choose the enhancement intensity. Click "Apply." That's it. Once active, your GPU will automatically upscale images depending on the "Quality" you chose. You may need to experiment to find the setting that works best for you and your setup. Some people say anything below intensity "4" doesn't provide noticeable (or satisfactory) results, so you might want to start there and work your way down. Since VSR relies heavily on AI, its results are hit-or-miss. While the feature can clean up old videos and images and make them look sharper and more legible, VSR is just as likely to mistake artifacts and noise for real parts of the original image and include them in the final product. VSR then cleans up the blemish, because AIs lack any critical thinking skills and sharpen everything they see. Sometimes, Nvidia RTX VSR just gets information wrong and adds details that go beyond mere artifacting. A finished video could include material textures that never existed in the first place, all because VSR misinterpreted certain aspects of an image. You might only notice these mistakes if you zoom in to any particular frame, so the average viewer probably won't realize VSR got something wrong. And that's assuming VSR actually works, as fast movements in videos receive little to no improvement. While Nvidia RTX VSR can upscale your older videos and make them clearer than ever, it can't work miracles. Your results ultimately depend on the source material and a bit of dumb luck. While Nvidia controls the lion's share of the computer graphics card market, many computer owners have switched from Nvidia to AMD. However, these exchanges aren't seamless, as users lose access to proprietary features such as Deep Learning Super Sampling. Thankfully, AMD adopters don't lose access to video upscaling, just the robustness of Nvidia's version. AMD chips have their own upscaling program known as FidelityFX Super Resolution (FSR). This feature's most obvious application lets users make older games look sharper, but it can also upscale low-resolution images and videos. Unlike VSR, FSR doesn't utilize AI; some AMD upscalers do, but not this one. Setting up FSR requires more work than VSR. Go to AMD's Adrenalin control panel, open the "Gaming" window, go to the "Graphics" tab, and enable "AMD FSR Upscaling" (if your computer doesn't do it automatically). You also need to open "Video playback" in your PC's settings menu and toggle "Process video automatically to enhance it". AMD also has several other image-sharpening technologies that can bring new clarity to fuzzy visuals, but they each have different applications that don't make them as universal as Nvidia RTX VSR.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. When it comes to ANC, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds are considered the gold standard. Featuring a chunky design, added ear fin, and ovoid-shaped nozzle, their passive noise isolation is already good. However, once the ANC is turned on, they cancel out most outside noise, like airplane engines, trains, or a rush-hour commute. Beyond noise cancellation, the earbuds also have a unique sound signature. The bass is punchy, the treble is pronounced, and the Bose app lets you tweak the EQ to your preference. While all of that is good, they have a few downsides as well. For one, the battery is subpar. At six hours of battery life, the QuietComfort Ultra are slightly below the industry standard. If you use the immersive audio mode, that battery life drops even further to four hours of continuous use. Additionally, the wireless charging case costs extra, users complain about occasional connection drops, and the mic is passable at best. Fortunately, the QuietComfort Ultra aren't the only premium earbuds on the market. If you're willing to spend a similar amount or even a little less, you can find a pair of earbuds that provide more value than the Bose. From the Apple AirPods Pro 3 to the Sony WF-1000XM6, each product wins in specific categories, while having a few trade-offs. Before you spend your money on a new pair of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, here are a few options to consider instead. Building on the success of the WF-1000XM5, the WF-1000XM6 are the latest flagship earbuds from Sony, priced at $329.99. Featuring high-end ANC, Sony's premium sound signature, and immersive app controls, they truly rival the QuietComfort Ultra. Similar to the Bose, the WF-1000XM6 cancel out noise across all frequencies. This means that most outside noise, like traffic and conversations, is filtered out. If you're a frequent traveler, the Sony WF-1000XM6 are effective at canceling out airplane or train engine rumbles as well. In terms of sound, the Sony earbuds have an edge over the Bose QuietComfort Ultra. The lows are deep and warm, the highs are energetic, and the vocal clarity is detailed. Sound, as a result, is more complete and nuanced. They also have support for higher-fidelity audio via LDAC. However, that feature only favors Android users, as iPhones are not compatible with the codec. Additionally, the Sony Sound Connect app contains a 10-band equalizer, EQ presets, and adaptive sound control, allowing you to tailor the sound to your preference. Battery also favors the Sony WF-1000XM6. Compared to Bose QuietComfort Ultra's six-hour battery life, the Sony earbuds can handle eight hours of continuous use with ANC on. In some cases, the playback might last up to nine hours as well. The only downside to the WF-1000XM6 is that the fit isn't great for everyone. Due to Sony's bulky design, the earbuds can cause discomfort in smaller ear types, and a good fit might be hard to achieve. Unlike the Sony WF-1000XM6, which go a little overboard with the price, the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro provide flagship qualities at a budget. Costing $169.99, they sit well below the price point of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra. But the ANC, sound quality, and overall performance are comparable to their more expensive competitors. According to SoundGuys' testing, at max ANC settings, they reduced outside noise by up to 84%. In similar tests, the Sony WF-1000XM6 benchmarked at 88%, whereas the Bose QuietComfort Ultra maxed out at around 90%. To ensure a perfect fit, there are five ear tips included in the box. The design also features an ear fin, similar to the Bose, and the buds fit comfortably in the ear canal. While the out-of-the-box sound is good enough for casual listeners, the Soundcore app features an eight-band EQ, letting you tailor the sound to your preference. The app also has a feature called HearID, which provides a listening test that builds a personalized EQ profile based on your hearing. If that isn't good enough, there are specific EQ modes as well. The playback time on the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro sits at 12 hours with ANC off and 6.5 hours with ANC on, slightly above the QuietComfort Ultra. LDAC is supported, and the app introduces a bunch of features like Dolby Audio, voice commands, live audio translation, and five levels of ANC. The case itself has a touchscreen, which can be used for managing the core functions, like changing audio modes. Overall, the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro deliver an immersive experience at a fraction of the cost. If you're deep into the Samsung ecosystem and own a Galaxy smartphone alongside other Galaxy products, getting the Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro will make the most sense. Priced at $249.99, they sit in the premium category. The ANC is similar to the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro and effectively blocks out most outside noise. Some high-pitched noises, however, can squeeze their way past the earbuds if you don't have a good fit. There are five levels of ANC in the Galaxy Wearable app, as well as an adaptive and ambient mode. The earbuds have a stem design and fit comfortably in the ear during longer hours of use. To provide a good seal, Samsung includes three tips in the box. The default sound is bass-heavy and tends to overemphasize the lows. However, for some, this might be ideal as punchy bass is considered a pro rather than a con. For the audiophiles, though, Samsung provides a nine-band EQ, which lets you play around with the frequencies. If you're a novice, there are a few default EQ options available as well. The battery, similar to the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, provides six hours of playback with ANC on and seven hours with ANC off. Wireless charging on the case is supported, and it holds enough charge to top up the battery at least three times. Glancing over the ecosystem features, the buds unlock SSC UHQ if you're running a Galaxy device with One UI 6.1.1 or above. This lets you enjoy better audio quality and streaming over Samsung's latest codec. The buds are also IP57-rated, have clear mic audio, and multipoint access between Samsung devices, making them ideal for Galaxy users. The Apple AirPods Pro 3 are a great choice of earbuds if you're a part of the Apple family. At $249.99, the AirPods Pro 3 provide premium ANC, a quality sound signature, and added features that set them apart from the competition. The design features the iconic stem, but the bulb is smaller compared to the Apple AirPods Pro 2. This allows the earbuds to sit deeper in your ear and create a good seal. As a result, the passive noise isolation is increased. When ANC is turned on, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 can massively reduce outside noise across all frequencies, putting them in the highest category of noise cancellation. In turn, sound is enhanced, and Apple's new drivers produce quality bass, detailed vocals, and deep reverbs. Instruments sound clean as well, and all the sounds complement each other rather than a specific frequency overpowering. The only downside is that Apple still doesn't let users tweak the EQ to their preference, and you're at the mercy of the set sound signature. Features are another cool part of the AirPods experience, and the AirPods Pro 3 include a heart rate sensor, live translation, and Apple Hearing Aid. High-quality Bluetooth codecs are unfortunately unavailable, making lossless audio on Spotify and Apple Music inaccessible. Battery life, however, is improved, and the earbuds provide eight hours of playback with ANC on, sitting comfortably above the Bose QuietComfort Ultra. The case also features wireless charging, transparency mode is enhanced, and transition between Apple devices is seamless. For the Apple ecosystem, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 provide premium sound while being convenient. Focusing on audiophiles, Sennheiser provides a package that outshines its competitors due to one specific reason: longevity. Priced at $299.95, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are expensive, but they feature user-replaceable batteries on both the charging case and the earbuds. This means that down the road, when your batteries degrade and die out, you can simply change them yourself. The process is straightforward, and all it requires is a PH00 screwdriver. Even though the earbuds don't have a fin design, the fit is deep and secure, increasing noise isolation. ANC is comparable to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro and Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro. The sound profile is catered towards audiophiles and delivers quality throughout all frequencies. Consequently, instruments are detailed, bass is impactful without being overpowering, cymbals aren't shrill, and the overall experience is nuanced throughout. Unlike Apple, Sennheiser includes an eight-band EQ, sound quiz, and default presets to play around with the frequencies. The controls on the earbuds are registered through taps, though sometimes they can be a little frustrating to use. Transparency mode, similar to the AirPods Pro 3, is excellent, and it doesn't feel unnatural. The battery lasts six hours with ANC on, and up to 12 hours with ANC off. High-fidelity Bluetooth codecs are also supported alongside multipoint, and the mic quality is clear. Overall, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are a great choice if you want earbuds that will last for a few years. To pick the best earbuds compared to the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, we focused on products that sit in the same premium category. This meant taking the highest-end flagship earbuds from top brands, including Apple, Sony, Soundcore, and more. Price was a major player, as the earbuds needed to be in a similar price range to the Bose. Beyond that, we focused on factors such as comparably effective noise cancellation, premium sound quality, extended battery life, comfortable fit, clear microphone, and ergonomic design. The included products delivered on all fronts, providing better value than the Bose in some areas while having trade-offs in others.

October 12, 2026 2 min read Lettuce engineered to produce meat proteins Protein-packed leaves might be the key to better meat alternatives By Lila Magbilang edited by Sarah Lewin Frasier Thomas Fuchs Join Our Community of Science Lovers! Perhaps you enjoy a burger in a lettuce wrap once in a while—but what if greens were also crucial to the patty? That’s the ultimate promise of new research showing lettuce can be engineered to produce myoglobin, a protein found in meat. Myoglobin (and its better-known relative hemoglobin) contains the compound heme, the red pigment in blood. Adding heme can give plant-based meat alternatives a meaty flavor and the ability to “bleed.” For example, Impossible Foods uses a compound called leghemoglobin (a heme protein derived from soybeans) to flavor its meat alternatives. But using myoglobin, which is found in animal tissue, could lead to vegetarian products that not only look and bleed like red meat but smell more like it, too. In the study, published in Frontiers in Plant Science, the researchers describe how they got lettuce and tobacco plants to produce myoglobin for the first time, says lead author Alexia Groff, who worked on the project as a Ph.D. student at Imperial College London. The team engineered the plants’ photosynthesizing chloroplasts—the cell structures that typically turn sunlight into food—to make them do the job. In previous attempts to make myoglobin using nonanimal sources such as yeast, the protein-production directions were placed in the nucleus’s genome, but Groff and her colleagues found that adding them to the chloroplast genome instead could yield more of it—perhaps producing myoglobin even more efficiently than animals do. Right now yeast fermentation is the standard method of producing heme (as leghemoglobin), but the sterile environment and industrial equipment necessary for manufacturing can be pricey. Plants are much easier to grow. “Row-crop protein production would likely be faster than fermentation-derived production,” says Adam Leman, a principal scientist at the Good Food Institute, who was not involved in the study. “If existing crop-processing equipment can be used, costs for isolating and purifying a myoglobin-rich fraction could be quite low.” Lettuce is especially promising: the medium itself is edible, meaning lettuce-produced myoglobin could move more easily through the regulatory steps that can slow down the path from laboratory to market. A more streamlined process could also mean less money spent in production—and far less energy use. The meat industry is a voracious energy consumer: 60 percent of agricultural energy use comes from farming and transporting animal products. Making meat substitutes less resource-intensive is a step toward more sustainable food systems—even if it means making meat proteins in a vegetable. “In science, there were things that we used to think were impossible that now are an everyday occurrence,” Groff says. “I’m very excited for what the future of this sector is going to look like.” Lila Magbilang is a California-based freelance science journalist who covers environmental and biological sciences. A group of senators, including some Republicans, pushed back on the agreement. President Donald Trump doubled down Monday on his decision to allow Russian diesel imports amid growing backlash, calling it the "right choice" and arguing that Europe has previously purchased energy products from Russia as well. Trump said in a Monday morning social media post that the "European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy" and added, "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump did not specify the period covered by $250 billion figure. Estimates from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air tracking how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the start of war with Ukraine roughly align with the figure Trump mentioned. Trump's comments come after a small group of bipartisan senators came out against the Trump administration's plan to lift Russian oil sanctions and import a new supply amid spiking prices in the U.S. The senators, in a statement on Sunday, urged the administration to reverse its decision due to the ongoing war with Ukraine and ban on Russian energy imports. "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," the senators wrote in the statement. Trump announced on Friday that he made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately import 300,000 tons of its diesel fuel, with a promise that millions more are coming. The statement was signed by Republican Sens. Susan Collins, Thom Tillis, John Curtis and Lisa Murkowski as well as Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. The senators also argued the move violates a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports and opens the door to allowing Russia to potentially benefit financially on its war against Ukraine. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute," the senators wrote in the statement. In April 2022, Congress passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, banning imports of Russian energy products. While the law does allow the president to lift the ban under certain conditions, it requires a justification to Congress before doing so, which the senators argue did not happen. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sharply criticized the decision, too, saying in an interview with ABC News over the weekend that the deal amounts to an "obvious weakness." "It plays into Russia’s hands -- allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said. "We count on America's fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine -- and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one." Trump's decision comes weeks after he signed the bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which authorizes tariffs on countries that continue to purchase Russian oil. Now, some senators, such as Tillis, say Trump's recent action runs counter to the efforts in the legislation. "I completely reject it," Tillis said on NBC’s "Meet The Press" on Sunday. "If President Trump wants to end the strain of energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran, and number two, recognize that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war. And it's Vladimir Putin who owns the responsibility for energy prices to the extent that they come from that part of the world." Tillis said the agreement to purchase Russian diesel is "essentially, I think, tarnishing Lindsey Graham's efforts to try and get those sanctions bill through." However, other Republicans are continuing to stand by Trump, including House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, who is a vocal supporter of Ukraine and previously voted to establish sanctions on Russia. Emmer told ABC News' "This Week" co-anchor Jon Karl on Sunday that the deal was "another example of our president thinking out of the box" to address the American public's concerns about high oil and gas prices by importing fuel to the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections. "He's listening to the American people, Jon. The American people are hurting because of this world market when it comes to diesel and fuel in general,” Emmer said. Emmer also hailed the deal as another tactic in Trump's attempt to broker a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. "I think this is just another step of trying to get that resolved," he said. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

India is now Skyscanner's largest market by users, with searches up 22% year over year against 17% globally, Neel Ghose of Skyscanner India told Skift. The bigger change is in the mix: three years ago about 80% of Skyscanner's India redirects went to domestic bookings and 20% to international, and the split is now 52% domestic and 48% international. Ghose said that reflects Skyscanner's effort to reach first-time international travelers and a broader change in how Indians approach travel, summed up as more intent to travel paired with a desire to spend better. Booking windows remain short at an average of 28 days, roughly half that of several other major markets, while average trip length has fallen to 3.1 days as travelers take shorter, more frequent breaks. That combination is squeezing ancillaries: interest in flight and hotel room upgrades has declined, and shorter stays are reducing expected spend on tours and activities. Currency is also in play, with about two-thirds of Indian travelers surveyed saying they would switch destinations for better value against the rupee, helping drive interest in Bishkek, Baku, and Tashkent alongside Japan and Vietnam. On AI, 87% said they are confident using it to help plan and book, but Skyscanner said accuracy remains a concern and does not yet have enough data to say travelers are routinely handing over the booking itself.

Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine  	Several chains of supermarkets in France have reportedly been hit by a cyber-attack targeting the refrigeration facilities of several stores across the country.  	Affected companies include Coopérative U, a retail cooperative encompassing supermarkets branded as Hyper U, Super U, U Express and Utile, Groupement Mousquetaire's Intermarché and Carrefour.  	In a post on X published on October 12, Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Cooperative U, confirmed the cyber-attack affected several stores in the network from October 11.  	“Our teams are fully mobilized, in coordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible. An investigation will be needed to shed full light on this attack,” he said.  	He also highlighted that refrigeration systems are “essential to preserving fresh products and supplying food to the French public” and said this attack is “of utmost gravity, unprecedented [and] unacceptable."  	Speaking to Infosecurity, an Intermarché spokesperson confirmed that 150 of its stores were affected by the cyber-attack, estimated the financial loss at "at least thousands of euros."  	Meanwhile, a Carrefour spokesperson said the incident "primarily affected 80 out of our 6000 stores" and Groupe Casino said 5% of Monoprix supermarkets are impacted by the attack.  	French news channel BFMTV reported that the compromised systems are administered by Danish refrigeration systems provider Danfoss. An Intermarché spokesperson has since confirmed these details to Infosecurity.  	The attackers targeted outdated versions of the manufacturer’s freezing and refrigeration control software, the spokesperson confirmed. Affected stores include those operating vulnerable Danfoss consoles with remote-control capabilities that lacked an adequately secured communication channel.  	“Hackers reportedly managed to remotely trigger forced defrost cycles in refrigeration systems at numerous supermarkets, with temperatures programmed to reach as high as 50 °C (122°F),” BFMTV reported.  	BFMTV reported that as a result of the incident two supermarkets alone, an Intermarché and Super U, have already recorded losses of €270,000 ($302,000) worth of merchandise in Haguenau, in the Alsace region of eastern France near the German border.  	Intermarché said it was yet impossible to estimate how much food would be wasted due to the attack.  	"Our legal and insurance teams have started investigating the incident," the spokesperson added.  	Other purportedly affected supermarket networks include E. Leclerc and Monoprix, Jonathan Le Borgne, author of the specialized retail news website Je bosse en grande distribution, has reported.  	E. Leclerc has acknowledged Infosecurity's request for comment but has yet to provide a response.  	Supermarkets in Belgium and the Netherlands were also reportedly affected.  	Additionally, research presented by Claroty’s Team82 at DEF CON 34 in August 2026 demonstrated how a compromised Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller could disable cooling while falsifying temperature readings, potentially concealing failures in the cold chain.  	A Shodan scan on Aug 19 still found 3726 of these controllers accessible from the public internet.  	These findings highlighted the real-world risks of exposing industrial refrigeration systems to the public internet without adequate security controls, authentication, and firmware updates.  	On October 13, the Danish company will be at Chillventa in Nuremberg, a three-day trade fair for refrigeration technology, where it is planning to showcase the new iC7-HVACR drive featuring “integrated cybersecurity features.”  This is a developing story. Coopérative U, Monoprix, Albert Heijn and Danfoss have been contacted but have not responded to our request for at the time of publication. This video can not be played What happens to unworn sports kit? For an elite athlete, pulling on Olympic kit can be the reward for years of sacrifice. But some of that clothing never makes it out of the packaging. Inside a warehouse on England's south coast, boxes are stacked with pristine Team GB clothing from Paris 2024 and Milan Cortina 2026. Tracksuit bottoms, jackets, hoodies and T-shirts sit untouched. Among them are garments created for Olympic opening ceremonies. All of it is unworn. Commercial constraints can make excess stock difficult to shift at scale. Now a new partnership means hundreds of items of surplus Team GB clothing and unsold merchandise will be resold through a specialist platform, with proceeds supporting the British Olympic Association's (BOA) charity arm, the Team GB Foundation. The initial launch will include 700 items from Paris 2024. It is one way of giving sportswear a second life. But why does that surplus exist, and why can perfectly usable clothing be so difficult to pass on? The BOA is far from the only organisation dealing with excess kit â elite sport in general struggles with kit wastage. 5thread, a consultancy specialising in sustainability, estimates that up to 100,000 items of sports kit end up in UK landfill every year. "It is a huge issue and it's also a complex issue," says Joanna Czutkowna, director of 5thread and a doctoral researcher in sports apparel and the circular economy. "A lot of this kit is bought before they know which athletes are going to complete in the sport or the event. So there's a lot of excess stock generated at the point of order. "Also, the types of contracts that you get for this have something called value in kind, so it's not a transactional contract. There's almost an incentive to get free product." Czutkowna is describing practices across elite sport, rather than Team GB's arrangements. Performance requirements also complicate efforts to reduce waste. Athletes need clothing designed to help them compete, so reducing quantities or changing materials is not always straightforward. The total surplus is difficult to measure. Kit can remain in warehouses or athletes' garages without entering a waste stream where it can be counted. The issue extends across sport, from clubs to countries. European football governing body Uefa estimates that up to 60% of professional team apparel, external is disposed of at the end of the season, although this figure has not been independently verified. The obstacles are not to do with the condition of the clothing. "Contracts can prohibit reuse because they don't want it on the market or there might be a particular innovation that they want to hold back," Czutkowna says. Adam Stevens, co-founder of Kitround, the specialist resale platform working with Team GB among others, says sponsorship and supply agreements remain financially important to sport, but there are ways to respect them while allowing clothing to be used again. "There are an awful lot of people, whatever sport they do, whatever teams they support, who simply can't afford to buy new," he says. British kitesurfer Lily Young training off the coast of Weymouth For British kitesurfer Lily Young, who is targeting a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the pressure to find a competitive edge can itself create surplus. Athletes preparing for major championships want to leave nothing to chance. "That does mean that we also end up with a lot of waste - a lot of things where you're like, 'this is basically brand new, but it's not quite good enough to maybe win'." Changes in sponsors can also leave athletes with clothing they can no longer wear. Young and fellow athletes have passed T-shirts to younger squad members and youth teams. Wetsuits and other equipment can also be passed on where they remain suitable. But equipment that no longer meets an elite athlete's needs could help someone else start, and more organisations such as Sail GP and the Royal Yachting Association are using specialist platforms to sell second-hand elite kit to the public at much lower prices. "We know that one of the main barriers to entry is cost," Young says. For Czutkowna, organisations need to think harder about how long their products can remain useful - and who could benefit from them. "A lot of this comes back to common sense," she says. "It's kind of a waste not, want not." Jen Rouse, managing director of the Team GB Foundation, says ordering is becoming more precise and the amount left over is reducing. Team GB is also considering producing some clothing without dates or event-specific names, so it could be used across more than one Olympic cycle. It is also exploring opportunities for athletes to return clothing they no longer need. She rejects the suggestion that excess clothing has previously simply accumulated unused. "It's not necessarily been sitting gathering dust in storage. It's always found a way out," she says. The partnership with Kitround creates another route, with sales supporting the Team GB Foundation. The aim is a circular economy for kit: keeping clothing and equipment in use through reuse, repair and resale. For Stevens, the principle behind finding kit another home is simple. "A kit was made to be worn. It was made to be out there on the field, on the water, in the pool, and it should be back out there. "That's really what underpins everything - making sure this kit doesn't go to landfill and that it can have a second life." Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins Use your first 30 days as a growth leader to assess where B2B buyers lose trust and reshape marketing channels around how they research and buy. Now more than ever, when growth leaders enter a company, they face unrealistic expectations around the numbers they’re supposed to reach, whether that’s pipeline or revenue. It creates huge pressure to perform out of the gate. Because of that, many naturally want to execute as fast as possible. That execution, in the era of AI, has become easier and easier. But it doesn’t guarantee success. In fact, in many cases, it runs counter to it. Part of the reason success lags, despite more execution, is that buyer behavior has changed dramatically, particularly in B2B. It’s important to take a step back and understand the repercussions for sales and marketing channels a company has typically used to build its success. There’s a new reality in which each channel could shift in its role in driving buyer engagement. What I’m advocating for here is to understand changes in your particular marketplace, and in some cases, look at specific channel needs in terms of retooling it with people, processes, tech, and deliverables that match the new realities of the way buyers now buy.  In a Gartner study, 73% of CMOs call growth expectations high to overly ambitious. Yet their budgets have been flat at about 7.8% of revenue since 2022. At that leadership level, there’s a realization that getting to expected results, given the resources, is going to be difficult. Spencer Stuart found that the average tenure was about 4.1 years. That’s one of the shortest in the core C-suite right now. There is an enormous amount of pressure on growth and marketing leaders. See also: Why The Last Year Has Been The Biggest Challenge For CMOs Deloitte found that 66% of companies reported AI productivity gains, yet only 20% report revenue gains. There’s a huge gap between the ability to use AI for automation and execution and the results it delivers. As an industry, our go-to-market teams get caught in this hamster wheel of producing more and more. AI has enabled us to do that. Yet Gartner says that 72% of sales orgs report low reinvestment of the time that AI saves. We produce more and more, but we don’t know how or where, or have the structure around creating something better. See also: AI Isn’t Delivering Marketing Efficiency, It’s Repeating Programmatic’s Broken Promise What’s changed in that buyer equation? Most importantly, buyer decisions are happening before your first call. In a 6sense study, they found the winner in any selection process was on the day-one shortlist 95% of the time. They also found that 94% of buying groups ranked that list before even contacting a vendor. That puts enormous pressure on traditional B2B marketing, which has typically focused more on visibility and education. Where do you reach buyers given that reality? Expectedly, Forrester found that 94% of buyers use AI in their buying process. Given that reality, it’s important to understand how buyers buy in your industry now versus several years ago. If you think a typical education play, where you create awareness volume, drive to an educational PDF, and fill your top of the funnel, will work, you may want to reconsider. Those days are over. Because of the way people find answers now, that might not be the best use of the specific channels or surfaces you have to convince a buyer to take the next step and interact with your team. See also: How To Leverage AI To Modernize B2B Go-To-Market If some channels in your mix help buyers find you, other channels help them believe in you. Maybe that’s a better framework for how you view your channels now vs. several years ago. In Pew Research, they found that searchers click 8% of the time when an AI summary shows up, 15% when none shows up. There’s an obvious click-through difference there. There’s also a big disconnect in what people say they want. Gartner found that 67% of buyers want a rep-free experience, yet 69% want a rep to confirm what AI told them. There are some really interesting things happening there between finding and researching, then validating and trusting or believing. Understanding that split and how channels interact or promote those things is paramount when you look at what is working and what is not. It also affects what you need to fix when you hit the ground running in an organization. 6sense also found that 62% of buyers need a seller or a vendor to answer AI-related questions that websites don’t. I believe even the role of our websites is now in question. What features, functionality, and promotional copy might be doing on the site now aren’t enough for many buyers who need deeper validation and understanding of a brand. You may have all of your channels operational. You may have a website operational. You may have paid advertising operational, and you may have other core parts of your go-to-market operation in play, but is it addressing your buyer in the right way? And is it moving them towards an interaction? Are all your efforts structured to do that? I recently had a CEO who was reaching out consistently through LinkedIn direct messages in a promotional way. The messages didn’t resonate. When he switched the channel approach to providing value (i.e., industry data and his perspectives), the interactions changed almost immediately. It’s easy to say a channel doesn’t work. But it’s important to reassess what the buyer needs from that channel and how you might adjust your approach. You’ll run into a huge consistency problem as you approach your work and as resource constraints tighten over time. McKinsey found that inconsistent information across teams is the top reason buyers switch vendors or suppliers. Knowing that changes the game even further. Do you have the resources necessary to create that consistency, especially when those channels aren’t targeting buyers in the right way? Channels that help buyers find you are typically best served by strong product marketing and content leaders who enable ops personnel to produce consistent touchpoints within a channel. If you need buyers to believe you, you need deeper sales cooperation, evidence within your customer base, and top-level thought leadership to power the right touchpoints. It might be worth pausing when you first join an organization to understand each go-to-market channel, whether it’s BDR outreach, SEO, paid advertising, events, etc. Does that channel have the right assets it needs, the right proof it needs to reach the buyer in a way that’s meaningful? If not, and you just have volume, then why do it? One asset we found particularly effective recently was an industry report that broke down data and lessons from one geo that could apply to another. Those insights resonated and produced deeper sales conversations in the new geo. It landed at exactly the right time in an event context, heightening the value of the interaction. The first 30 days as a growth leader may be best spent finding out where the buying process breaks. Do you have enough top-of-funnel volume to be seen? Are GEO and paid ad efforts, for example, doing their job in making buyers aware of what you do? Are you seeing a high bounce rate on your website and not deeper interaction that would indicate buyers are getting questions answered? Are you creating the surfaces that validate the research buyers are doing, and creating moments where trust and belief can take shape? Are you running events in a way that your salespeople aren’t just telling people about a product they already know, but are instead enabling them to answer deeper questions? Are buyers who are ready to engage getting validation, and do they trust you in those moments to buy? As a fractional marketing leader, I was recently asked to help a company get its first 10 customers in a new geo. A key assessment I did helped me understand what channels we had available, how the sales team was interacting with buyers, and what we could do to build top-level thought leadership across the board to drive better results. Telling that thought leadership story in email and social, combined with effective BDR outreach and a central event to drive buyers, produced a much better result. It’s enabling us to hit targets. If we just did a traditional approach of spending paid ad money or leveraging BDRs separately, we wouldn’t have gotten the same result. Thinking about channels from the perspective of the new buyer reality helps you shape marketing channels, create better sales experiences, and produce better outcomes. Use those first 30 days to assess your channels and design new buyer interactions that will enable your company to scale over time. Week 5: It was a week of terrible plays and a week of terrible plays that immediately were forgotten as more terrible plays happened. Here are the instant takeaways, including a lot of Texans thoughts and some young players getting major upgrades due to injury.  I’ve mostly ignored the idea that Marks would be some sort of league-winner with David Montgomery as the lead back. It conflicted with my priors, for one thing. But for another: Nobody on this team can run the ball anyway. There were a pair of events that took place in Sunday’s 26-3 Texans win that changed my mind. One of them is that Montgomery was ruled out with a groin injury – ominous, at best, news. Marks would seem likely to assume a major role in the running game if Montgomery were sent to injured reserve. Even if Montgomery wasn’t, though, Marks would get a little added value. DeMeco Ryans said after the game that Montgomery could miss some time. The other is … The Texans didn’t give a single carry to another back after Montgomery left. Dare Ogunbowale wasn’t used at all. I don’t think Marks will get 100 percent of the carries again next week; nobody does that. But he has to be regarded as a favorite for at least 70 percent of the Texans backfield touches, if not more. Even given the bad situation, Marks probably walks into a low-end RB2 role for the short-term. Bernard was already going to be heavily involved after Michael Pittman hit injured reserve, but you know how Aaron Rodgers treats rookie wideouts. It was hard to believe that Bernard would be the one to buck the trend. Germ moving the chains ⛓️ @oti_germie pic.twitter.com/DqcQU9xqAP However, Rodgers and Mike McCarthy had their hands forced in Week 5. Roman Wilson got hurt. Ben Skowronek got hurt. And Bernard responded by leading the team with nine targets and converting it for 6/80. Does that mean Bernard is a WR3? Probably not, though with bye weeks coming and the general state of the receiver position as down bad as we’ve seen it, there’s probably not much separation between WR3 and WR4 right now anyway. But somebody must be a reliable short-area target here, and Bernard has a chance to be that while Pittman, Skowronek, and Wilson heal up. With Marvin Harrison Jr. now sent to the Texans – we’ll get into that in a second – the Cardinals have space for another fantasy option. If you’ve seen any Arizona Cardinals football this year, you’ll recognize that a) their defense is so bad that they’ve made the Jacoby Brissett fantasy football conversation relevant weekly and b) that hasn’t meant much for Harrison. But that doesn’t necessarily need to be the case for Bourne, who was a priority free-agent target for Mike LaFleur and had an 8/75 game in the opener with five first downs. Clearing out Harrison’s target share should get Bourne involved enough to be a reasonable FLEX play going forward. And hey, bye weeks are about to hit big. I don’t know that we need to have higher expectations than that for Bourne – who has shown some fantasy use with Mac Jones last year – but the Cardinals have enough fantasy volume to feed a third wheel. Especially if they’re going to run the ball as poorly as they did against the Lions on Sunday. It’s been a few weeks since De’Von Achane tore his ACL. Let’s check in on the snap counts and production for Gordon and fellow Dolphins runner Jaylen Wright since then: Week 4Wright: five carries, seven yards, 12 offensive snaps. Gordon: nine carries, 100 yards, one touchdown, 22 offensive snaps Week 5Gordon: 18 carries, 88 yards, one touchdown, 43 offensive snapsWright: six carries, 11 yards, nine offensive snaps Another strong run up the middle by Ollie Gordon, although his knee was down before the ball broke the plane of the end zone pic.twitter.com/HR59Roj0BW Is some of that about the fact that Wright re-injured his foot in practice this week? Probably. But is it also true that the Dolphins, with Malik Willis, seem to always generate good rushing lines and that Gordon is now heavily entrenched as the head of a committee? I think so. In fact, I think he’s closer to a low-end RB2 than a FLEX play now. So for the second time in two weeks, Gordon’s stock climbs.  Here’s the thing about Justin Herbert, and it really can be as simple as this: They started four rookies and Cole Strange on the offensive line in Week 5. You might be thinking “ah, another person making excuses for Herbert, how convenient.” And that’s fine. I wouldn’t exactly say he’s played well this year. He barely threw for 100 yards today! But what we thought would be a good situation with a healthy Rashawn Slater, Joe Alt, and Tyler Biadasz in the preseason has now devolved into something that’s unworkable for any NFL quarterback. Yes, Mike McDaniel is struggling. Yes, Herbert has made some dumb mistakes while pressing. But it’s the offensive line that is the straw that stirs the Herbert stick over the past four years. When it died last year, his fantasy prospects went with them. Nik Bonitto chases down Justin Herbert to get the sack 💪@DENvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/aAKporoasY And so … yeah, he’ll be a reasonable QB2. I’m not advocating anybody to flat out drop him in a superflex league or anything. But whatever talent is here is in such a poor situation that it’s just impossible for anything good to come out of it right now. I have done every Texans game for Rotoworld’s blurb team this year, which means I am privy to some things about how dumb this team is.  One of those things is that they have weirdly split playing time between the wideouts in a way that has nerfed fantasy value for everyone. It’s not uncommon for Nico Collins to play 70 percent of the snaps and for everybody else to not even reach that. Kayshon Boutte led all non-Collins Texans wideouts with 39-of-65 snaps on Sunday. So here comes a wideout in the middle of the season with no past with this offense. Is he going to suddenly be featured? I don’t think so. I thought there was at least a chance he’d bounce back to long-term relevance with the Cardinals. But if he’s going to be out here for 60 percent of the snaps and not be a focal point of the offense, well, I don’t know that there’s a lot to be optimistic about here. I’m not completely down on Harrison’s talent. I think there’s a chance he turns it around in Houston at some point. But the short-term value here looks bleak enough that I don’t think I’d recommend holding him. Good running backs don’t lose carry battles to Samaje Perine. Maybe this was kind of a weird game – it is a game against an opponent that has given up on fielding a real team this year right before a bye week – but on the heels of last week’s nine-carry, 10-yard thud against the Jaguars, I’m a little concerned. Perine has always siphoned off just enough usage from Brown to be an interesting FLEX play at times, but this isn’t exactly an endorsement to use FAAB on Perine. This is an anti-endorsement of Brown, who probably is falling into the high-end RB2 ranks at this point. The Bengals have overcome it by sitting on the Texans in Week 2 and turning over Baker Mayfield and Malik Willis several times, but their run offense moving under center has not worked in any real way. I’m curious if they’ll come out of the break with a new game plan. Skattebo left Week 5’s game with 13 carries to Najee Harris’ nine, but between his backbreaking fumble and what feels like an incredibly open running back room, it’s hard to feel like this is running out well for him. Skattebo played 56 snaps, while Tyrone Tracy played 17 and Najee Harris played 16. That’s two straight weeks where Skattebo has ceded at least 10 snaps to both of his backups. CHAOS IN OVERTIME Cam Skattebo fumbles, and Washington recovers!📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/LeMXcD6EOI The Giants have played enough plays in those games that Skattebo’s overall lines still look decent, but Skattebo hasn’t cracked 60 yards since Week 1. His PPR value, after 32 targets in just eight games in 2025, is in the dumps. He enters Week 6 with 12 targets in five games. He’s fumbled four times in five games. I don’t think Skattebo is in any danger of losing his RB1 job here – John Harbaugh said he had a “hell of a game” before the fumble. But the walls have closed in on this role enough that it simply isn’t worth as much as we thought it could be in the preseason. No Dart, no receiving value, and the running room has not been delivered either. It’s a tough scene. A Division of NBCUniversal. Who knew one of the more solid streetwear drops this season would consist of, quite literally, just clothes? The first drop from Seoul-based and Reddit-adored streetwear label thisisneverthat features a campaign with basic product shots.  Instead having a model animating a garment, the pieces are featured rumpled, stacked, and levitating on hangers in a way where each garment  comes alive as its own subject. The concept is reminiscent of a quasi-stunt concept that Demna (and Guram…RIP to the partnership) pulled off back when he had a last name. In 2017, the designer produced Vetements window displays for both Saks and Harrod’s composed of masses of unwanted clothing — out-of-season stock mixed with closet discards from each store’s employees. Designed to grow as time passed, the mounds becoming piles becoming mountains represented the amount of waste implicit in luxury markets. This drop’s point is that you can hint at humanity without actual humans.  thisneverthat executes this especially well with the weathergear puffers, depicting each rolled up into accompanying cylindrical carrying bags. One fashionably ruddy green-gray anorak is posed with its hood angled down left, the better to resemble someone giving or receiving a dap, for example. Drop two came later last week with more clothes — like a suite of Pertex jackets and fleece vests done in neutral grey cheetah prints and lavender plaids — that assume the position, so to speak. Props to thisneverthat for  letting the clothes be just great clothes, and taking it upon themselves to depathologize the drop. Their recent collaboration with IYKYK Japanese audio-and-streetwear brand Surplus Research says as much, that the best stuff is a secret to most. Michael Saylor’s Strategy said Bitcoin holdings reached 848,250 BTC after its latest purchase, while maintaining a $4.88 billion cash reserve. Strategy bought 250 Bitcoin for $21.5 million last week, marking a second consecutive weekly decline in purchases as its Bitcoin holdings reached 848,250 BTC. The company funded $21 million of the purchases through sales of its common stock and the remaining $500,000 with existing cash between Monday and Sunday, according to an announcement published on Strategy’s website. Strategy also continued repurchasing shares of its STRC preferred stock, spending $192.4 million during the week, up from $176.3 million the previous week. RNZ / News / World Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/world/1865776%2Ffrench-supermarkets-suffer-refrigerator-shutdown-after-unprecedented-cyberattack Major French supermarket chains said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security. Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented". "Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality". At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements. Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires. BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores". Those branches that were affected will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarche told AFP. Specialist French retail sector news website jebosseengrandedistribution.fr said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected but the companies have yet to confirm this. E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores". A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted. Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates". Intermarche said branches would have to throw away fresh and frozen products. AFP / Fred Tanneau It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware". It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures of how many systems were affected. A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cyber security agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor". "It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread", the source added. The chief executive of Cooperative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as "unprecedented" and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since Sunday night. "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he wrote on X. He added that the company's teams were "fully mobilised" to restore the situation as quickly as possible. "An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack," he added. The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires", the prosecutor's office said. Intermarche condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures. Customers enter an Intermarche supermarket in Issy-les-Moulineaux, on the outskirts of Paris, on 12 October 2026, following a cyberattack that heated fridges and sparked fires. AFP / Dimitar Dilkoff BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products". The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by malicious actors carrying out cyberattacks. President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure from Russian "hybrid attacks". Industrial equipment such as refrigeration units, long isolated from the internet, are now connected via sensors or remote monitoring systems, Antoine Hautin of cybersecurity consultancy Almond told AFP. By likely affecting hundreds of units simultaneously, the attack demonstrated "a certain level of sophistication," he added. - AFP Sign up for Ngā Pitopito Kōrero, a daily newsletter curated by our editors and delivered straight to your inbox.
