POPULAR SEARCHES                         BROWSE BY            Sunday's NFL slate somehow had a little bit of everything. We arguably had the best game of the young season, with the San Francisco 49ers taking down the Seattle Seahawks in a thriller to remain undefeated. The Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars had two lead changes in the final 15 seconds of their game in London. Sunday also brought us our first tie of the year, and a rare headliner trade on a game day that helps set the course for an interesting trade deadline.  Suffice it to say, Sunday brought us a lot of things we could overreact to. Which overreactions are legitimate, and which ones aren't? Let's break it down.  With the win over the Seahawks, 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan erased the perception that he can’t defeat a Mike Macdonald-led defense. And with the win, the 49ers are 3-0 against the Broncos, Seahawks and Rams this season, becoming the first team since the 1981 Broncos to record three wins in their first five games against teams that reached a conference championship game the previous season. It’s the third time San Francisco has started the season 5-0 under Shanahan. The previous two instances (2019 and 2023), the 49ers reached the Super Bowl. The 49ers also easily handled the Super Bowl champions of the offseason, defeating the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in Australia to start the year. Brock Purdy is the frontrunner for league MVP, even though he struggled at times against one of the best defenses in the league on the road at Seattle. And receiver Mike Evans has been one of the best free-agent additions of the offseason, finishing with game highs in receiving yards (113) and receptions (7). Through the first part of the regular season, the 49ers have shown the NFC goes through Levi’s Stadium.   Kenneth Walker played his best when the games mattered most, leading the Seahawks to a championship last season. That was particularly true in Super Bowl LX, when he ran for 135 yards and earned the game's MVP honors.  But that wasn't enough for Walker to stay in Seattle this offseason. The Seahawks promptly let Walker go in free agency, where he signed a three-year, $45 million contract extension to join the Kansas City Chiefs this offseason. Paired with quarterback Patrick Mahomes, Walker has been the most dominant running back in the NFL, leading the league in rushing yards. That move has led to some second-guessing in Seattle, which drafted Jadarian Price with its first-round pick in April's draft. The Seahawks are also awaiting the return of Zach Charbonnet, who is still on injured reserve due to a knee ailment he suffered last season.  Price has failed to come close to Walker's production so far, dealing with fumble issues (he's lost two fumbles) before recently landing on IR due a chest injury. With Charbonnet still out, the combination of free-agent pickup Emanuel Wilson and George Holani hasn’t produced the same explosive running game with Walker in the backfield last year. That wasn't apparent in Sunday's loss to the 49ers. The Seahawks were averaging 110 rushing yards a contest entering Week 5 and had just 86 in a loss to San Francisco. Holani had two costly fumbles, including one recovered by San Francisco rookie defensive lineman Gracen Halton for a touchdown. During the team’s Super Bowl run, the Seahawks averaged 130 rushing yards a contest and did not turn the ball over in the postseason. With the running game falling short, Sam Darnold has had to deal with a larger burden. That hasn't produced great results, with Darnold throwing two interceptions on Sunday. Of the three games Darnold has started and finished this season, he's thrown multiple interceptions in two of them — and both resulted in losses.    The Cardinals finally pulled the trigger by trading Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans. The Cardinals received pretty good compensation, netting a second- and sixth-round pick while also sending a seventh-rounder with Harrison to consummate the deal. With the move, the Cardinals give up on developing the No. 4 overall selection in the 2024 draft just three years into his NFL career, while Harrison gets a chance at a fresh start in a new environment with someone he had a lot of success with at Ohio State in Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud. But will the deal help change the course of the Texans' season?  Considered the best receiver in his draft class and one of the best receiver prospects in years, Harrison has to take some ownership and accountability for things not going well in Arizona. But he also wasn’t the only one to blame, as the Cardinals did not do a great job of putting Harrison in positions to excel based on his skill set and surrounding him with proper talent.  That said, there are now no excuses for Harrison. He must figure out how to produce for a new team in a new offense, and that transition will likely take some time. And there isn't much time for the Texans to figure it out. Sure, they won on Sunday, but they're 1-4 and face the 4-1 Jacksonville Jaguars in London next week.    In a week where folks openly questioned whether the Eagles have given up on the season, Nick Sirianni made another questionable decision that led to an improbable 57-yard game-winning field goal by Jaguars' kicker Cam Little. The loss dropped the Eagles to 2-3 on the year, marking another woeful defeat in a year where the NFC East feels very winnable.  The Eagles appeared to have won the game after Jalen Hurts marched the offense into scoring position and Jake Elliott drilled a 48-yarder with eight seconds left. However, instead of instructing Elliott to kick the ball into the end zone, he placed it in the field of play and Ameer Abdullah returned it 53 yards to put Jacksonville into field goal position for the winning score. Bottom line: Philadelphia lost a game it should have won, and Sirianni is shouldering the blame for the loss. Sirianni has had success in Philadelphia, winning two NFC titles and a Super Bowl in five seasons, but Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie is more concerned about what his head coach has done for him lately. And through five games this season, it’s been a hot mess for Philadelphia. But this is when teams led by Sirianni are usually at their best — when everyone counts them out and their backs are against the wall. And after Lane Johnson’s retirement and the trade of center Cam Jurgens, it appears that everyone will shovel dirt over the Eagles' season, especially after Sunday's loss. However, if Sirianni is going to orchestrate an in-season turnaround this year, he's going to need to overcome some early obstacles. The Eagles continue to struggle in the second half of games. In 18 drives in the second half this season, Philadelphia has 10 three-and-outs and is 2-of-20 on third down, per FOX Sports Research. Philadelphia has managed just three points in the second half all season. While the defense has kept them competitive, Sirianni has struggled to get the offense right. And down three starters on the offensive line, two running backs and No. 1 receiver DeVonta Smith, the Eagles have failed to consistently find answers under offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. And Sirianni might end up paying the price.    In a rivalry game where both head coaches don’t like each other, Jordan Love finally played like the MVP candidate NFL prognosticators expected to see this season. Love completed 80.6% of his passes for 367 yards and two scores in the Green Bay Packers' decisive win over the Chicago Bears. For the second time this season, Love didn’t throw an interception.  Christian Watson (143 yards) and Matthew Golden (123) both had 100-yard receiving performances, as the Bears struggled to defend the deep ball. Green Bay’s much-maligned offensive line did a decent job of keeping Love upright for the most part, as he was sacked just twice. Love finished with six completions of at least 20 yards. As good as Green Bay’s passing game looked, it still struggled to run the football. Other than bulldozing his way for two scores, MarShawn Lloyd finished with just 31 rushing yards. Entering Sunday’s contest, the Packers were rushing for a league-low 58 yards per game. The running game didn’t look any better against the Bears, as they ran for 70 yards on Sunday. Also, rookie kicker Trey Smack missed two field goals and an extra point. With the inevitable close games that playoff-contending teams play late in the year, the Packers are going to need more consistency from their young kicker.   The Las Vegas Raiders lost their second game in a row, and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins wasn’t at his best. Cousins completed 67.9% of his passes for 243 yards and a touchdown, posting a 106.7 passer rating. But his numbers were better than his play might suggest, with the Raiders scoring just 10 points through the first three quarters.  As a result, the Raiders were boat-raced by the New England Patriots, 45-17, and No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza got his first taste fo regular-season action when he closed out the day. He finished 6 of 8 for 48 yards in mop-up duty, getting into the red zone in his only drive before turning the ball over on downs.  The Raiders paid Cousins good money for a reason, and that was to take the pounding in the tough part of the first half of the schedule. And with the Raiders getting off to a surprising 3-2 start, Cousins should be the quarterback for the next six games as they face the Bills, Rams, Seahawks, Broncos and 49ers. It’s better for Cousins to see if he can get through that gauntlet in one piece and give Mendoza two weeks to prepare for his first start after the bye in Week 12. More importantly for Cousins and Mendoza is the Raiders figuring out how to effectively run the football to create balance on offense. Las Vegas finished with just 38 rushing yards against New England.   Needing a jumpstart on offense, the Jaguars leaned on Washington to create some big plays, and he produced. Washington finished with six receptions for 124 yards and two touchdowns, one of which was a 51-yard score to start the game, while the other was a pretty, one-handed catch for a score in the fourth quarter. Washington entered Sunday tied for third in touchdowns (4) and ninth in receiving yards (352). Should a performance like Sunday's solidify Washington's spot among the game's top pass-catchers?  My colleague and Jaguars radio announcer Bucky Brooks has pointed out Washington’s consistent work ethic and compared him to another explosive playmaker: Carolina Panthers icon Steve Smith Sr. Washington led the Jaguars in receiving last season and is one of the reasons quarterback Trevor Lawrence is in the MVP conversation for a second straight season.  Now, it looks like the duo might be ready to take the next step.

Share A sushi meal sparked a medical crisis that left Ecuadorian influencer Yuli Vargas fighting for her life and experiencing paralysis affecting parts of her face and body.  In August 2025, Yuli’s condition severely deteriorated, leaving her hospitalized for 23 days after she ate sushi at a restaurant. Since surviving the ordeal, the influencer has shared her harrowing experience in detail and warned viewers not to make the same mistake she made. Amid growing concern over her ordeal, a medical expert explains how foodborne infections can become life-threatening, why raw seafood carries risks, and which symptoms should prompt urgent medical attention.  yulivargasc_ Vargas, who shares content about chronic illness and health awareness, described the experience as a turning point in her life. “It all started when I ate sushi… which triggered a series of complications and diagnoses,” she told Need to Know in an October 2025 interview about her hospitalization. In August 2025, she contracted severe Salmonella and typhoid fever infections after eating contaminated sushi.  What began as food p**soning rapidly worsened her health.  yulivargasc_   Yuli said the complications included pangastritis, moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, pancreatitis, and gallbladder inflammation. She also underwent an endoscopy and a colonoscopy during the same week. “I went through countless tests, procedures, and finally, an extremely risky surgery where I had to face reality: the odds of me making it out of the operating room alive were slim,” Yuli said. She recalled, “The pain and fear I felt throughout my hospitalization is something I don’t know how to explain.” “I endured nights of incessant pain where no medication worked; not even heavy sedation could calm me.”  yulivargasc_ She was kept in intensive care for monitoring during part of her hospitalization.  “In those moments, between pain and despair, I was unable to sleep or drink water, unable to breathe properly because of the pain, and I went without food for 16 days because I was given assisted feeding,” Vargas shared. She said doctors initially placed the feeding line in her arm, but it caused considerable pain. They later inserted a central line through her jugular vein to continue providing nutrition, “which ended up causing an infection several days later, and they had to remove it as an emergency.”  yulivargasc_ Yuli said her elevated pancreatic enzymes made the gallbladder operation especially risky.  “[The doctors] didn’t want to operate on me, and I had to accept that I might not survive,” she said. Hours after the procedure, she suffered an ischemic stroke, according to her account.  The stroke left her with paralysis affecting the right side of her body and face, adding another frightening complication to an already difficult hospitalization. “The doctors were at a loss for what to do,” Vargas said. “After multiple tests and examinations, they came up with the following diagnoses: pangastritis, moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus affecting the nervous system and pancreas.”  yulivargasc_ Systemic lupus erythematosus, commonly called lupus, is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues.  It can affect different organs, and its symptoms and severity vary widely between patients. Dr. Alexander Acosta, an infectious disease expert, told Bored Pandathat Salmonella can be transmitted through raw seafood, but linking an infection to a particular meal requires evidence. “Salmonella can come from raw seafood. That said, doctors must have evidence tying Salmonella to a particular food item, and this is often not known,” he explained.  yulivargasc_   Acosta pointed to a 2022 Salmonella outbreak the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) investigated.  Of 18 people interviewed, 13 reported eating raw fish, sushi, or poke.  Investigators also found the outbreak strain of Salmonella at a fresh-fish supplier.  The findings supported a link between the outbreak and the contaminated seafood. Typhoid fever presents a related but distinct food-safety concern.   MICHEL/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) It is caused by Salmonella Typhi, which spreads through food or water contaminated with infected human feces. “Typhoid is commonly transmitted by food/water contaminated by human waste,” Dr. Acosta said. “This could include food handled by someone with Typhoid and/or shellfish (e.g., oysters) living in typhoid-contaminated waters.” He explained that identifying an infection’s source may involve examining symptom timing, stool-culture results, recently consumed foods, and whether others became sick after eating the same food. Dr. Acosta said serious infections can trigger complications beyond the digestive system, particularly when a patient becomes severely dehydrated or bacteria enter the bloodstream.  nicoletaionescu/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) “Signs that doctors worry about and seek the cause for include severe dehydration, worsening inflammation, and bacteria leaving the gut and entering the bloodstream,” he explained. “When the germs enter the blood, what starts as a stomach ache can turn into a medical emergency.” He also cautioned against assuming that an infection explains every subsequent complication in a particular patient. “Yes, severe infections can plausibly contribute to all three, since they cause inflammation and make other complications more likely,” Dr. Acosta said, referring to pancreatitis, colitis, and gallbladder problems as experienced by Vargas.   yulivargasc_ But he added, “I’m not able to opine on Ms. Vargas’ case as I do not have all of the facts about her illness.” He noted that pancreatitis is a rare complication of typhoid colitis.  He also explained that Salmonella Typhi can live in the gallbladder, and gallstones may help the bacteria persist there.  Moreover, foodborne illnesses can range from mild, short-lived symptoms to infections that require urgent medical attention.  Dr. Acosta warned, “It’s a commonly held belief that food p**soning is not a big deal, but in fact some people need to seek medical attention when they develop diarrhea/vomiting.”  LIGHTFIELD STUDIOS/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) He highlighted several warning signs identified by the CDC, including bloody stools, diarrhea lasting more than three days, a fever above 102°F (approximately 39°C), vomiting that prevents someone from keeping fluids down, and signs of dehydration. “Severe dehydration can result in kidney injury and can also cause your blood pressure to drop, leading to shock,” the expert explained. He added that confusion or an inability to keep fluids down for hours should prompt same-day medical evaluation, potentially in an emergency department. Older adults, young children, pregnant people, and those with weakened immune systems face a higher risk of serious foodborne illness and may need medical attention sooner.  Dragana Gordic/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) Acosta also challenged the assumption that fresh-looking seafood is necessarily safe. “It’s commonly believed sushi and raw fish/shellfish in general are safe to consume if they’re fresh. However, bacterial contamination cannot be seen or smelled,” he said. “You may eat at the cleanest, shiniest restaurant and if the fish is contaminated, nothing they do will remove the bacteria.” Freezing fish can eliminate parasites, he explained, but it does not reliably eliminate Salmonella.  As a result, people at higher risk of severe foodborne illness should avoid raw fish and shellfish.  Nishihama/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) For Vargas, leaving the hospital was only the beginning of another difficult stage: recovering from the stroke, rebuilding her strength, and learning to manage a chronic illness. “I’m currently recovering from surgery and paralysis; I’m trying to get back to walking, eating, and moving,” she told her fans in a statement.  “I’m learning more about lupus and living it to the fullest, because when it hurts, it really hurts,” Vargas said. “I’m being treated with several dr*gs, including some that block the sensation of pain in the brain.” Notably, while her account highlights how rapidly a serious illness can change someone’s life, it does not establish the exact cause of each complication she experienced. The stock market's best-case scenario could be brewing, Goldman Sachs says. Strategists at the Wall Street bank are eyeing a Goldilocks situation for markets, a dream configuration where economic growth is neither too hot nor too cold. The idea is that the economy is growing at just the right pace to fuel investor optimism while keeping a lid on inflation. It's a setup that looks poised to spark a fresh rally in stocks as well as bonds in the coming months, the bank wrote in a note to clients on Monday. Goldman said it's shifted back to an overweight stance on stocks for the next three months and to an overweight stance on bonds over the next 12 months, citing a strong backdrop for economic growth and cooling inflation. Earnings are also expected to surprise to the upside for the third quarter, strategists added, estimating that the S&P 500 would post 18% earnings growth in 2027, when excluding "other income" related to the revaluation of equity shares. "Our macro baseline remains constructive: growth should stay healthy, especially for earnings, recession risk remains low, and inflation momentum should moderate into 2027. This combination of resilient growth and easing inflation points to more of a 'Goldilocks' backdrop, which should be more supportive for balanced portfolios," a team led by the bank's Christian Mueller-Glissman wrote. Some Wall Street strategists took a Goldilocks scenario off the table in recent month as inflation remains elevated. Energy prices saw a big mid-summer surge, largely due to the war in Iran and higher oil prices. The market has also been rattled lately by a historic sell-off in government bonds, which has pushed yields to levels that haven't been seen in decades. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield remains near its highest level since 2002, surging in recent weeks as investors recalibrate their expectations for interest rates.  While the major stock indexes remain near records, market breadth has deteriorated sharply. More than half of all stocks in the S&P 500 have fallen at least 20% below their recent peaks, falling into bear market territory. But there are a handful of underlying economic indicators that suggest growth will remain strong. The economy is expected to grow 3.6% for the third quarter, according to the latest GDPNow estimate from the Atlanta Fed. The job market has also remained resilient. Job gains fell far below expectations in September, though the US added a robust 133,000 jobs in August. The unemployment rate also remains near a historic low, at 4.2% in September. Consumer price growth held steady in August at a 3.4% year-over-year pace. A 60/40 portfolio — a classic investment strategy where 60% of a portfolio is allocated to stocks and 40% is allocated to bonds — tends to perform the best when inflation is falling, the bank added, adding that it saw "less downside risk" for the 60/40 mix over the next year. "The main near-term downside risk to equities remains higher rates and energy prices — also, US midterm election uncertainty could lead to a pick-up in equity volatility from current low levels," strategists wrote. The bank said it favored a barbell strategy, balancing high-growth global tech stocks with rate-sensitive, low volatility, high-dividend, or "bond proxy" stocks. A barbell strategy involves exposure to both high-growth and defensive investments, the idea being that losses on one side of the barbell could be offset through gains on the other side. Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins Google is planning to make Discover an AI concierge. The goal is greater usefulness; the risk is less traffic for publishers. A new job posting for a Principal UX Lead for Discover, appears to indicate that Google is planning a substantial transformation of Discover, their recommendation engine for articles. The posting strongly suggests that Google plans to overhaul Discover into an AI-powered experience to become more deeply personalized. The job posting shows that Google may be planning to change Discover into an AI-powered experience that anticipates users’ interests, helps them accomplish goals, and connects them with content and services across Google’s ecosystem. It describes a Discover that more interactive, deeply personalized, and more competitive with social media feeds. It’s possible that some of the changes are already being tested because I recently experienced suggestions for Meta Threads in Discover. If these changes come to pass, this may mean a change to how publishers and creators reach audiences through Discover because what’s described is more than an effort to improve content recommendations. Google is describing a different purpose for Discover that leans more toward helping users act on information. One of the most consequential changes to Discover is the re-conceptualization of it from a recommendation engine to a concierge. A concierge is a person that arranges services and obtains things on behalf of another person. The clue is explicit in the job description: “Lead the design vision and execution to transform Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience that helps users make progress on their goals.” The phrase “proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience” suggests Google wants Discover to anticipate what users need rather than simply recommend articles based on past search patterns that indicate user interests. What that means is that instead of recommending articles about a topic, Discover could recognize an ongoing interest or goal and recommend information, products, services, and next steps for accomplishing the task that’s inherent in the interest. This is a strong match for how Google’s CEO Sundar Pichai envisions the future of search, what he refers to as Agentic Search that fits within a task-based paradigm. Google CEO Pichai described the future of search: “I feel like in search, with every shift, you’re able to do more with it. …If I fast forward, a lot of what are just information seeking queries will be agentic search. You will be completing tasks, you have many threads running.” The full job posting for that section outlines the direction Google Discover is taking: “Lead the design vision and execution to transform Discover into a proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience that helps users make progress on their goals. Balance AI capabilities while centering human voices and sources. Develop thoughtful, user-first strategies for making Discover a more impact experience that serves a scaled consumer base and helps existing users go deeper, moving seamlessly from inspiration to action.” The phrases “concierge experience,” “make progress on their goals,” and “inspiration to action” describe a radical change away from how Google Discover’s current function as a recommendation engine. A 2026 Google research paper describes a recommender system that identifies a user’s semantic intent, particularly for understanding soft attributes, which are highly subjective and personalized. The research paper explains: One thing that won’t change with Discover is that it will still mine user interaction data, but that how that data is interpreted will be redefined. The job posting gives a clue: “You will lead strategic design initiatives to redefine feed interactions, content formats, and AI-driven exploration experiences.” Another clue is that Google intends to innovate new feed formats with AI that are focused on engagement but also with showing more human creators, which should be good for publishers. This is the clue: “Evolve feed formats by scaling AI enabled formats, designing new engagement mechanisms, and elevating human voices and perspectives in the feed.” Discover is currently tightly associated with Search, as some of the hints about what users are interested are derived from their search patterns. That’s probably why Discover is considered a subset of Search in Google Search Console. The job posting indicates that the person hired must be able to work together with other parts of Google, including YouTube. The posting explains: “You will partner closely with executive leadership across Product Management, Engineering, Data Science, UX Research, and cross-organization partners (YouTube, Shopping, Chrome, and Android) to deliver a unified experience.” Another interesting takeaway is how they will be targeting youth. The posting didn’t indicate how young this targeting will reach. The job posting describes this focus: “Proven track record of defining product strategy for youth demographics and driving product-market fit in competitive content ecosystems.” That phrase “product-market fit” is a reference to how well a product meets the expectations of the demographic it was designed for. The insight here is that Google is looking for a person who can make Discover more attractive and younger audiences and increase engagement and stickiness. Hat tip to @AndellDam for spotting the job posting and sharing it on X. Over the last several months I have been tracking AI guys trying to create vibe coded clones of popular apps, especially Adobe’s apps which have always been the most pirated apps since the 90s.  There are now about a dozen vibe coded attempts to clone Photoshop and some other Adobe apps, not including dozens of forks of them. People like this aren't just openly copying Adobe's apps. It's Microsoft, Avid, Autodesk and whoever else is in their sights next including game devs big and small. Here’s just one example from last week of an individual game developer who discovered someone reverse engineered his game, repacked it and added their own strings to it.  Automated or semi-automated cloning to steal revenue away from developers isn’t new. In the early 2000s when Google released Adsense hundreds of Adsense filled spam sites sprung up and cluttered the search engines. If your own site ever had a popular page or article, bots would clone your pages and republish your content on spam sites, stealing traffic away from you. That’s the same unethical and spammy behaviour we are seeing today when AI guys vibe-clone a copy of your apps.   Directly stealing the look and feel of a product but changing the name is what the counterfeit goods market does. This is the same thing but in software.  The amount being spent in AI tokens (API costs) is in the thousands of dollars per project. The largest attempt to vibe clone Adobe’s apps has over 70 devs at the time of writing (update: 165 now, it is rising daily) using Claude to submit 100s of pull requests per day. The amount they are spending on tokens must be over $50,000 in the last two weeks. I will not name this project and don’t want to give them traffic that they do not deserve. Those dozens of devs will be spamming all the social media platforms with their alt accounts anyway.  Yet despite this not one of these vibe coded projects has been able to create a brush engine that matches Photoshop’s brush engine. The performance of their brushes collapses once the canvas size is over 8K x 8K pixels. Photoshop’s brushes work smoothly even when you’re working with 100 megapixel images out of a Hasselblad or Phase One camera. If you’re trying to build a Photoshop competitor in the year 2026 you should be building the engine first and then adding all the advanced features on top later, not the other way around. Unless your intention is just to generate headlines and promote an AI business.  In the Photoshop clone that is getting the most attention, on the billboard size canvas test above Copy/Paste and the Undo stack is extremely slow and momentarily freezes the application each time. This is basic stuff that decent software developers had working well 25 years ago when we had single core computers and nowhere close to 1GB of memory. If you can't get decent performance today on multicore multi gigahertz computers with many gigabytes of memory you or your AI are not doing a good job.  Those defending the poor performance of vibe coded apps have parroted the famous lines AI guys used in the past - “It is only days old” and “this is the worst it gets”. They make the mistake of equating human app development time with generative AI development time (hundreds of times faster). A vibe coded app is, in human hours, not only a few days old but closer to two or three years old. If a brush engine or transform tool works badly after the human equivalent of three years of development that is a demonstration of bad planning or an AI model not doing a good job.  Brush performance aside, each of these projects struggle with 100% file format compatibility and lossless image editing. Image previews while applying filters are downscaled to low res previews to maintain usable speed. Colour profile rendering and soft proofing is hit and miss. Support for the vast number of colour profiles and print profiles is bare. On some platforms many common fonts aren’t available because they require licensing. So instead of innovating and pushing forward they have successfully rewinded the clock back to 1996 when there was a lack of industry standardisation, compatibility and quality.  They’re spending minimum $2K (this is what the dev of Photoshop clone ‘Photon’ claimed to have paid in Claude API costs for his first release version not including further running costs) to vibe code a Photoshop competitor when Affinity Photo is free and Photoshop costs $200 a year. Not very smart economics.  They rant and claim the era of subscription software is finished, but they are subscribed to AI services and AI software. The amount they are paying to AI companies is far higher than the cost of Adobe, Autodesk, Canva or Maxxon applications, and the result is barely usable vibe coded apps that will need to be continually maintained at high cost.  Vibe coders brag about their app binaries being much smaller than Adobe’s app binaries, as if that has something to do with the quality of the code. It does not. Application code (which is just text) takes up very little disk space in any application. What takes up the most amount of disk space are the frameworks, libraries, models and media assets an app ships with. The more advanced and capable an app is the larger it will become. But the size on disk is largely irrelevant in the age of terabyte+ size disks. The size of an app in memory, the app’s performance and its stability are how you judge the quality of an application.  Continuing from the last point, they and internet commenters have often made claims that Adobe’s apps have “bloat” in them, but if you ask them to qualify what they mean by bloat they cannot. They will revert to application binary size again. These are mostly people who have no knowledge of programming and parrot each other. An app either has good quality code that performs well or it doesn’t. An app can have tons of redundant functions in it but functions do not run unless they are called by a tool.  Whether software is vibe coded or not, open source software has rarely challenged commercial software. Krita has been around for years and is a decent application, but Clip Studio Paint’s subscriptions earn Celsys millions of dollars a year. Nobody is giving up Clip Studio Paint for software that has rough edges. Blender is a fantastic application, but expensive high end apps like Maya are still the 3D animation applications of choice for larger studios and commercial productions.   In a 2026 survey of 150 CG production companies in Japan, when asked for their main 3D animation suite 58% named Maya, 17% 3ds Max, 12% Blender, and 7% Cinema 4D.  The picture is similar elsewhere.    Commercial apps innovate and lead. Open source apps like Blender follow the lead. Innovation costs a lot of money. Clip Paint Studio, Maya, 3ds Max and Cinema 4D, btw, are all subscription applications. But because those apps aren’t in demand by pirates Autodesk has not experienced the hate and bullying campaigns that Adobe has received.  And when it comes to customer support things become even sadder looking. One or two guys in a Discord chatroom cannot support a global user base, especially when those two guys are hunting for underage children to speak to on Discord (yes, I have seen what vibe coders do). Here we see Photoshop versus vibe-cloned copies of Photoshop. We test brush stroke performance on a billboard-size canvas with the brush set to 1000 pixels size. Photoshop handles this with no issue. The vibe-coded clones perform badly (basically unusable) because Claude can only give them off the shelf solutions it was trained on. The saddest part in all this is how it feeds into the ignorance and online hate campaign against Adobe that we have seen in the last 5 or so years. Some have labelled it ‘Adobe derangement syndrome’, but whatever it is it is a mix of stock market manipulation (some admit it) and anger that Photoshop has been getting harder to pirate ever since cloud services were integrated into Adobe’s application suite.  An  example above of the kind of misinformation spreading low-lifes that infest Reddit and LinkedIn. We should clear the air here. Subscription software exists when cloud services and cloud compute are integrated into a software suite. It is the only way to pay for the running costs at wide scale. If you remove these modern services there is limited progress in software development. You'll have to move all high cost compute locally which is impractical because most users cannot afford a high end workstation GPU or cloud server.  Instead of hurling hate speech and bile at thousands of software engineers who lead innovation at large companies (Adobe, Autodesk, Maxxon, Celsys, and others), show them some gratitude for their efforts. They are the engineers who innovate and everyone else follows. Just because they work at a big company doesn't mean they are committing human rights abuses. We have a generation brainwashed by envy and hate instead of urging everyone to be greater and bigger.  If some people have an issue with companies being large, they now have the tools to compete against them. But instead of vibe cloning poor quality rip offs why not build new original creative applications around fresh ideas that have never been tried before? But then again, vibe cloned piracy is a demotivating force. It ruins the incentive to create. Why create new original apps and games if someone comes along and rips you off? You’re giving yourself too much credit Brandon. There are dozens of people in your GitHub repo and they are all subscribed to a chatbot that is doing almost all the coding after being fed screenshots of Adobe’s apps. Update: this blog post was linked to on ycombinator and the discussion that followed was exactly what I pointed out above - tired parroted talking points, cliché anti-corporate rants and conspiracy theories. Not one comment about the innovation that scientists and engineers pursue at the companies above that benefits millions of users and the economy or the technologies that trickle down to the open source communities. One comment even insisted that Adobe should only add features that ‘people ask for’. If the tech sector worked like that we would be many years behind. A leaked factory notice allegedly claims the RTX 5080 24GB will become the top GeForce card Nvidia has reportedly stopped manufacturing the GeForce RTX 5090, including the D variants made for the Chinese market. The claim comes from a leaked notice from an unnamed factory, shared by leaker @hongxing2020 and reported by Tom's Hardware. A second leaker, @Zed__Wang, reportedly backed the claim, saying the GB202 chip behind the RTX 5090 will only go into data center and professional cards from now on. "According to a notification from the factory, Nvidia will no longer manufacture any RTX 5090 models, including the D variants," the message from @hongxing2020 reads. "Going forward, the highest-end GeForce graphics card will be the RTX 5080 24GB, while the RTX 5080 16GB version will be discontinued. Please spread the word." Nvidia has not announced the change, and Tom's Hardware said the company had not responded to its request for comment. An RTX 50 Super refresh, rumored to include a 24GB RTX 5080 Super, has reportedly been delayed by memory supply constraints, according to Tom's Hardware. Rumors put the arrival of Nvidia's Rubin-based RTX 60-series at late 2027 at the earliest, and possibly 2028. The industry-wide memory shortage has already affected other hardware. Emily Henry fans are in luck. On September 22, Henry revealed her next romance novel will be released on April 6, 2027. She unveiled the title, "Modern Classic," by posting it on movie theater marquees across the US and UK. "Modern Classic" will be Henry's seventh romance novel to date. She smashed onto the romance scene in 2020 with "Beach Read" and has written five more books since then, each of which has made The New York Times' bestseller list.  Henry's summer romance books often approach love with a sense of honesty and fun that the genre needs to thrive. Her characters may be enemies who find themselves living next door to each other or best friends who are scared to risk it all for something more, as was the case in "People We Meet on Vacation," which was turned into a Netflix film released in January 2026. Henry has yet to release a cover or description for "Modern Classic," but the marquee announcement and title have fans wondering whether the book will have anything to do with movies. It will be a while, though, before readers know for sure. Luckily, there are plenty of other romance books to pass the time with, including Henry's earlier works if you haven't read — or reread — them yet. In Henry's 2020 novel "Beach Read," which is being adapted into a film, author January Andrews is in a writing rut. She can't seem to think of her next big idea for a romance novel, so she decides to retreat to the beach house she inherited from her father, hoping inspiration will strike. To her dismay, January discovers Augustus Everett, an acclaimed literary author who happens to be her college archnemesis, is living next door.  January plans to steer clear of Augustus for the duration of summer — until she finds out he's having writer's block, too. They decide the solution to their problem is for each of them to try their hand at each other's writing style. Augustus will have to show January the ropes of capital-L literature, and she'll have to make him fall in love with writing about love.  However, falling for Augustus was never part of the plan. As you dive into "Beach Read," it's easy to see how it turned Emily Henry into a household name. No one expected Alex and Poppy to become best friends less than Alex and Poppy. After a fateful road trip in college, free-spirited Poppy and buttoned-up Alex become inseparable. To keep their friendship alive after graduation, the pair agreed to take a trip together every summer, exploring a new place side by side. The trip is Poppy's favorite week of the year, but when "People We Meet on Vacation" begins, they haven't been on a trip — or spoken — in two years, distance growing between them after one night changes everything. As Poppy feels more bogged down than ever by her life in New York, she knows reuniting with Alex would make everything better. So Poppy proposes one more trip, hoping a week together can get their friendship — and her life — back on track. Will Poppy or Alex be willing to face the feelings that sent them running from each other in the first place? "Book Lovers" is Henry's third summer romance book, and it's both an epic love story and an ode to books themselves.  Nora Stephens doesn't think anything is missing in her life. She loves her job as a literary agent, her apartment in New York, and living near her sister, Libby, and her nieces. When Libby asks Nora to escape to Sunshine Falls, North Carolina, for a month, Nora can't say no, especially since Libby is several months pregnant at the time. Libby has big dreams of small-town romance for Nora during their getaway, but instead of finding a local man to have a fling with, Nora keeps running into Charlie Lastra, a grumpy New York editor she's never gotten along with.  Despite their less-than-romantic history, Charlie and Nora keep crossing paths in Sunshine Falls, making the ever-growing list of things they have in common harder to ignore. And when Nora discovers her life as she knows it is about to change, Charlie might be the exact thing she needs. Henry is at her best in "Happy Place," a novel that ruminates on what it means to fight for love. Harriet has spent her entire adult life loving Wyn. Their relationship consumes her, and the fact that she met him through her best friends, Sabrina and Cleo, only makes her love him more. Between Wyn and her friends, Harriet found the family she had always wanted in college, and she plans to spend her entire life with them. When Wyn abruptly breaks up with her after she starts her medical school residency, Harriet is heartbroken and terrified she's going to lose everyone she loves. She manages to avoid telling Sabrina and Cleo what happened for five months, planning to burst their bubble on their annual group trip to Maine. Then Wyn shows up, telling her they'll have to pretend to be a couple for the duration of the trip, since it's the last vacation the group will ever spend in the house they've loved for years. Harriet doesn't want to cause her friends pain, so she's willing to torture herself for a week. All she has to do is stop herself from asking Wyn what went wrong for seven days, but as his displays of fake affection start to feel more and more real, Harriet might have to face her fear of rocking the boat if she wants a true chance at happiness. In "Funny Story," Daphne Vincent thought she had everything figured out. She was going to marry her doting fiancé, Peter, quietly thrive at her dream children's librarian job, and settle down in his hometown of Waning Bay, Michigan. Then, Peter leaves her for his childhood best friend, Petra, leaving Daphne at a crossroads. As she tries to recalibrate her entire future, Daphne moves in with Petra's ex, Miles Nowak, a wild spirit with whom she doesn't think she has much in common. She plans to avoid Miles as much as she can in their tiny apartment. Then, a night of drinking leads the pair to realize they may be able to help each other get over their breakup embarrassment if they let their exes think there's more between them than just a shared living space. Daphne knows their plan is temporary, but when she starts to develop real feelings for Miles, she may have to rethink everything she knows about what it means to be in love. Henry's latest book, "Great Big Beautiful Life," takes place in the summer and features a love story, but it marks a departure from her typical romances. Journalist Alice Scott is ready for the biggest challenge of her career to date: convincing the elusive heiress Margaret Ives to let her write her biography. Sunny-dispositioned and thoughtful Alice is sure she can make Margaret comfortable enough to share the story of why she disappeared from public life years ago. However, when she arrives in Little Crescent Island, Georgia, to meet Margaret, she finds she'll be competing against Hayden Anderson, a grumpy and inconveniently handsome writer who happened to win a Pulitzer Prize for his last biography, to tell Margaret's story. Beating out Hayden for the role might be an uphill battle, but Alice isn't going down without a fight, even after she realizes Margaret is picking and choosing what she tells each of them after getting them to sign strict NDAs. And as they try to unweave Margaret's history, it will become more and more difficult for Alice and Hayden to ignore the heat between them. Bolu Babalola's "Honey & Spice" doesn't feel like a debut novel, as she writes romantic chemistry with a deftness Henry herself may envy. Kiki Banjo has made a name for herself at Whitewell University with her radio show "Brown Sugar." She's staked her reputation on her ability to suss out players, warning her peers in the African-Caribbean Society against dating men who aren't worth their time. Then she risks it all by kissing Malakai Korede in front of everyone after writing him off as "The Wastemen of Whitewell" on her show. Kiki is terrified her show is going to slip through her grasp, so she makes a deal with Malakai to pretend to be a couple in the hopes that Kiki can save her show and Malakai can change his reputation on campus. Kiki expects the duration of their fake romance to be torture, but as she and Malakai eat, study, and spend time together, she's unsettled to discover there seems to be more to him than meets the eye. Will Kiki be willing to let go of her preconceived notions for a chance at something real? Like Henry, Taylor Jenkins Reid is a master at writing about yearning and epic love, as is obvious in "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo." Monique Grant's career as a magazine writer is at a standstill when famous — and famously private — film star Evelyn Hugo says she wants to do a tell-all interview with Monique, and only Monique.  Monique doesn't understand why Evelyn would want to work with her of all people, but she can't say no, especially when Evelyn starts opening up to her about her path to fame and the forbidden love that changed the course of her life. Monique feels like Evelyn has handed her the opportunity of a lifetime. When she finds out why Evelyn chose her for the tell-all, Monique will have to face truths about their shared history she never expected. If you've already read Henry's "Great Big Beautiful Life," you'll swoon for "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo." Lydia Bird's life is turned upside down when the love of her life, Freddie, dies in a car accident. After months of mourning and wanting to go back in time, Lydia begins to move on with the help of her sister and Freddie's best friend. Then she's given a way to return to her old life with Freddie, a life where the tragedy never occurred. Her heart is pulled in two directions as she struggles to choose between going back to the familiar and embracing the unknown, where someone new wants to love her.  Poignant and fresh, Josie Silver's "The Two Lives of Lydia Bird" is a story of love and hope that strikes a similar tone to Henry's works. On the night before Drew Nichols is set to be a groomsman in his ex-girlfriend's wedding, he gets stuck in an elevator with the pretty and funny Alexa Monroe, the first bright spot in what he believes will be an unbearable weekend. Impulse leads him to ask her to be his date to the wedding, and the duo surprises themselves by having more fun together than they bargained for. They plan to part ways after the wedding, neither interested in a long-distance relationship, but fate might have other plans for them.  Jasmine Guillory writes about romance with reverence and joy, making "The Wedding Date" an ideal read for Henry lovers. Dannie Kohan's plan is on track. In one day, she performs well at the job interview of a lifetime and agrees to marry her long-term boyfriend. Then, when she goes to sleep that night, she wakes up five years in the future, with a different man beside her and his ring on her finger. Dannie has only one hour in the future before she's yanked back to the present, and she tries to push the experience aside as a vivid dream. Then, she meets the man from her dream four and a half years later and discovers he's dating her best friend. Dannie will have to confront what she really wants and decide whether she's willing to change her plans to find true happiness.  Rebecca Serle's "In Five Years" explores time, grief, and all-consuming love, both romantic and platonic, in the same way Henry's books do, challenging readers to ask how far they would go for true happiness. Although Sally Rooney's beloved "Normal People" has a darker tone than Henry's books, the protagonists, Connell and Marianne, have a chemistry and a yearslong history that Henry fans will love. Connell and Marianne meet in high school, when Connell is a popular jock, and Marianne is, well, the opposite. The two bond despite their differences, setting them on a course that will shape their lives, drawing them back to one another over and over again. Rooney's novel shows the inevitability of love, finding words for the often inexplicable reasons people need each other. You can also stream the Hulu series once you finish the book. Like Henry, Carley Fortune captures the angst and ecstasy of summer love in "One Golden Summer." Alice can trace back her successful photography career to one photo: a candid shot of three teenagers on a bright yellow speedboat. She captured the shot during the one summer she spent at Barry's Bay with her Nan when she was 17, and it shifted the trajectory of her life. Fifteen years later, Alice should be living her dream as a professional photographer, but six months after a breakup, she feels stuck and uninspired. When Nan breaks her hip, Alice thinks spending another summer at Barry's Bay might be good for them both. Her vision of a tranquil summer with her grandmother gets upended by Charlie Florek, one of the teens from Alice's famous photo. The glimpse of Charlie that she got across the lake all those years ago was intriguing, but adult Charlie is so devastatingly handsome and thoughtful that he almost scares Alice. As they spend the summer together, Charlie heals wounds in Alice that she didn't know were there. If he lets her in, Alice might just do the same for Charlie. Ilya Rozanov and Shane Hollander are supposed to hate each other. Not only have they been competing against each other in hockey since they were 18, but they're also total opposites. Canadian Shane is cautious and focused, while Russian wild card Ilya isn't afraid to embrace his bad boy reputation on the ice. They have one big thing in common, though: the secret hookups they can't seem to resist every time they see each other. If the world found out about their relationship, both Ilya and Shane's careers could be in jeopardy, but they may decide it's worth the risk for a chance at something real with each other. Rachel Reid's "Heated Rivalry" was adapted into a hit TV show, so you can stream the series if you want more from the characters when you finish the book. Christina Lauren has written dozens of books, and their 2018 novel "Love & Other Words" is perfect for Henry fans who love friends-to-lovers plots. Macy Sorensen has been white-knuckling her way through life for nearly a decade, but she's content with the safe world she's constructed for herself. A pediatric resident and newly engaged to a kind man who makes her feel mostly nothing, Macy thinks her heart is safe from the turmoil she experienced in her adolescence — until Elliot Petropoulos literally walks back into her life. Macy met Elliot as a teen shortly after her mother died, and he quickly became her center of gravity as she visited the small town he called home on weekends. Christina Lauren tells their story from the past and present, showing readers how they became fast friends over books and adolescent secrets, how they fell into life-changing love, and the wreckage they were both left with when it all fell apart. After 10 years of no contact, Macy may finally be ready to tell Elliot why she went radio silent on him after one fateful night. They'll both have to decide if they can move on from the pain of the past for a chance at a joy-filled future, together. Achingly romantic and surprisingly funny, "The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston is about meeting the right person at the wrong time, literally. Clementine West has been adrift since her beloved aunt died. She thought living in the Upper East Side apartment she inherited from her would make her feel closer to her, as the apartment's magic had always drawn her in. Instead, she feels like she's just waiting for her aunt to walk through the door. Then, one day, Clementine comes home to find a man she doesn't know standing in her kitchen. Except, he thinks the apartment is his, for the summer anyway. He exists seven years in the past, staying in the apartment over the summer while Clementine and her aunt were in Europe. Clementine isn't ready to be hurt by love again, but she might not be able to keep up her defenses against the sweet chef staying the summer. And if she does let herself fall, will they work together if she finds him again in the now? Justin and Emma are having the same dating problem. Everyone they date meets their soulmate immediately after they break up with them. When Emma sees Justin's viral Reddit post about his problem, she reaches out, and they decide to go on a date in hopes of breaking their curse. Emma, a traveling nurse, plans to stay in Minnesota for the summer and enjoy a fling with Justin during her short stay. The last thing either expects is to get immediately attached, especially when they both have family members counting on them come fall. Despite their best-laid plans, Emma and Justin's curse might have been leading them to each other all along in "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez. To the world, romance novelist Eva Mercy and acclaimed literary author Shane Hall have nothing to do with each other. That's because the only two people who know their books are inspired by each other are Eva and Shane. For their entire careers, Shane and Eva have been writing secret love letters to each other, as the week they spent as teens glued to each other's sides in a rush of love still haunts them both years later. They finally come face-to-face again when they both speak on a Brooklyn literary panel, and despite the years since they've seen each other, their chemistry is undeniable. Eva doesn't trust Shane after the way things went down between them, though, and as a single mom, she can't risk getting hurt again. Still, Eva has always been curious to know why Shane disappeared, and reuniting with him might be the key to breaking her writer's block. The second-chance romance in Tia Williams' "Seven Days in June" will hit the spot for Henry's fans. Ali Hazelwood is a prolific romance author, and the coming-of-age story and yearning in "Deep End" will scratch the itch for lovers of Henry's books. Nearly every moment of Scarlett Vandermeer's life at Stanford is accounted for. She spends her days in the pool as a member of the diving team or studying, laser-focused on achieving her goal of getting into medical school. A relationship or even a fling is the last thing on Scarlett's mind. Then, she finds out Lukas Blomqvist, Stanford's world champion swim captain who thrives on control, has similar interests to her when it comes to intimacy, and she thinks she might be able to make time in her busy schedule for something casual. Lukas and Scarlett agree to explore their attraction together, deciding not to tell almost anyone about their arrangement. Scarlett doesn't think keeping her relationship with Lukas to herself will be a problem until she realizes the last thing she feels about him is casual. "Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan offers another take on second-chance romance. Sam's family's beach house on Long Island was her happy place in her childhood. She spent every summer there, and she was never happier than she was with her toes in the sand. Then, at 17, Wyatt broke her heart, and Sam couldn't face a summer there without him. She hasn't been back for more than a long weekend since. At 30, Sam is making the trek from the city back to the beach, and she isn't the girl she was at 17. She's determined to succeed at her high-powered job and plan the perfect wedding with her fiancé, Jack, whose tendency to over-schedule their lives has become a comfort. Only when she arrives, Sam discovers that Wyatt has returned to the house next door, and the entire adult life she created for herself begins to crumble. As old feelings come rushing back, Sam will have to take stock of who she is, who she wants to be, and who she really wants to live her life with. When Phoebe Stone arrives at the Cornwall Inn in Rhode Island, she's dressed to the nines and doesn't intend to ever check out. Her plans immediately go awry, though, when she discovers the entire hotel has been rented out for a wedding, and the attendees immediately assume she's one of the wedding people. Soon, Phoebe has no choice but to participate in the wedding festivities, especially because she and the bride keep telling each other their darkest secrets. After months of depression, the fanfare and plot twist of a stranger's wedding might show Phoebe her own path forward. Slightly more melancholy in tone than Henry's works but still beautifully romantic, "The Wedding People" by Alison Espach is about the surprises life can bring when you least expect it. If you're looking for another romance work that has been adapted for the screen, you can check out "The Deal" by Elle Kennedy, known as "Off Campus" on Amazon Prime. Hannah Wells is thriving at Briar University. She's killing it in her music classes, and she has the best friend a girl could ask for. Her crush, Justin, has no idea she's into him, though, and Hannah doesn't know where to start on figuring out how to flirt or date. Enter Garrett Graham, a hockey captain bound for the NHL. His GPA is in trouble, though, and Hannah is the only one who can help. The duo strikes a deal, with Hannah agreeing to tutor Garrett in school if he helps her make Justin jealous with a fake relationship. Garrett expects that pretending to date Hannah will be a breeze, but when he develops real feelings for her, he'll have to come up with a new plan to get the girl. Bitcoin buying is back. Corporate crypto heavyweight Strategy announced Monday that it bought over $21 million worth of Bitcoin last week, bringing its total holdings to roughly $70 billion. The company, led by flamboyant billionaire Michael Saylor, funded the purchase by selling more than 125,000 shares of its common stock and using $500,000 in cash. It also spent roughly $192 million to repurchase nearly 2 million shares of STRC, a type of preferred stock that makes regular payments to investors. The latest purchase extends Strategy’s return to Bitcoin buying, marking its fifth purchase since August. Bitcoin broke out of a prolonged trading lull in mid-August, climbing to around $77,000 for the first time since May. It has largely held above that level since and was trading at $82,600 Monday morning. The rebound followed a steep downturn that pushed Bitcoin from a high of $126,000 last October to a low of $58,000 in June. Amid the slump, Strategy—which holds roughly 4% of Bitcoin’s circulating supply—sold portions of its stockpile on four occasions. As Bitcoin’s price rebounded, Strategy stopped selling and returned to stockpiling. Strategy isn’t the only big player wading back into Bitcoin. Other companies have recently added crypto to their balance sheets, breathing life back into corporate crypto buying.  Earlier this month, Strive, the asset manager cofounded by billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, announced a $169 million purchase of 2,000 Bitcoin, bringing its stockpile to roughly $2.4 billion. Robinhood, the crypto trading platform led by CEO Vlad Tenev, also joined the ranks of corporate Bitcoin buyers and recently disclosed a $25 million investment for its own balance sheet. Metaplanet, the Japanese investment firm and world’s second-largest publicly traded Bitcoin treasury company, announced this month that it sold 10,000 Bitcoin and bought 11,000 in the third quarter to demonstrate to credit markets that it could convert its holdings into cash when needed. But companies aren’t just stockpiling Bitcoin. Bitmine, a Bitcoin miner turned into an Ethereum treasury company, announced this month that it had added roughly $41 million worth of the cryptocurrency to its treasury. The purchase brought its holdings to about 6 million tokens—nearly 5% of Ether’s total supply. The renewed buying comes as Bitcoin’s recovery fuels hopes of further gains. The cryptocurrency has held up despite recent interest rate hikes in the United States and renewed tensions in the Middle East. Opinion: The Apple Upgrade program is a net positive for consumers, but there are knock-on effects that could yet have a lasting impact  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Where were you when the first iPhone went on sale back in 2007? I remember clearly that I was working for Phones4U — a third-party phone reseller in the UK — and the iPhone launch completely decimated the business, as suddenly Phones4U wasn't a reseller of the most popular phone on the market. The same existential threat applied to all carriers except AT&T and O2, which had exclusive launch rights to the iPhone in the US and UK, respectively. Fast-forward 19 years, and Apple has repeatedly proven that the iPhone's popularity gives it considerable power over its carrier partners — customers are no longer loyal to the carrier providing the mobile service, but to the brand behind their favorite phone. Apple's newest commercial venture, the Apple Upgrade program — which was announced earlier this year and is, at the time of writing, still only available in the US — is the latest dagger to the heart of major MNOs (Mobile Network Operators). But despite being a fantastic deal for customers and Apple itself (and make no mistake: I believe it's a net positive move), the Apple Upgrade program could yet prove a double-edged sword for the mobile industry as a whole. Let me explain.      To understand what the Apple Upgrade program is, you have to first understand how the industry worked before the original iPhone. To say that Apple has irrevocably changed the carrier business model on numerous occasions may seem like hyperbole, but it’s hard to overstate the company's lasting effect. Before the original iPhone, carriers were integral to a phone's success. Carriers controlled which phones were sold in stores, which phones received the bigger marketing pushes, and which were “certified” to work with that carrier. This meant that all phone makers had to focus more on acquiescing to carrier requests — including shipping customized devices with several preloaded apps and even carrier-specific branding — than meeting their customers' needs. In many ways, carriers were the customer rather than the end-user itself, and they proved even more integral, as each carrier also controlled when software updates were released to its phones. I remember clearly how customers would blame the phone maker for software-related shortcomings rather than the carrier, even if the software update was delayed by the carrier’s own internal testing. The power of carriers was inevitably going to be replaced by a different model, but the iPhone had a marked effect on the power wielded by carriers in more ways than one.      If you’ve seen the BlackBerry movie, you’ll remember the line used to describe the original iPhone before it went on sale: it had the "highest interest of any consumer electronic item in history". To go further, its original $499 / £269 price also made it the most expensive phone in history at the time. But contrary to industry standards at the time, the exceptional consumer interest in the original iPhone meant carriers were clamoring to stock it, rather than Apple having to entice them to sell it. This complete reversal of established norms also meant Apple was able to stamp out many of the key controls carriers had, and the effect was stark. The iPhone had a marked effect on the power wielded by carriers in more ways than one. Let’s consider each of the previous requests that carriers would make of a phone maker. Branding on the phone itself or in the software? Gone for the iPhone. Preloaded carrier apps and other bloatware? Gone for the iPhone. A software update schedule controlled by carriers? Apple releases updates to all phones at the same time globally. Customized models? Carriers should be grateful they get to stock the iPhone at all. However, Apple's unique position went even further. Phone makers used to have to discount phones and offer incentives, but for many years, Apple did not. Granted, we are now in an era in which Apple competes through trade-in promotions and works closely with its carrier partners, but it was the last major phone maker to embrace promotional pricing of any kind. It's not just Apple that has benefited from these changes; as Apple established new ground rules, companies like Samsung, Google, and LG have all benefited from a different playbook than in the pre-smartphone era. Now, with the Apple Upgrade program, Apple again holds outsized control over the customer journey. For many, this is a great program, but for other stakeholders, it’s decidedly not. Here’s why.      The Apple Upgrade Program is a leasing program provided by Apple, with financing by Klarna. It lets you lease a new iPhone, Mac, iPad, or Apple Watch and pay for it monthly over a fixed lease period (between 12 months and 36 months). At the end of the lease, you can opt to return the item to Apple at no charge or buy it out for the remaining value; the latter is a particularly attractive offer for customers. Most lease programs have you spending more money over the course of the lease compared with buying the item outright. This arbitrage is how the financing lender makes their money, but with the Apple Upgrade program, you’ll never pay more in total than the outright purchase value. This is crucial: Apple is effectively offering 0% financing across its range of products, and while it likely pays Klarna directly for providing these services, it does not pass any additional costs on to the customer. In essence, you can still buy any Apple item you plan to, but you now have a more flexible way to pay for it, with no credit card or specific credit limit needed.      The current state of RAMageddon — aka the soaring cost of all technology due to the shortage of RAM modules — meant it was inevitable that Apple would have to increase its product prices, which it did by a considerable margin in both June and September this year. Despite Apple customers traditionally being less price-sensitive than Android customers, rising prices during a global cost-of-living crisis would inevitably have impacted its financial statements and, therefore, its share price. The Apple Upgrade program changes this reality in a big way: in the US at least, it’s now far easier for customers to buy Apple products (and more of them) than they used to be able to, and Apple itself gains far more valuable numbers to present to its shareholders: the number of customers on subscriptions; the dollar value of those sold; and the number of customers. More than that, the Upgrade Program offers Apple predictable revenue numbers for quarters and years into the future, and allows it to launch more products across the year without worrying as much about established launch cycles and windows. It also makes all of its new products far more accessible to the masses, which is particularly prescient given the now-confirmed $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499 launch price of the iPhone Duo, which begins shipping next week.      For all its positives, there are two areas where the Apple Upgrade program could have a negative effect — and both stem from its potential impact on carriers. Like the now-discontinued iPhone Upgrade program before it, an iPhone purchased via the Apple Upgrade program is seemingly unlocked for use on any network. It still requires activation with one of the Big Three carriers — Verizon, T-Mobile US, or AT&T — at the point of sale, but once you complete said activation, you can switch to a different carrier of your choosing. This undoubtedly reduces the need to be locked into a long-term, multi-year contract with your carrier and, crucially, removes a key source of revenue from locked devices: roaming fees. Together, they will impact carriers’ revenue, inevitably leading to several knock-on effects for the consumer. The Apple Upgrade program is a deal that's too good not to take advantage of. First, customers will inevitably end up paying more for their service plans, whether through higher plan costs, higher add-on costs, or even increased out-of-bundle charges. Second, the above will lead to an even more booming MVNO (Mobile Virtual Network Operator) market, but as we’ve seen with Mint Mobile, these MVNOs will also inevitably be acquired by the aforementioned big carriers they rely on. The biggest impact will be felt in network technology and retail footprint. Verizon, T-Mobile US, and AT&T are publicly traded and have a fiduciary responsibility to their shareholders. They might pay even more for future spectrum holdings, but the adoption and rollout of future technologies could be much slower if the Apple Upgrade program takes off in the way Apple clearly hopes. This isn’t just hyperbole; we’ve already seen this happen with the 5G rollout and the LTE rollout before it. The impact will be even more acute for those who like to frequent carrier retail stores. T-Mobile has already made some services fully digital, and, like other industries, phone retail seems to be undergoing a managed decline. Further pressure on carriers’ revenue sources will simply accelerate this shift, leaving vulnerable customers most likely to feel the effects. So, yes, the Apple Upgrade program is a fantastic deal for most people involved, but I am concerned about the impact it will have on carrier operations, and specifically how these operations might impact consumers in the long term. Having said all that, my next Apple purchase will almost certainly be through the Apple Upgrade program — it’s a deal that’s too good not to take advantage of, especially if you’re buying one of Apple's higher-spec models.
